Argatroban (hepatic clearance) and bivalirudin (substantial proteolysis plus renal effects) have different implications with liver/renal dysfunction. Surgery for stable active HIT should be delayed if possible, whereas emergency surgery requires specialist risk acceptance and a detailed non-heparin bypass plan. The distinction between suspected HIT, confirmed HIT, subacute HIT and remote antibody-negative HIT changes what anticoagulant options are reasonable; not all phases justify the same blanket rule.

## Post-CPB platelet fall is not automatically immune HIT

An early fall in platelet count after CPB (usually first 1–3 postoperative days) is common from haemodilution, circuit consumption and surgery. Immune HIT classically creates a later second platelet fall around day 5–10, or rapid thrombocytopenia with recent heparin exposure; assess a >50% fall from the patient’s postoperative peak and new thrombosis rather than relying on the absolute count alone. Apply the 4Ts clinical probability score; a negative/low probability result generally makes HIT unlikely. A positive PF4 immunoassay does not prove platelet-activating HIT—confirm with a functional assay where appropriate.

If acute HIT is suspected, stop all heparin sources, including flushes and coated equipment, and agree non-heparin anticoagulation with haematology. For urgent CPB, bivalirudin requires a perfusion-specific protocol, knowledge of drug metabolism and a management plan for stagnant blood in the circuit. Remote HIT after negative antibody/function testing is a different risk category. Avoid blanket advice that bivalirudin is “preferred in renal failure”: part of its clearance is renal and dosing/monitoring must be adjusted.

## Reversing heparin with protamine

Protamine is a positively charged polypeptide that electrostatically binds negatively charged heparin, producing an inactive complex. It **does not reverse bivalirudin**. A conventional maximum neutralisation calculation is around **1 mg protamine for every 100 units of heparin**, but this may substantially overestimate requirements because heparin has been redistributed/metabolised. Current practice often uses measured heparin concentration and lower protamine:heparin ratios, such as ≈0.6–1 mg per 100 units of relevant circulating heparin, rather than automatically neutralising every unit ever given. Give **slowly IV** with invasive BP monitoring and communication to surgeon/perfusionist. Excess protamine itself impairs platelet function and coagulation and can cause hypotension; more is not necessarily better.

**Protamine reactions: recognise three clinically important patterns.**

| Reaction                                  | Mechanism and presentation                                                                                        | Immediate management                                                                                                                                                                                  |
|-------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Rapid systemic hypotension                | Vasodilation, especially with fast infusion                                                                       | Stop/slow protamine, support MAP with vasopressor, assess bleeding/ventricular function; distinguish from anaphylaxis and haemorrhage.                                                                |
| Severe anaphylaxis/anaphylactoid reaction | Immune or non-IgE mediator release; hypotension, bronchospasm, rash/angio-oedema may occur                        | Stop protamine, call help, **adrenaline** per perioperative anaphylaxis algorithm, oxygen, appropriately titrated fluid, support circulation; consider re-heparinisation/return to CPB when required. |
| Acute pulmonary hypertension / RV failure | Complement/thromboxane-related pulmonary vasoconstriction, sudden high PAP, RV dilation, low LV filling and shock | Stop infusion, support systemic/RV coronary pressure, optimise oxygenation/ventilation/acidosis, consider pulmonary vasodilator and inotropy, re-establish CPB urgently if refractory.                |

**Check for prior protamine reactions and use of protamine-containing insulin. Fish allergy or vasectomy history alone is not a reliable predictor of a reaction. Document exposure and timing, take timed tryptase as indicated and refer suspected anaphylaxis. Assess residual heparin using an appropriate test and clinical bleeding before repeating protamine. Heparin rebound may reflect redistribution.**

## Protamine: think of three different physiology problems, not one allergy label

If hypotension appears during reversal, pause the infusion and rapidly assess rhythm, TOE, arterial pressure, PAP/CVP if present, airway pressures, oxygenation and skin signs. **Simple rate-related vasodilation** produces systemic hypotension with relatively preserved ventricular contractility and no severe PVR surge. **Severe anaphylaxis** may produce vasoplegia and bronchospasm with or without rash under drapes. **Acute pulmonary vasoconstriction** produces a suddenly distended/failing RV, falling LV filling, rising PAP and profound systemic hypotension; this can become a circulation-threatening emergency even without cutaneous features.

For vasodilation, stop/slow protamine and support the circulation; for anaphylaxis, administer **adrenaline** and follow the ANZCA/ANZCOR perioperative algorithm; for RV failure, oxygenate, correct hypoxia/acidosis/hypercarbia, provide perfusion-pressure support and discuss inhaled pulmonary vasodilator/reinstitution of CPB immediately. In a catastrophic reaction with bypass cannulas still present, return to CPB may save the patient while the reaction is treated. **Do not give an uncritical large crystalloid load to a dilated congested RV.** If inadequate reversal leaves unsafe bleeding, balancing a further protamine attempt against recurrence requires consultant-led discussion and alternative strategies.

## Why cardiac surgical patients bleed after bypass

The patient can have **surgical bleeding** (anastomosis, cannulation, sternum) or **microvascular coagulopathic bleeding** (platelet dysfunction/consumption, reduced fibrinogen, dilutional factor deficiency, hyperfibrinolysis, hypocalcaemia, acidosis/hypothermia or excess heparin/protamine). These may coexist. Diffuse oozing from multiple raw surfaces suggests coagulopathy; brisk/continuous localised drain output, early haemodynamic instability or retained clot suggests a surgical source, even if coagulation tests are abnormal.

**A logical blood-management pathway:**

- **1.** **Before surgery:** correct anaemia/iron deficiency where time permits; review antiplatelets/anticoagulants, bleeding history and blood conservation consent. Group/crossmatch and assess transfusion need.
- **2.** **During surgery:** meticulous haemostasis, minimise unnecessary haemodilution, cell salvage where appropriate, maintain temperature and ionised calcium, avoid excessive crystalloid and monitor haemoglobin/oxygen delivery.
- **3.** **Antifibrinolytic:** **tranexamic acid (TXA)** inhibits plasminogen–fibrin interactions, reducing fibrinolysis. Commonly used in cardiac surgery, but regimen varies and high exposures/renal impairment increase seizure risk. **ATACAS** showed reduced transfusions/re-exploration but more postoperative seizures; choose renal-adjusted local dosing, avoid indiscriminate high-dose escalation.
- **4.** **After protamine:** examine surgical field and chest drainage; send FBC/fibrinogen/INR and use **ROTEM/TEG-based algorithms** to direct treatment of actual bleeding. Correct fibrinogen deficiency with cryoprecipitate/fibrinogen concentrate, platelet dysfunction/deficiency with platelets, coagulation-factor deficiency with plasma or selected concentrates per protocol. Distinguish residual heparin using heparinase paired tests before giving more protamine.
- **5.** **Re-explore early** for suspected surgical source/tamponade rather than giving repeated haemostatic products and allowing ongoing haemorrhage.

**ROTEM interpretation example:** prolonged clotting time (EXTEM CT) suggests coagulation factor deficiency or anticoagulant effect; reduced FIBTEM amplitude suggests inadequate fibrinogen contribution; low EXTEM amplitude relative to preserved FIBTEM suggests platelet contribution; a correction of abnormalities in heparinase-modified channels suggests heparin effect. Numeric cutoffs and products are **instrument-, test- and institutional-algorithm-specific**. The 2025 ANZCA Blue Book chapter by Hegde and colleagues makes exactly this point: treat a **bleeding patient with a demonstrated deficit**, not every abnormal tracing.

## Tranexamic acid: why it works, and why dose still matters

CPB activates endothelial and contact pathways and can increase conversion of plasminogen to plasmin. **Plasmin degrades cross-linked fibrin**, causing premature dissolution of newly formed clot. Tranexamic acid (TXA), a synthetic lysine analogue, blocks plasminogen/plasmin lysine-binding sites and inhibits fibrin binding and fibrinolysis. It therefore prevents clot breakdown; it does **not** reverse UFH or replace fibrinogen/platelets when these are deficient.

The large **ATACAS** trial found less major bleeding/reoperation with TXA in coronary surgery, but more seizures; it did not demonstrate an overall mortality benefit. Convulsions are plausibly related to concentration-dependent CNS glycine and GABA-A receptor inhibition; high dose and renal impairment increase concern. **Do not memorise a single universal cardiac TXA regimen.** Centres use lower- or higher-dose schedules, sometimes an IV loading dose followed by infusion and/or pump-prime supplementation. Select dose and timing according to local cardiac protocol, renal function, seizure risk and the operation, rather than automatically adopting a dose from orthopaedic or obstetric surgery. Routinely distinguish prophylactic antifibrinolysis from therapeutic response to active hyperfibrinolytic bleeding. [ATACAS](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1606425).

## Treat post-bypass bleeding by locating the defective step in clot formation

A patient bleeds briskly after protamine. The correct first question is **‘Is this a surgical source or diffuse coagulopathy?’** A persistently filling surgical field/one rapidly draining mediastinal tube can indicate a bleeding anastomosis; widespread oozing from cannulation sites suggests acquired haemostatic impairment. Either can coexist, so request early surgical inspection while sending appropriate blood tests. Examine actual blood loss, perfusion status, temperature, pH, ionised calcium and pre-existing antithrombotic exposure.

| Finding / investigation                                                                                   | What it suggests                                                                       | Rational treatment (if clinically bleeding)                                                                                                                 |
|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Heparinase and non-heparinase clotting traces differ substantially; ACT remains prolonged after protamine | Residual UFH or heparin rebound (consider also protamine excess and test interference) | Confirm with paired measurements/heparin assay, give **carefully titrated** additional protamine only when indicated; excessive protamine worsens bleeding. |
| Low FIBTEM functional fibrinogen or low Clauss fibrinogen                                                 | Fibrinogen depletion or impaired fibrin polymerisation                                 | Fibrinogen concentrate or cryoprecipitate per protocol; repeat the assay and check clinical response.                                                       |
| Poor TEG MA / ROTEM EXTEM clot firmness with adequate fibrin contribution                                 | Reduced platelet number or function, including antiplatelet effect                     | Platelets if significant bleeding and a documented functional/quantitative deficit; consider P2Y12 exposure, hypothermia and high shear.                    |
| Prolonged clot initiation after excluding residual heparin                                                | Coagulation-factor depletion                                                           | Plasma or selected factor concentrate according to validated protocol; beware prothrombotic rescue therapy.                                                 |
| Rapid late lysis on TEG/ROTEM                                                                             | Hyperfibrinolysis                                                                      | Confirm TXA exposure and dose, correct cause, give antifibrinolytic according to protocol.                                                                  |
| Firm/near-normal viscoelastic clot but substantial chest-drain bleeding                                   | Surgical source, platelet defect not measured by routine assay, local site bleeding    | Return attention to surgeon and operative field; do not treat the monitor instead of the patient.                                                           |

**Interpretation caveat:** ROTEM EXTEM, INTEM, HEPTEM and FIBTEM are different assay channels. An institutional algorithm may use A5/A10 or MCF with validated thresholds; values are not interchangeable between instruments or centres. Viscoelastic tests can guide targeted treatment but cannot reliably diagnose every P2Y12-associated platelet defect. This is the practical point of the ANZCA Blue Book 2025 chapter by Hegde and colleagues on viscoelastic haemostatic assays: identify the deficient clot component and **choose the corresponding therapy**, rather than blindly giving one unit of every blood product. [ANZCA 2025 Blue Book](https://www.anzca.edu.au/safety-and-advocacy/advocacy/college-publications/australasian-anaesthesia-%28the-blue-book%29).

## Transfusion thresholds and the evidence

For stable adult cardiac surgical patients, restrictive RBC strategies around Hb **75 g/L** have been supported by **TRICS III** (non-inferiority for major clinical outcomes versus liberal thresholds in the trial population). That is not a mandatory trigger in active shock, ongoing major haemorrhage or myocardial ischaemia. Balance Hb against active bleeding, oxygen delivery, SvO₂/lactate and clinical context. A normal ACT does not mean normal platelet function; a ‘normal’ fibrinogen before prolonged CPB does not guarantee adequacy after dilution. Avoid the common exam mistake of prescribing a fixed FFP–platelet–cryo package without assessing the bleeding phenotype and coagulation data.

**Evidence anchors:** [Cartwright & Mundell, BJAEd 2023 Part 1](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2022.12.003), [Part 2](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2023.03.008), [2024 cardiac PBM guideline](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12257489/), [2025 ANZCA Blue Book goal-directed haemostasis](https://hdl.handle.net/11055/1387).

## Transfusion decisions: an evidence-informed floor, not a reason to ignore physiology

**TRICS III** supports restrictive RBC transfusion in many adults undergoing cardiac surgery: **Hb trigger 75 g/L** was non-inferior for a composite clinical outcome compared with a more liberal strategy, but this does not mean every patient with ongoing graft ischaemia, severe shock or poor DO₂ on pump must tolerate Hb 75. Assess bleeding rate, oxygen extraction, cerebral/somatic perfusion, coronary ischaemia and the ability to increase pump flow. More plasma or platelets are not substitutes for RBCs when the principal problem is oxygen-carrying capacity. Conversely, if the patient is euvolaemic with a reasonable Hb but is bleeding because of fibrinogen depletion, RBCs will not fix that mechanism. [TRICS III](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1711818).

**The endpoint of the bleeding algorithm is not normal blood tests: it is haemostasis and organ perfusion without avoidable transfusion harm.** After haemostatic therapy, repeat clinical assessment and selected tests. Reassess whether ongoing chest drainage warrants prompt surgical re-exploration rather than repeated product administration in ICU.

## Aprotinin and interpretation of post-bypass bleeding

For 2007.2 Q9, explain both the evidence for reduced bleeding and transfusion and the safety signal from the 2006 observational study. Confounding by indication matters because higher-risk patients were more likely to receive aprotinin. The later BART randomised trial raised a mortality signal versus lysine analogues. Some jurisdictions now authorise restricted use. First answer the historical question using the evidence available in 2007, then explain how later evidence and local availability change current decisions.

For active bleeding, a low fibrin-based clot amplitude supports targeted fibrinogen replacement when appropriate. Weak whole-blood clot strength with relatively preserved fibrin contribution raises platelet deficiency or dysfunction. Improvement in a heparinase channel compared with the corresponding heparin-sensitive assay supports residual heparin. Normal ACT or clot strength cannot independently exclude a surgical source, platelet drug effects or evolving tamponade. Reassess after therapy and coordinate early re-exploration where indicated.

[ANZCA Blue Book 2025](https://doi.org/10.60115/11055/1305) · [BJA Education CPB anticoagulation, 2023](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2022.12.003) · [Cardiac patient blood management guideline](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12257489/) · [BART](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa0802395)

items.title: 6. Myocardial, cerebral and whole-body protection on bypass
items.body:
Mapped LOs: SS_CS 1.1 (hypothermia and circulatory arrest), SS_CS 1.17 (myocardial protection, cerebral effects, aortic cannulation, reperfusion and ischaemic preconditioning).

## What cross-clamping and cardioplegia actually mean

The aortic cross-clamp creates an isolated segment of the aorta so the surgeon can operate without continuous blood flow through the heart. But **if normal coronary blood flow stops, myocardial cells still need ATP**. If unprotected, ion pumps fail, calcium rises and ischaemic injury begins. **Cardioplegia** is a protective fluid delivered to the coronary circulation that commonly contains extra potassium: it stops normal electrical activation and contraction, dramatically reducing myocardial energy demand. Cold solution can reduce metabolism further, while some preparations also supply oxygenated blood and metabolic substrate. The heart is arrested but not dead; cardioplegia must reach all vulnerable myocardium and be replenished according to the technique.

**Antegrade** means flowing the normal way: solution enters the aortic root or coronary ostia and travels along coronary arteries. **Retrograde** means travelling backwards via the coronary sinus (a cardiac vein), allowing some regions beyond severe coronary stenoses to be reached. Severe AR can cause aortic-root cardioplegia to leak back into the LV, while retrograde methods may incompletely protect the RV. These are surgical reasons to select or combine routes, not trivia to memorise.

**Reperfusion** means coronary blood flow resumes after unclamping; the heart can exhibit ventricular fibrillation, transient weakness (stunning), electrolyte shifts or injury from abrupt oxygen reintroduction. **Venting** drains blood or air from the LV or aortic root, preventing a stopped ventricle from becoming distended and making de-airing safer. A distended LV on bypass may mean inadequate venting, not a need to increase a diuretic. The advanced cardioplegia table below develops these basic relationships.

## Myocardial protection: how can an arrested heart survive?

The heart needs ongoing ATP to maintain ion gradients, calcium handling and myocyte viability. Coronary flow is interrupted during aortic cross-clamping, so unprotected warm ischaemia rapidly causes ATP depletion, acidosis, intracellular Ca²⁺ accumulation, contracture and reperfusion damage. **Cardioplegia** chemically arrests the myocardium, usually in diastole using high extracellular potassium, while cooling and delivery of oxygenated substrate reduce metabolic demand. ‘Stopping the heart’ is not itself protection; it is the combination of rapid arrest, adequate distribution, appropriate temperature and intermittent replenishment that prevents damage.

| Strategy                                              | Physiological effect                                                                                  | Clinical limitation                                                                                         |
|-------------------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Antegrade cardioplegia via aortic root/coronary ostia | Physiological coronary direction; rapid uniform delivery with patent proximal arteries                | Severe proximal stenoses or severe AR can impair distribution; aortic root delivery may leak into LV in AR. |
| Retrograde via coronary sinus                         | Perfuses many myocardial regions despite proximal stenosis; useful adjunct in severe coronary disease | RV/anterior territories may be less reliably protected; risk of coronary-sinus injury/overpressure.         |
| Cold blood or crystalloid solutions                   | Cooling reduces O₂ demand, potassium arrest                                                           | Very cold techniques can affect microcirculation; re-dose as required.                                      |
| Warm blood cardioplegia                               | Delivers O₂/substrate and supports metabolic recovery                                                 | Myocardium consumes more O₂ at higher temperature; requires reliable continuous/intermittent delivery.      |
| Venting and topical cooling                           | Prevent LV distension and improve myocardial protection                                               | LV distension raises wall stress and subendocardial demand even during bypass.                              |

**After removing the clamp**, coronary reperfusion may cause ventricular fibrillation, transient stunning, hyperkalaemia from cardioplegia washout, oxidative stress or calcium-mediated injury. **Ischaemic preconditioning** describes brief, nonlethal ischaemia inducing endogenous protective pathways (mitochondrial signalling, kinase activation and altered reperfusion response), while postconditioning refers to brief interruptions around reperfusion. Although biologically attractive, clinical outcome benefits of anaesthetic/remote conditioning strategies have been inconsistent; do not claim a specific volatile agent guarantees cardiac protection.

## Myocardial protection in practice: match the delivery route to the operation

After the aorta is cross-clamped the myocardium can no longer rely on normal coronary perfusion. **Cardioplegia converts an actively contracting, energy-consuming heart into a deliberately arrested heart** while providing some combination of cooling, substrate, oxygen and buffer. Potassium-rich solution depolarises cardiomyocytes and prevents normal action potential propagation; reduced cross-bridge cycling drastically reduces ATP demand, but basal membrane-pump and metabolic demand persist. Arrested myocardium is therefore protected, not metabolically inert.

Antegrade cardioplegia travels through the aortic root into coronary ostia and is often efficient when the aortic valve is competent and coronary distribution permits it. Severe proximal coronary stenoses may impair delivery to threatened territories, and **severe aortic regurgitation** can divert root cardioplegia into the LV, distending it rather than perfusing the coronaries. Selective coronary ostial delivery or **retrograde coronary-sinus cardioplegia** then becomes valuable. Retrograde delivery is especially useful for areas beyond stenoses or during valve surgery, but perfuses the RV variably and depends on correct sinus cannulation; it does not replace careful visual assessment of myocardial protection. For a long clamp interval the team must know the redosing schedule, temperature and whether the perfusate is crystalloid or blood-based.

![Visual guide 3 — How antegrade and retrograde cardioplegia protect an arrested heart. Schematic for teaching; not to scale.](set13-ch6-1.png)

**Venting is itself myocardial protection.** When the heart is arrested, bronchial/coronary venous return and any aortic regurgitant flow may fill the LV. LV distension increases wall tension, subendocardial pressure and oxygen demand, worsens myocardial oedema and increases risk of impaired separation. A left-heart vent through the pulmonary vein/LA or aortic root (at the appropriate stage) prevents distension and facilitates de-airing. A suddenly full LV on TOE despite CPB is a signal to evaluate venting and valve incompetence, not automatically a reason to give diuretic or increase inotrope.

**Reperfusion injury** adds to ischaemic injury when the clamp is removed. Oxygen-derived reactive species, sudden calcium influx, mitochondrial permeability-transition pore opening, endothelial dysfunction and inflammatory activation can cause myocardial stunning, rhythm disturbance and microvascular dysfunction even with technically successful grafts. Rewarm and reperfuse deliberately; check potassium and acid–base balance, treat ventricular fibrillation, support coronary perfusion pressure and distinguish transient stunning from persistent mechanical/graft obstruction. Ischaemic preconditioning and volatile ‘conditioning’ have attractive mechanisms but inconsistent hard-outcome clinical evidence, so they supplement—not replace—adequate cardioplegia, time management and perfusion.

## Reperfusion injury and ischaemic preconditioning: mechanisms that inform separation

Following cross-clamp removal, return of oxygenated coronary blood restores ATP generation but also creates reactive oxygen species, calcium overload and mitochondrial permeability-transition pore opening. Endothelial and microvascular dysfunction, inflammation and intracellular oedema produce temporary myocardial stunning; more severe injury can cause infarction, arrhythmia and low output. The anaesthetist should distinguish transient global stunning after ischaemia/reperfusion from new regional dysfunction due to inadequate cardioplegia, graft failure or coronary air.

Ischaemic preconditioning describes protection induced by brief non-lethal ischaemic episodes before a longer insult; remote limb conditioning has plausible mechanisms but has not produced consistently important outcome improvements in major cardiac-surgery trials. Do not promise it prevents injury. Practical myocardial protection still depends on effective antegrade/retrograde cardioplegia where indicated, adequate reperfusion, avoidance of excessive cross-clamp time, temperature management and rapid correction of mechanical coronary problems. During reperfusion, watch for potassium and calcium shifts, ventricular arrhythmias and transient impairment of contractility.

## Aortic atheroma and safe cannulation

A diseased ascending aorta is a major source of embolic stroke, especially during cannulation, cross-clamping, side-biting clamps and de-airing. Review aortic imaging and palpation/epiaortic ultrasound; **epiaortic ultrasound is particularly useful for identifying plaque not reliably appreciated by palpation or TOE** (distal ascending aorta has a TOE blind spot). Options include choosing a clean aortic site, axillary/femoral arterial return, no-touch anaortic CABG or altered surgical plan. Retrograde perfusion from femoral cannulation can dislodge distal atheroma or be unsafe in aortic dissection; axillary perfusion offers different advantages and complications. The principle is to minimise **manipulation of diseased aorta**, not routinely to use one cannulation site for everyone.

## Why cooling protects organs, and how this differs from cardioplegia

Cooling reduces metabolic demand throughout the body; a cold brain can tolerate a temporary interruption of flow better than a warm brain, but it is never completely protected from ischaemia. **Deep hypothermic circulatory arrest (DHCA)** is an intentional period in which systemic flow is stopped, usually for complex aortic arch surgery where the surgeon needs an open, bloodless arch. This differs from routine CPB, during which pump flow still perfuses organs, and from cardioplegia, which mainly protects the heart.

If the arch is being repaired, **antegrade cerebral perfusion (ACP)** may send oxygenated blood forwards into carotid/innominate circulation even while the rest of systemic flow is interrupted. **Retrograde cerebral perfusion (RCP)** sends blood backwards via cerebral venous pathways, with less predictable nutritive flow. Brain temperature, cerebral oxygenation and time without effective perfusion must be tracked. Rewarming too rapidly may increase oxygen demand before adequate circulation has recovered and may create harmful temperature gradients.

**Alpha-stat versus pH-stat** sounds abstract, but the difference is about CO₂ and cerebral blood flow during cooling. Alpha-stat uses gas values measured at 37°C without correcting them to the colder body temperature, tending to preserve cerebral autoregulation. pH-stat adds CO₂ during hypothermia to achieve a temperature-corrected PaCO₂ target, dilating cerebral vessels and increasing cerebral blood flow and uniformity of cooling, with potential embolic-flow trade-offs. Understand the effect of CO₂ on cerebral vessels first; the names become much easier to remember.

## Hypothermia: why cool, and what are the costs?

Temperature determines enzyme kinetics and the rate at which tissues consume O₂. A traditional approximation is a **6–7% fall in cerebral oxygen metabolism per 1°C** fall, but this is not linear across the entire temperature range. Controlled hypothermia extends tolerance of temporary reduced cerebral/visceral perfusion, making complex aortic operations possible. It is not a substitute for adequate oxygen delivery on ordinary CPB, nor does it prevent embolism.

**The 2024 EACTS/EACTAIC/EBCP CPB guideline defines cooling categories (core temperature):**

| Classification | Temperature | Typical context                                                                |
|----------------|-------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Mild           | 28.1–34°C   | Many routine operations or selected cerebral-protection strategies             |
| High-moderate  | 24.1–28°C   | Selected aortic surgery, often with cerebral perfusion                         |
| Low-moderate   | 20.1–24°C   | Complex arch surgery depending on cerebral perfusion plan                      |
| Deep           | 14.1–20°C   | Deep hypothermic circulatory arrest (DHCA) for selected arch/aortic procedures |

**Trade-offs:** hypothermia reduces oxygen consumption but causes platelet dysfunction, delayed coagulation, altered drug metabolism, electrolyte shifts and cardiac irritability. Rewarming can cause cerebral hyperthermia, increase oxygen demand and contribute to gaseous microemboli. Maintain controlled arterial–venous/heat-exchanger gradients according to perfusion protocol; the updated CPB guideline advises that the heat exchanger–arterial inflow difference should not exceed **10°C** during cooling/rewarming. Use appropriate nasopharyngeal and bladder/rectal/core sites because rapid brain and slower body temperature changes diverge.

## Deep hypothermic circulatory arrest (DHCA): rationale and steps

**The purpose is cerebral and end-organ protection during a period when normal systemic circulation must stop**, typically for open distal ascending aorta or arch work in which a cross-clamp/cannula would obstruct the field. This is not ‘the same as cardioplegia’ and not ‘ECMO’.

- **1.** Establish CPB, anticoagulation and cerebral monitoring; cool slowly to the agreed deep-hypothermic range (often **18–20°C**, patient/protocol dependent).
- **2.** At adequate cooling and myocardial protection, stop systemic pump flow for the necessary period, while the surgeon opens/repairs the arch; provide agreed selective **antegrade cerebral perfusion** (ACP) or retrograde cerebral perfusion (RCP) if used.
- **3.** Re-establish perfusion as soon as feasible, de-air meticulously, rewarm slowly and avoid overshoot hyperthermia or large arterial–venous temperature gradients.
- **4.** Monitor return of cerebral oximetry/electrical activity, coagulation and renal/neurological complications.

**Safe time is not a single magic number:** isolated DHCA without perfusion has limited cerebral protection, with guideline discussion suggesting neurological risk rises substantially beyond approximately **30–40 minutes**. ACP enables longer arch reconstruction at moderate temperatures by delivering targeted cerebral blood flow; the proper strategy depends on the arch repair, collateral circulation and institutional experience. Bilateral versus unilateral ACP, NIRS trends and cannulation are selected case-by-case. RCP may help remove embolic debris and provide cooling but delivers less nutritive cerebral flow than ACP; it is not an equivalent substitute in every patient.

**Why some patients still develop neurological injury:** atheromatous or air emboli, cerebral malperfusion from arch vessels, low oxygen delivery, prolonged arrest, hyperthermia and reperfusion injury, as well as pre-existing vascular disease. Use multimodal protection: minimise aortic manipulation, suitable perfusion pressure/flow, arterial filtration, blood gas/haematocrit control, NIRS and EEG where appropriate, and deliberate rewarming. Historical alpha-stat versus pH-stat CO₂ management alters cerebral flow and autoregulation; routine adult deep-hypothermia practice often favours alpha-stat, but paediatric and selected cooling strategies differ. Explain the strategy rather than memorising one universally superior choice.

**ANZCA examiner relevance:** the 2019.2 SAQ on DHCA specifically found that some candidates confused the technique with ordinary cardioplegia, passive post-arrest cooling and ECMO. A good answer must state the **surgical indication, cerebral metabolic rationale, physiological consequences and protective/perfusion strategy**.

## Cooling, circulatory arrest and cerebral blood flow: join the physiology to the technique

The **point of deep hypothermia is to lengthen the brain’s tolerable no-flow interval** while the surgeon opens the aortic arch. Cerebral metabolism falls with temperature, but it does not cease completely; cooling kinetics and tissue temperatures are uneven. A surface/core reading alone does not tell you the precise temperature of every brain region. Hypothermia also slows myocardial, hepatic and renal metabolism and changes drug distribution and clearance. During rewarming, tissues regain oxygen demand more quickly than some vascular beds recover normal autoregulation. This explains why low DO₂ and brain hyperthermia on rewarming can negate benefits gained during cooling.

**Describe a deep-hypothermic circulatory arrest operation as a planned sequence:** adequate heparinisation and cannulation → controlled CPB cooling with temperature and cerebral oxygenation surveillance → myocardial protection and aortic exposure → temporary systemic circulatory arrest with surgeon-directed arch reconstruction → selective cerebral perfusion when used → secure anastomosis, de-airing and systemic reperfusion → gradual rewarming and metabolic/coagulation correction. The aortic root and LV need venting, and arch-vessel perfusion must be actively assessed. The circulatory-arrest phase is not a period of oxygenated ECMO flow to the whole body; if selective ACP continues, the brain receives flow while other territories may remain ischaemic.

**Antegrade cerebral perfusion (ACP)** delivers oxygenated blood into innominate and/or carotid circulation during arch surgery. Unilateral ACP relies on an adequate circle of Willis; bilateral ACP is considered if collateral flow is unreliable or arrest is prolonged. **Retrograde cerebral perfusion (RCP)** infuses via the SVC in the reverse venous direction and may improve cooling/air or debris clearance, but nutritive brain perfusion is less predictable. DHCA without adjunct flow has a relatively short safe interval, often conceptualised in tens of minutes rather than hours; no single ‘30-minute rule’ guarantees preservation. Aim to minimise systemic arrest time, and judge protection with operative time, anatomy, NIRS/EEG as available and clinical risk—not a blanket duration.

**Alpha-stat versus pH-stat is an examinable distinction:** alpha-stat maintains uncorrected gas values and tends to preserve autoregulation and less vasodilated cerebral circulation; pH-stat adds CO₂ during cooling to increase cerebral flow and promote uniform cooling, potentially also increasing embolic delivery. Neither is an absolute rule for every age or temperature. The relevant viva explanation is how **PaCO₂ changes cerebral vascular resistance**, and therefore why gas management is part of cerebral protection.

## Cerebral protection and neurocognitive outcomes after CPB

Postoperative neurological problems include **stroke**, delirium and delayed neurocognitive recovery. Cognitive changes are multifactorial; avoid asserting that all delayed cognition is ‘pump-head’ from inflammatory cytokines. Risk factors include age/frailty, prior stroke, AF/aortic atheroma, cerebral hypoperfusion/embolisation, low oxygen delivery, infection, prolonged surgery, sedatives and sleep disruption. Confirm any acute focal deficit urgently with a stroke pathway and imaging; delirium prevention uses reorientation, analgesia, early mobilisation, sleep, sensory aids and minimisation of avoidable sedatives.

**When NIRS falls:** first determine whether unilateral (malpositioned cannula/arch vessel) or bilateral (systemic flow/MAP/Hb/SaO₂/PaCO₂) and check for artefact. Improve effective cerebral oxygen delivery rather than giving red cells automatically. NIRS has outcome limitations and should not replace clinical/other perfusion monitoring.

## Prevent neurological injury before it becomes a postoperative problem

Stroke after cardiac surgery has multiple mechanisms and cannot be reduced to ‘CPB causes microemboli’. Atherosclerotic emboli can arise from cannulation, cross-clamping and proximal graft work; air embolism from left-heart opening/de-airing; hypoperfusion from low DO₂ or malperfusion; haemorrhage from antithrombotics/coagulopathy; and postoperative AF adds embolic risk. Risk is amplified by prior stroke, carotid disease, age, aortic atheroma, surgery complexity and prolonged bypass. **Aortic manipulation is a modifiable part of risk**, which explains the role of CT, epiaortic ultrasound and ‘no-touch’ techniques in selected patients.

During CPB, monitor bilateral NIRS where employed, watch the trend from the patient’s own baseline and respond in a physiological order: confirm sensors and head position → assess pump flow and arterial pressure → check SaO₂, Hb, PaCO₂ and temperature → evaluate cannula/arch vessel obstruction or asymmetry → correct the specific deficit. Transfusing blood for a single unexplained NIRS decline without first evaluating circuit flow and malperfusion is not appropriate. NIRS can detect regional imbalance but normal frontal values do **not** exclude embolic posterior circulation stroke; it is one component of monitoring, not a neurological guarantee.

Postoperatively distinguish focal neurological deficits needing an **urgent stroke pathway** from delirium and delayed neurocognitive recovery. These have different mechanisms and management. Prevent delirium with pain control, early wakefulness/mobilisation, sleep and sensory aids, avoiding unnecessary benzodiazepines and treating infection/hypoxaemia; do not describe all postoperative cognitive changes as a permanent inflammation-mediated ‘pump-head’ syndrome.

items.title: 7. Separation from cardiopulmonary bypass: the high-yield chapter
items.priority: P2 HIGH (1 parent LO) + P3 MODERATE (1 parent LO)
items.body:
Mapped LOs: SS_CS 1.19 (difficult weaning, P2 HIGH), SS_CS 1.17 (safe separation), SS_CS 1.7 (haemodynamic goals), SS_CS 1.9 (internal defibrillation).

## The six questions to ask before choosing a drug at separation

Coming off bypass is the moment when the machine stops doing the patient's cardiac work. The heart has been cooled, arrested, operated on and reperfused. It may need time before it generates enough native flow. The most useful beginner framework is to ask six questions in order: **(1) Is it actually beating in a useful rhythm? (2) Is there enough blood entering it? (3) Can the LV contract? (4) Can the RV move blood through the lungs? (5) Is there an obstruction or surgical problem? (6) Is the blood pressure low despite adequate cardiac output because arteries are dilated?** Each question suggests a different treatment.

**Small, vigorous ventricles:** often underfilling, although an obstruction can mimic this; consider returning blood from the bypass reservoir in small reassessed amounts and investigate blood loss. **Dilated weak LV:** consider myocardial stunning, inadequate coronary reperfusion, graft problem, new valve pathology or excessive afterload; use TOE to find the cause, support contractility and return to CPB if necessary. **Big struggling RV and small LV:** suggests RV failure, raised pulmonary vascular resistance or pulmonary outflow obstruction; oxygenate, optimise ventilation, maintain systemic pressure, support RV contraction if needed and avoid automatic large fluid loads. **Vigorous ventricular function but low MAP:** consider vasoplegia, meaning that systemic blood vessels are excessively dilated; a vasoconstrictor is more logical than a large dose of an inotrope. **New severe valve leak/obstruction or intracardiac air:** drugs will not repair the lesion.

**The drug distinction.** A **vasopressor** (such as noradrenaline or vasopressin) mainly supports systemic vascular tone and MAP. An **inotrope** (such as dobutamine) chiefly increases contractility, but may also lower SVR and cause hypotension. An **inodilator** (such as milrinone) improves contractility while reducing vascular resistance (including PVR), making it useful in selected RV failure but potentially dangerous without pressure support. **Adrenaline** can increase both inotropy and vasoconstriction but also raises heart rate, lactate and myocardial oxygen demand. Think of the physiological deficit before naming a drug. Multiple deficits can coexist.

**An example:** MAP is 45 mmHg when pump flow is reduced. TOE shows a normal, strongly contracting LV and RV with reasonable filling. Giving more dobutamine is unlikely to solve isolated low SVR; noradrenaline may restore pressure. If instead the LV is huge and barely moves, treating the MAP alone could disguise persistent low cardiac output. This distinction is at the centre of the ANZCA difficult-weaning questions.

## What TOE is trying to tell you at the point of separation

TOE is not merely a way to report an ejection fraction. Before leaving CPB, use it as a structured bedside explanation for **why forward flow may fail**. First ask whether each ventricle has enough preload without being overdistended; next assess global and regional contractility; then check whether valves are competent and there is new obstruction; finally consider pericardial compression or an aortic/cannulation problem. A **small empty LV with a dilated RV** suggests RV afterload or RV contractility is preventing LV filling; a **small hyperdynamic LV with low MAP** may suggest underfilling or vasoplegia. A **full poorly contracting LV** suggests pump failure or ischaemia. Drug choice follows this diagnosis rather than the pressure number alone.

A newly repaired valve is usually reassessed by TOE **before protamine** and before all surgical access is lost: unexpected severe regurgitation, stenosis or dynamic LVOT obstruction may require returning to CPB rather than escalating catecholamines. If the patient cannot safely separate, discuss temporary mechanical support early rather than repeatedly attempting a failing wean.

## Why separation is difficult

When CPB provides almost all systemic flow, the patient can have a satisfactory MAP while the heart is still stunned, empty, obstructed or unable to generate meaningful cardiac output. **Weaning tests whether the newly repaired heart can now sustain systemic oxygen delivery**. This requires adequate myocardial recovery, a functional repair, appropriate loading conditions, effective rhythm/conduction, gas exchange and tolerable systemic/pulmonary vascular resistance. Failure to separate means one or more of these prerequisites are missing. The correct response is to identify the missing physiology—not simply give more fluid or increase every inotrope.

![Teaching diagram B — The differential for hypotension when returning from bypass.](set13-ch7-1.png)

## Prerequisites: do not reduce pump flow until they are met

| Requirement                  | What to confirm                                                                                      | Why it matters                                                                                                       |
|------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Adequate myocardial recovery | Cross-clamp removed, coronary reperfusion, acceptable rhythm/ventricular function, no major new RWMA | Stunning improves with time; unresolved ischaemia or graft/repair problems do not.                                   |
| Rewarming                    | Core temperature commonly >35–36°C per local protocol, temperature gradient controlled              | Hypothermia causes bradyarrhythmia, poor contractility and impaired coagulation; rewarming increases metabolic need. |
| Electrolytes / acid–base     | Correct significant K/Mg/Ca problems, acidosis and severe hyperglycaemia                             | Hyperkalaemia or hypocalcaemia after cardioplegia/transfusion can impair capture and contraction.                    |
| Ventilation and oxygenation  | Ventilator on, appropriate tidal volume/PEEP/FiO₂, lungs recruited, ABG acceptable                   | The lung must resume gas exchange when the pump stops; aggressive PEEP can reduce RV output.                         |
| Rhythm and pacing            | Sinus or effective paced rhythm, AV synchrony if useful, pacing leads/tested generator               | Severe bradycardia/complete heart block can alone prevent output.                                                    |
| Loading conditions           | Plan to restore blood from circuit to patient, avoid gross hypovolaemia or LV/RV distension          | An empty ventricle cannot eject; a severely dilated one may fail or generate MR/TR.                                  |
| Vasopressors/inotropes       | Titrated drugs available/started when indicated, arterial pressure monitoring and TOE                | Hypotension from vasoplegia is different from low-output shock.                                                      |
| Surgical repair/de-airing    | Surgeon confirms repair, adequate de-airing, TOE assessment of valves/grafts/air                     | Significant residual lesions or intracardiac air must be corrected before full separation.                           |

## Standard separation: the choreography

- **1.** **Communicate readiness.** Identify the most vulnerable chamber/territory beforehand, agree pressure, rate and vasoactive plan and who will call a pause.
- **2.** **Warm and ventilate.** Re-establish gas exchange, check ABG, potassium, ionised calcium, haemoglobin and depth of anaesthesia. Inspect TOE for residual air and ventricular size.
- **3.** **Restablish electrical performance.** Allow intrinsic rhythm if appropriate or pace. If VF persists, defibrillate safely (internal technique below), consider residual air, hypothermia and electrolytes.
- **4.** **Restore cardiac filling gradually.** Reduce venous return diverted into the circuit so more blood fills the heart; progressively reduce CPB pump flow while monitoring arterial pressure, chamber size, RV/LV function, CVP/PA pressures if available and oxygen delivery. Communicate with perfusionist because apparent ‘low preload’ may be a venous-drainage problem rather than true intravascular deficiency.
- **5.** **Evaluate the repair and whole heart under load.** TOE: LV and RV size/contractility, regional wall motion, valve/prosthesis function, RVOT/LVOT obstruction, septal position, pericardial effusion, retained air; consider pulmonary venous/venous return problems where applicable.
- **6.** **Commit only after an adequate assessment.** If stable at low pump flow and then full separation, maintain a measured period off bypass before giving protamine; avoid premature reversal if likely to return to CPB.

![Figure 2. A physiological decision tree for difficult separation from cardiopulmonary bypass.](set13-ch7-2.png)

## When BP falls: diagnose with physiology rather than reflex treatment

**First question:** does the heart look empty, failing, obstructed, or mechanically compressed, and is the systemic circulation dilated? TOE, arterial waveform, CVP/PAP and the surgery performed are more useful than any isolated MAP.

| Haemodynamic phenotype             | Clues                                                                                                                   | Targeted response                                                                                                                                                                                             |
|------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Underfilling**                   | Small hyperdynamic ventricles, low filling, recent bleeding, excessive circuit drainage                                 | Transfer blood from reservoir/appropriate volume **in reassessed increments**, find bleeding; avoid unnecessary crystalloid.                                                                                  |
| **LV systolic failure / stunning** | Dilated poorly contracting LV, low output, rising LA/PA pressures; new RWMA if ischaemic                                | Exclude graft/air/coronary problem and inadequate reperfusion. Consider dobutamine/milrinone or carefully titrated adrenaline, maintain MAP with noradrenaline, optimise loading, re-establish CPB if needed. |
| **RV failure**                     | Dilated RV, septal shift into LV, rising CVP, low LV filling, high PAP/PVR                                              | Avoid hypoxaemia/hypercapnia/acidosis/high airway pressures. Maintain systemic/RV perfusion (noradrenaline/vasopressin), consider inotrope and inhaled NO/epoprostenol; **avoid reflex large fluid boluses**. |
| **Vasoplegia**                     | Low SVR, warm/high-flow state, relatively preserved LV/RV contractility, low MAP despite adequate filling               | Noradrenaline then selected vasopressin; assess bleeding/anaphylaxis/sepsis; no need to treat every low MAP with inotrope.                                                                                    |
| **New ischaemia / graft failure**  | New regional wall-motion defect, ST change, ventricular arrhythmia, new severe MR                                       | Restore coronary perfusion, correct air/hypotension, examine graft/anastomosis, discuss revascularisation/return to CPB.                                                                                      |
| **Mechanical lesion**              | Residual severe valve obstruction/regurgitation, paravalvular leak, prosthesis problem, SAM/LVOTO, new shunt, tamponade | Diagnose with TOE and **correct the lesion**; drugs alone will not solve a mechanical obstruction.                                                                                                            |
| **Rhythm / conduction**            | AF, VF, profound bradycardia, complete heart block, AV dyssynchrony                                                     | Cardioversion/defibrillation or pace with appropriate AV timing; correct K/Mg/temperature.                                                                                                                    |

## A difficult wean: turn TOE findings into the next action

![Visual guide 4 — Recognising common TOE patterns during difficult CPB separation. Schematic for teaching; not to scale.](set13-ch7-3.png)

There is an important difference between a patient who **cannot leave bypass at all** and one who **separates but develops low cardiac output** over the next 10–30 minutes. In the first situation, maintaining or re-establishing adequate CPB flow prevents repeated cycles of organ hypoperfusion while the team diagnoses the cause. In the second, the patient may have ongoing afterload, rhythm or ischaemic problems that emerge only when full cardiac output and pulmonary blood flow resume. Both require the same physiological framework but different urgency for returning to bypass.

**Interpret ventricular size before choosing a drug.** A small LV and small RV suggest underfilling or excessive circuit drainage, although regional abnormalities and mechanical compression must be excluded. A distended poorly contracting LV with high LA pressure suggests LV pump failure, graft-related ischaemia, inadequate cardioplegia or excessive afterload. A large RV with a flattened septum and small LV suggests RV failure/PVR problem or obstruction of pulmonary outflow; giving fluid may worsen ventricular interdependence. Normal vigorous contractility with low pressure and apparently adequate flow is more consistent with vasoplegia. An obstruction pattern (prosthesis problem, tamponade, dynamic LVOTO) may require surgical correction rather than inotropy.

**Why the pressure response can mislead:** noradrenaline may restore MAP even when cardiac output remains low; an inotrope can increase measured output while reducing arterial pressure and coronary perfusion; high PEEP may improve oxygenation while worsening RV preload/afterload. Therefore reassess pulse pressure, mixed or central venous saturation, lactate trend, end-organ perfusion and TOE after every major change. No one CVP or PAOP value predicts fluid responsiveness. Be explicit when proposing a small fluid test: what variable will demonstrate benefit, what will demonstrate harm, and when will you stop?

## A careful right-ventricular approach after CPB

The RV is designed for low pulmonary afterload. After long CPB, hypoxia, acidosis, pulmonary vasoconstriction, protamine, residual mitral disease or pulmonary air/embolus may abruptly raise PVR. RV dilation then pushes the septum leftward, reducing LV filling; systemic hypotension reduces RV coronary perfusion and creates a vicious cycle.

**Step by step:** look for acute RV dilatation and septal flattening on TOE; review PAP/CVP trends, ABG and the surgical result. Correct ventilation/oxygenation, acidosis, high airway pressure and avoid nitrous oxide. Support systemic MAP using noradrenaline or selected vasopressin; if low output persists, add dobutamine/milrinone with pressure support. Inhaled nitric oxide or epoprostenol can selectively reduce PVR, but monitor pulmonary oedema when left-sided filling pressures are high. True underfilling can justify a small test bolus; a congested RV will usually worsen with more volume. Re-establish CPB and consider RV-specific support or VA-ECMO if refractory. This is different from treating primary LV stunning.

## Right ventricular pressure and output after bypass

Read RV size, free-wall function, septal position, LV filling, arterial pressure and measured flow together. PA pressure may fall as the failing RV loses pressure-generating capacity. Falling PA pressure with rising CVP and worsening output is therefore concerning. TAPSE and tissue Doppler change with loading and pericardiotomy. Use serial multiplane TOE and haemodynamics. With new inferior ischaemia, review RCA graft flow and coronary air. If severe failure starts during protamine, stop the infusion and prepare phenotype-directed rescue. Return to bypass after adequate re-heparinisation if reversal has already occurred.

[ANZCA Blue Book 2021, RV dysfunction chapters](https://www.anzca.edu.au/safety-and-advocacy/advocacy/college-publications/australasian-anaesthesia-%28the-blue-book%29) · [Adult CPB guideline](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947607/)

## Dynamic LVOT obstruction after mitral repair: the classic trap

A patient separates after mitral repair with hypotension, a small vigorous LV and worsening MR. This is not necessarily ‘poor contractility’. **Systolic anterior motion (SAM)** of the repaired anterior leaflet may narrow the LVOT and produce dynamic obstruction. Higher contractility, tachycardia, low preload and low SVR worsen the gradient. **Do not reflexively give dobutamine or adrenaline.** Confirm SAM/LVOTO on TOE, restore afterload using phenylephrine/vasopressin, correct actual underfilling, reduce catecholamine stimulation and slow the HR with carefully selected beta blockade after perfusion is supported. Severe persistent obstruction can require surgical revision.

## TOE-based failed-wean differential: one pressure, three completely different treatments

Hyperdynamic small LV + low SVR/high flow suggests vasoplegia, but consider dynamic SAM/LVOTO if an LVOT gradient, anterior leaflet motion and posterior MR jet are present. Distended weak LV or new regional wall-motion abnormality suggests myocardial stunning, graft dysfunction, coronary air, valve dysfunction or outflow obstruction. Dilated RV with septal shift, raised venous pressure and underfilled LV suggests RV afterload or contractile failure. Each mechanism directs different choices of vasopressor, inotrope, volume and surgeon intervention.

With SAM, avoid worsening obstruction by reflex adrenaline or dobutamine. Restore afterload using an appropriate vasoconstrictor, adjust preload cautiously, slow tachycardia when stable and consider beta-blockade. For ischaemic LV dysfunction, preserve coronary perfusion, ask the surgeon to inspect graft/coronary flows and return to CPB to correct any mechanical lesion. For RV failure, correct hypoxia, hypercarbia, high airway pressure and acidosis; maintain right coronary perfusion; use pulmonary vasodilators and appropriate inotropic support. Escalate to MCS if recovery is unlikely without it.

## Internal defibrillation (SS_CS 1.9)

VF after aortic unclamping is relatively common and may respond after further reperfusion, electrolyte correction and electrical therapy. With the sternum open, **internal paddles** are placed on the myocardium with conductive surfaces appropriately positioned, avoiding coronary grafts, delicate tissue and personnel contact. Confirm everyone is clear and synchronise communication with surgery/perfusion. Internal defibrillation generally uses **much lower energies than external transthoracic shocks**, commonly starting around **10–20 J biphasic** according to device/local protocol, escalating as recommended if unsuccessful. There is no single universal internal energy setting across equipment. For unstable organised tachyarrhythmia use synchronised cardioversion where appropriate; for VF deliver an unsynchronised shock. Avoid prolonged pauses in perfusion or indiscriminate repeated shocks without addressing ischaemia, potassium, temperature and air. Confirm return of effective mechanical contraction, not just an organised ECG.

## Epicardial pacing to facilitate separation

Temporary atrial and ventricular wires may be placed at surgery. An initial rate around **70–90/min** may be useful after bypass when the intrinsic node is recovering from cold/ischaemia; select according to output, lesion, diastolic filling and pacing tolerance rather than assuming 80 is obligatory. In complete heart block with intact atrial activity and available atrial/ventricular wires, **DDD** can preserve AV synchrony and optimise output; if only a ventricular wire or unreliable atrial sensing/capture is available, **VVI** provides ventricular backup. In operating theatre interference, asynchronous AOO/DOO may prevent inappropriate inhibition while diathermy is active, but must be used deliberately; do not leave a competing asynchronous mode unattended when intrinsic rhythm returns. Set sensitivity and output based on tested thresholds, generally output with a safety margin of at least twice capture threshold; examine the lead, connector, generator and patient if intermittent capture occurs. These detailed pacing principles build on Set 12; they matter here because failure of AV synchrony may be the sole cause of failed weaning.

**ANZCA examiner point:** the 2026.1 SAQ on epicardial pacing in a complete-heart-block patient found candidates lost marks by giving generic pacing advice without specifying/justifying **mode and rate** or considering backup pacing modalities. Contextualise every programming choice to haemodynamics.

## A practical ‘difficult wean’ script for the viva

> “I would promptly communicate with the surgeon and perfusionist, resume or maintain partial bypass flow to protect organ perfusion, and use TOE to classify the problem as inadequate filling, LV failure, RV failure, vasoplegia, rhythm or a mechanical complication. I would correct temperature, oxygenation, acid–base/electrolytes and pacing; treat the specific haemodynamic mechanism; verify the repair and de-airing; and reattempt a graded wean only when the cause is corrected. For persistent shock I would escalate early to selected mechanical support rather than repeatedly attempting an unsafe separation.”

This structure is more useful than a list of drugs. It connects **what you see** → **what it means** → **what you do**.

## When to stop repeated weaning attempts and escalate support

Persistent new territorial RWMA should prompt graft/ostial assessment before repeated pharmacological attempts. Persistent severe valve regurgitation, prosthesis malfunction, intracardiac air, SAM/LVOTO or bleeding/tamponade requires direct treatment. Profound biventricular failure or refractory RV failure may require temporary MCS as a **bridge to recovery or a definitive decision**, not after many unsuccessful attempts have produced acidosis and coagulopathy.

Device choice follows the failing organ. **IABP** modestly unloads an ejecting LV and augments diastolic aortic pressure but provides little independent forward flow and cannot support refractory arrest. **Microaxial LV pumps** provide more LV unloading/flow, but need suitable aortic valve/root anatomy, adequate RV filling and anticoagulation; haemolysis and vascular injury are relevant. **VA-ECMO** provides cardiopulmonary support when the circulation and/or oxygenation are profoundly inadequate, but raises LV afterload and can cause LV distension/pulmonary oedema unless unloading is addressed. **RVAD** is a more targeted option for predominant RV failure, with or without oxygenator depending on pulmonary support needs. None is automatically superior in all postcardiotomy shock; involving a shock/perfusion team early avoids the wrong circuit being chosen for the wrong phenotype.

**Final safety gate before protamine:** the surgeon and anaesthetist must be confident the repaired heart is supporting perfusion, there is no major unexplained TOE abnormality, no significant intracardiac air remains and an agreed rhythm/temporary pacing plan exists. Protamine is not an arbitrary step once the pump is switched off; reversing UFH while an urgent return to bypass is likely complicates rescue.

items.title: 8. Mechanical circulatory support: IABP and ventricular assist devices
items.priority: P2 HIGH (1 parent LO) + P4 LOW (1 parent LO)
items.body:
Mapped LOs: SS_IC 1.39 and SS_CS 1.28; connects to difficult CPB weaning and postoperative shock.

## Why mechanical support may be preferable to escalating catecholamines

Inotropes can improve contractility but also raise myocardial O₂ demand, provoke arrhythmias and worsen ischaemia. A pump can temporarily maintain perfusion, unload a ventricle, or bridge to correction of an underlying lesion, recovery, durable VAD or transplantation. **Device choice follows the failed chamber and the clinical purpose**: isolated LV, RV, biventricular or combined heart–lung support. No device is a generic answer to all cardiogenic shock, and insertion itself introduces bleeding, vascular and thrombotic risks.

## Mechanical circulatory support: which part of the circulation is the problem?

A drug can only help the patient's own heart pump better or alter vascular resistance. **Mechanical circulatory support (MCS)** adds an external or implanted device that changes pressure, flow or ventricular work. The key question is whether the patient needs (a) a modest reduction in LV workload, (b) substantial independent LV forward flow, (c) RV forward flow, or (d) both circulation and gas exchange supported.

An **intra-aortic balloon pump (IABP)** is a balloon in the descending aorta. It **inflates in diastole** (after aortic valve closure) to augment aortic diastolic pressure and may improve coronary perfusion; it **deflates just before systole** to lower resistance against which the LV ejects. It does not itself pump litres of blood to the body, cannot oxygenate and needs the patient's heart to keep ejecting. That is why it is a modest support device, not a complete rescue for refractory cardiac arrest.

An **Impella** pump is a microaxial pump that crosses the aortic valve, drawing blood out of the LV and delivering it to the ascending aorta—directly unloading and augmenting forward flow. A **ventricular assist device (VAD)** is the broader name for an artificial pump supporting the LV, RV or both. A **right VAD** typically draws from the right atrium and returns to the pulmonary artery. **VA-ECMO** drains venous blood and pumps oxygenated blood into a systemic artery; it can maintain systemic circulation during major cardiac failure, but the retrograde aortic return increases the pressure the LV faces and may distend the LV. The next chapter compares VA with VV-ECMO from first principles.

When asked what device you would use, start by naming the failed chamber and whether the lungs can oxygenate, then explain what that device supplies and what new problem it creates. Do not memorise a device brand as the response to every episode of shock.

## Intra-aortic balloon pump (IABP): understand the timing

![Visual guide 5 — IABP diastolic inflation and pre-systolic deflation timing. Schematic for teaching; not to scale.](set13-ch8-1.png)

A balloon catheter lies in the descending thoracic aorta with its tip just distal to the left subclavian origin (confirm position by imaging), avoiding major aortic branches. It **inflates immediately after aortic valve closure** (at the dicrotic notch), raising diastolic aortic pressure and potentially coronary perfusion, then **deflates just before systole**, lowering end-diastolic aortic pressure and resistance to LV ejection. This simultaneously attempts to **increase coronary O₂ supply and reduce LV O₂ demand**. The gain in cardiac output is modest (often approximately 0.3–0.5 L/min and highly patient-dependent); IABP cannot replace native ventricular ejection or independently oxygenate blood.

**Waveform in 1:2 mode:** compare the unassisted and assisted beats. An effective inflation produces a new diastolic augmentation peak just after the notch; assisted end-diastolic pressure is lower than the unassisted equivalent, and assisted systolic pressure should be lower owing to unloading. Diastolic augmentation may exceed the native systolic peak but does not have to. Timing errors matter:

| Timing error    | Arterial waveform clue                                  | Consequence                                                              |
|-----------------|---------------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Early inflation | Inflation before the dicrotic notch                     | Premature aortic valve closure, increased LV afterload or regurgitation. |
| Late inflation  | Inflation well after notch; weak diastolic augmentation | Less coronary perfusion benefit.                                         |
| Early deflation | Diastolic pressure falls too soon                       | Loss of augmented coronary perfusion; may encourage retrograde flow.     |
| Late deflation  | Balloon remains inflated at onset of LV systole         | Increased systolic afterload, higher myocardial demand and poor output.  |

**Indications:** selected refractory LV failure/low output after cardiac surgery, bridge in mechanical complications of MI (e.g. acute MR or VSD) and selected ischaemia despite optimal medical therapy. **Not routine** after successfully revascularised infarct-related cardiogenic shock: IABP-SHOCK II did not show survival benefit. Inability to generate pulsatile output or profound biventricular failure may require more powerful support.

**Contraindications:** moderate/severe aortic regurgitation (diastolic inflation worsens backward flow), aortic dissection and severe aortoiliac/vascular disease or aneurysm at risk of rupture; active uncontrolled bleeding/coagulopathy and local limb perfusion issues may also limit feasibility. Complications: leg ischaemia, arterial injury/dissection, bleeding, thrombocytopenia, balloon rupture, infection, poor positioning/renal artery obstruction. Monitor distal pulses/perfusion, catheter position, device alarms and anticoagulation plan. **Optimise performance** with accurate timing/trigger (ECG or arterial pressure), adequate preload and coronary perfusion pressure, avoidance of severe tachyarrhythmia and correcting underlying myocardial ischaemia.

## Past SAQ 2022.1 Q8: map aortic waveform points A–F to physiology

At 1:2 augmentation compare the unassisted and assisted cardiac cycles. The officially reported labels are: A = unassisted systolic pressure (chair report prints “assisted systole/unassisted systole”), B = dicrotic notch/aortic valve closure, C = unassisted aortic end-diastolic pressure, D = augmented diastolic pressure, E = assisted aortic end-diastolic pressure, F = assisted systolic pressure. Inflation at B raises aortic diastolic root pressure and can increase coronary perfusion; deflation before F lowers assisted end-diastolic pressure and LV afterload. The examiner specifically cited weak cardiac-cycle language, so name valve events and supply/demand effects, not just the relative peak heights.

The balloon is typically sited in descending thoracic aorta distal to the left subclavian. Performance depends on appropriate size/volume, correct position, timing, native ventricular activity and trigger reliability. Irregular rhythm can challenge ECG timing, but the device may trigger from arterial pressure. Early inflation opposes LV ejection; late inflation loses augmentation; early deflation loses sustained diastolic effect; late deflation raises systolic afterload. Major adverse effects include limb ischaemia, vascular injury, bleeding, thrombocytopenia and device rupture. Significant AR and aortic dissection are important contraindications.

Source check: Original IABP figure in 2022.1 ANZCA Final Chair Report p.18; see revised Set 13 SAQ bank and companion PNG.

## Ventricular assist devices (VADs) and temporary percutaneous pumps

![Visual guide 6 — IABP versus Impella versus VA-ECMO: physiological differences. Schematic for teaching; not to scale.](set13-ch8-2.png)

| Device / configuration                                     | What it does                                                                                                 | Best use / important limitations                                                                                                                                                        |
|------------------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Impella (microaxial LV pump)**                           | Draws blood from LV across aortic valve into ascending aorta; actively unloads LV and increases forward flow | Selected LV shock, refractory low output. Risks haemolysis, limb ischaemia, bleeding, pump malposition; LV thrombus/mechanical AV/important AR are problems. Needs adequate RV preload. |
| **TandemHeart (standard transseptal LA→arterial circuit)** | Drains LA and returns to artery, bypassing LV                                                                | LV unloading/support, but requires transseptal access and anticoagulation; not intrinsically an RVAD.                                                                                   |
| **Dedicated temporary RVAD**                               | RA→PA support (e.g. ProtekDuo configuration)                                                                 | Isolated severe RV failure with adequate lungs; pulmonary oxygenation may require an oxygenator and other configuration.                                                                |
| **VA-ECMO / ECLS**                                         | Venous drainage → pump + oxygenator → systemic artery                                                        | Rescues severe biventricular/cardiopulmonary collapse; increases LV afterload with peripheral retrograde flow and may worsen LV distension/oedema.                                      |
| **Durable LVAD**                                           | Implantable pump supports systemic LV flow, often as bridge to transplantation or destination therapy        | Chronic advanced HF; preload/RV dependent, often low pulsatility, needs antithrombotic/device-specific care.                                                                            |

**Selecting support after failed weaning:** Isolated severe LV dysfunction with acceptable RV function may suit IABP if modest assistance suffices, or a stronger LV pump. Severe RV failure may require RVAD or VA-ECMO depending on oxygenation and left-sided function. Biventricular failure plus major gas exchange impairment often favours VA-ECMO. If VA-ECMO produces a distended LV with absent aortic opening and pulmonary oedema, address **LV unloading** (vent, selected IABP or microaxial pump) while accounting for device-specific hazards.

**Evidence needs precise interpretation:** [IABP-SHOCK II](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24011548/) showed no routine survival benefit for IABP after MI-related shock in an early-revascularisation population. [DanGer Shock](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38587239/) found selected STEMI-related shock patients receiving Impella CP had lower 180-day mortality (45.8% versus 58.5%) **but** higher composite safety events (24.0% versus 6.2%), bleeding, limb ischaemia and renal replacement therapy. These results cannot be extrapolated to every postcardiotomy shock patient. [ECLS-SHOCK](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37634145/) did not demonstrate routine 30-day mortality benefit from early VA-ECMO in all infarct-related shock, while bleeding/vascular complications increased. A **multidisciplinary shock team, phenotype and timing** govern decisions.

## Durable continuous-flow LVAD: perioperative planning and HeartMate 3 evidence

A durable LVAD (e.g. magnetically levitated HeartMate 3) drains LV blood to the ascending aorta; it is preload dependent, afterload sensitive and reliant on adequate RV function. A patient may be poorly pulsatile: Doppler opening pressure can approximate MAP and an arterial line may be needed for complex procedures. Evaluate flow, speed, power, pulsatility indices, driveline/infection, RV function, aortic regurgitation, anticoagulation and ICD settings with the LVAD team. Pneumoperitoneum, head-up positioning, vasodilatation and positive-pressure ventilation may reduce venous return and trigger a suction/low-flow state; evaluate volume, RV function and pump settings before changing speed.

Do not assume HeartMate 3 always requires aspirin plus warfarin: the ARIES-HM3 randomised trial found aspirin avoidance with a vitamin K antagonist reduced nonsurgical bleeding without increased thromboembolic events in studied patients. Neither routine bridging nor a fixed interruption/reversal regimen applies to every operation; agree drug decisions with the VAD service based on thrombosis risk, surgical bleeding and local protocols. Other complications include GI bleeding/acquired von Willebrand syndrome, pump thrombosis, stroke, haemolysis, RV failure and infection. Assess perfusion in an arrest without assuming an absent pulse means no flow; follow device-specific emergency guidance.

Source check: Falland & Allen BJA Education 2023: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10501881/ ; ARIES-HM3 JAMA 2023: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10640705/

items.title: 9. ECMO and extracorporeal support beyond conventional cardiac bypass
items.priority: P3 MODERATE (1 parent LO) + P4 LOW (1 parent LO)
items.body:
Mapped LOs: SS_CS 1.16 (CPB/ECMO in non-cardiac surgery), SS_IC 1.62 (respiratory ECMO), supporting SS_IC 1.39.

## ECMO in one diagram: the return location determines its main purpose

**ECMO** means extracorporeal membrane oxygenation: blood leaves the body, passes through a pump and membrane oxygenator, then returns to circulation. It resembles the CPB circuit but is typically used for longer support with different cannulas, circuit features and anticoagulation. The critical distinction is where the blood returns.
