items.title: 2026.1 Q7: Epicardial pacing in complete heart block before separation from bypass
items.q: A patient is in complete heart block prior to separation from cardiopulmonary bypass. a. Outline the programming considerations for epicardial pacing in this patient. (30%) b. Describe your approach to troubleshooting intermittent capture of the pacemaker in this patient who is pacing-dependent in the ICU. (70%)
items.model:
## a) Programming considerations

**Mode.** The patient is in complete heart block, so the ventricle must be paced. With atrial and ventricular wires and a sinus atrium, **DDD** (AV sequential) is best, because atrial systole contributes up to 25% of ventricular filling and AV sequential pacing generally improves ejection; AAI is relatively contraindicated in high-grade block. With ventricular wires only, or AF, use **VVI**. On weaning from bypass, an asynchronous mode (**DOO or VOO**) is acceptable while diathermy is in use and the chest is open, then change to a demand mode (DDD) afterwards, because asynchronous pacing risks R-on-T.

**Rate.** About **70 to 90 per minute**, chosen because the intrinsic rate is absent and a stunned, oedematous ventricle has a relatively fixed stroke volume so output is rate dependent; individualise to the output and ischaemia. **AV interval** 160 to 200 ms.

**Output.** Measure the **capture threshold** with experienced assistance, continuous ECG/arterial monitoring and effective backup pacing. In a dependent patient, do not deliberately provoke prolonged loss of capture to test the system. Under 5 mA is acceptable, 5 to 10 mA warrants discussion with the surgeon about new wires, over 10 mA is unacceptable. During supervised wire assessment/closure the surgeon may use a specific threshold-check protocol; the dependent ICU patient needs a reliable safety margin, commonly at least twice the measured capture threshold, with reassessment as thresholds change. **Sensitivity:** the sensing threshold can only be measured if there is an intrinsic rhythm, which a block may not allow; a dependent patient may need an asynchronous mode or close monitoring. Confirm mechanical capture on the arterial waveform.

## b) Intermittent capture in a pacing-dependent ICU patient

**Safety first.** Is the patient stable? If bradycardic or hypotensive, restore pacing immediately and use adrenaline or isoprenaline as a monitored bridge if required; atropine may be ineffective in complete/infranodal block and must not delay pacing, apply **transcutaneous pacing** pads, call for help, and start CPR if asystolic. Keep a defibrillator at the bedside.

**Systematic approach: patient, leads, generator.**

| Domain | Causes | Action |
|---|---|---|
| **Patient** | Rising threshold (oedema, ischaemia, fibrosis; thresholds vary most in the first 48 hours), hypothermia (aim above 36 degrees), hypo or hyperkalaemia, acidosis, pericardial effusion or tamponade, drugs | Correct K, Mg, pH and temperature; echocardiogram; review drugs |
| **Leads** | Wire migration or fracture, loose connection at the wire, cable or box | Check from patient to box: wires at the skin, wire-to-cable, cable-to-box; replace the cable; try another wire or pole |
| **Generator** | Box off, flat battery, wrong mode, **output too close to threshold** so respiratory variation causes intermittent capture; oversensing (shivering, T waves, diathermy) inhibiting output; undersensing | Perform a full pacing check; raise output; reduce sensitivity setting for undersensing or raise it for oversensing; correct shivering; use an asynchronous mode if inhibited; change box and battery |

Intermittent pacing may also reflect a native escape rhythm competing with the paced rate: assess with experienced staff and a backup method; do not lower the rate or stop pacing unsafely in a dependent patient. Adjust the pacing rate only while preserving perfusion.

**Alternative modalities** if capture cannot be restored: transcutaneous pacing, a **transvenous wire**, or new epicardial wires; electrophysiology review, and a permanent pacemaker if block persists. If an R-on-T arrest occurs, pause the pacemaker, defibrillate, and follow cardiac surgical life support; do not leave a poorly sensing system running on a ward.

## Distinguish capture, sensing and output failure

**No pacing spikes** suggests inhibition/oversensing, cable/generator failure or an inappropriate rate/mode; **spikes without QRS** indicate failure to capture; **QRS without an arterial pulse** means absent effective mechanical output and requires resuscitation/diagnosis. Increase output promptly for capture failure while correcting causes. For oversensing, a higher numerical mV setting makes the box less sensitive; for undersensing, a lower mV setting makes it more sensitive. Do not assume every intermittent beat is a lead problem. Replace faulty equipment without interrupting effective pacing. Only measure a sensing threshold when intrinsic activity is present and doing so is safe.

DDD requires reliable atrial and ventricular sensing and is not automatically the safest mode with poor atrial sensing. Reassess rate and AV interval against arterial pressure, filling and ischaemia, rather than treating 70–90/min or 160–200 ms as universal prescriptions. Continue continuous monitored care, record mode/rate/output/sensitivity/thresholds and arrange specialist review before ICU discharge.

**Examiner linkage:** the 2026.1 report requires a justified mode/rate, a structured patient–leads–generator assessment, and alternative pacing to ensure safety; rate justification and rescue alternatives were common omissions.

> **Marking note:** educator-created 10-mark schedule, not an official ANZCA rubric. Award partial credit within each domain; a numerical total does not establish an ANZCA pass.
rubric: **3 marks** — Justifies mode/rate/output/sensitivity/AV interval and confirms mechanical capture safely (part a)
**2 marks** — Stabilises the dependent patient and provides backup pacing
**3 marks** — Systematically assesses patient, leads and generator with capture versus sensing distinctions
**2 marks** — Corrects the fault and provides transcutaneous/transvenous/new epicardial alternatives and specialist follow-up

items.title: 2025.1 Q3: Discuss the perioperative management of an adult patient who underwent
items.q: Discuss the perioperative management of an adult patient who underwent heart transplantation three years ago and now requires an appendicectomy.
items.model:
## Preoperative assessment and preparation

Clarify appendicitis severity, perforation/sepsis, urgency, fasting/vomiting and need for source control. Contact the transplant team and review graft function, recent echo/ECG, functional capacity, rejection episodes, coronary allograft vasculopathy, arrhythmias and recent admissions. Absence of angina does not exclude graft ischaemia because cardiac afferents are denervated. Three years after transplant, opportunistic risk depends more on current immunosuppression/rejection therapy than on the date alone.

Review immunosuppressants and take an explicit plan for continuing them at the correct time, with an alternative route if oral absorption is unreliable. Tacrolimus/ciclosporin need attention to renal function, levels and CYP interactions; mycophenolate/azathioprine can cause cytopenia, and steroids cause diabetes/infection risk and possible adrenal suppression. Check FBC, renal/electrolytes (particularly potassium/magnesium), glucose and tests guided by illness. Do not independently stop anti-rejection drugs because surgery is urgent; severe sepsis may require a specialist-agreed modification. Continue usual steroid and provide stress supplementation when indicated by adrenal risk/stress.

Give effective appendicitis antibiotics guided by local flora, allergy and severity, with cultures if septic and no treatment delay. Use strict asepsis, quantify aspiration risk, consent to increased cardiovascular/infectious risk and plan postoperative monitoring. Resuscitation and source control proceed together; do not delay an urgent operation for every historic transplant record.

## Intraoperative management

The denervated heart has a higher resting rate, a reduced rapid reflex response to hypotension and a slower response to circulating catecholamines. Maintain adequate venous return, afterload and contractility; avoid abrupt vasodilatation, hypovolaemia, severe bradycardia and excessive fluid. Limited reinnervation can occur, so responses are not identical in every recipient.

For a stable patient with a full stomach, carefully titrated general anaesthesia with a cuffed tracheal tube is usually suitable; modify induction for shock and have direct-acting vasoactive drugs ready. Atropine and indirect sympathomimetics may be unreliable; use appropriate direct-acting agents and pacing if clinically needed rather than assuming routine prophylactic pacing. Monitor ECG, capnography, oxygenation and temperature; add an arterial line for significant sepsis/graft dysfunction/instability, not automatically solely for transplantation.

Laparoscopic pneumoperitoneum and position can reduce venous return, increase SVR and airway pressures, and alter CO2; ask for the lowest appropriate insufflation pressure, monitor tolerance, and agree conversion/desufflation if needed. Use protective ventilation and quantitative neuromuscular monitoring. Choose drugs with regard to organ function/interactions and avoid nephrotoxins. Preserve normothermia and glucose control.

## Postoperative management

Disposition reflects graft reserve, sepsis severity, surgery and haemodynamic support: monitored recovery may suffice for an uncomplicated stable case, whereas organ dysfunction/vasopressors require HDU/ICU. Ensure analgesia/antiemesis, early enteral drug delivery and documented immunosuppressant administration; monitor renal function, electrolytes, glucose, rhythm, infection and graft dysfunction. Communicate antibiotic and transplant-drug interactions with pharmacy. Involve the transplant team for an unexpected deterioration or missed anti-rejection doses.

The examiner specifically expected transplant physiology/pharmacodynamics, immunosuppressant management and postoperative care; an answer dominated by pacemakers misses the problem.

**Sources and review basis:** Official 2025.1 report, BT_PO 1.5; explicitly shared Master map. Blue Book 2019 cardiac-transplant chapter is background only unless read separately; current infection principles and transplant-team drug management inform the model. This is not an assertion that all cardiac-transplant questions belong to Set 4.
rubric: **2 marks** — Surgical urgency/sepsis and current graft/rejection/vasculopathy assessment.
**2 marks** — Specific continuation/route/interactions of immunosuppressants.
**2 marks** — Denervation and appropriate haemodynamic/drug implications.
**2 marks** — Anaesthetic/laparoscopic plan and appropriate monitoring.
**2 marks** — Postoperative disposition, organ/medication surveillance and handover.

items.title: 2022.1 Q8: IABP pressure trace at 1:2 augmentation
items.q: Identify the points labelled A to F on this intra-aortic balloon pump (IABP) pressure-time trace at the commencement of 1:2 augmentation. (30%) Outline the aims of IABP placement and discuss the underlying physiological principles. (70%)
items.model:
## a) Identify A–F (30%)

The official report labels the trace as follows: **A** = unassisted systolic pressure (the original report prints “assisted systole/unassisted systole”); **B** = dicrotic notch, marking aortic valve closure; **C** = unassisted end-diastolic aortic pressure; **D** = diastolic augmentation (peak pressure after balloon inflation); **E** = assisted end-diastolic aortic pressure; **F** = assisted systolic pressure. In a 1:2 trace compare the unassisted and next assisted beats and describe the cardiac-cycle events, not merely whether peaks are higher or lower.

## b) Aims and physiological principles (70%)

The balloon lies in the descending thoracic aorta, just distal to the left subclavian artery, and is synchronised to the cardiac cycle. **Inflation immediately after aortic valve closure** displaces blood proximally and distally, creating an elevated aortic diastolic pressure. The proximal rise may increase coronary perfusion pressure and myocardial oxygen supply, particularly where coronary perfusion is pressure dependent. **Rapid deflation before the next systole** reduces aortic end-diastolic pressure and the pressure against which the LV ejects, reducing LV wall stress, stroke work and myocardial oxygen demand. These effects improve the myocardial oxygen supply–demand balance; any cardiac-output augmentation is modest and depends on underlying ventricular function.

Timing matters. **Early inflation** (before valve closure) opposes LV ejection, raising afterload. **Late inflation** loses part of diastolic augmentation. **Early deflation** forfeits sustained augmentation and may impair useful pressure support. **Late deflation** leaves an inflated balloon opposing LV ejection, raising assisted systolic pressure. Set 1:2 to compare waveforms and correct the inflation/deflation markers.

Performance depends on balloon size relative to aortic diameter, full balloon volume, correct position, reliable triggering, haemodynamic state and appropriate assist ratio. ECG triggering may be unreliable with arrhythmia, but arterial-pressure triggering can be used; a perfectly regular rhythm is **not** an absolute requirement. Consider IABP for selected ischaemic low-output states or inability to wean from CPB, remembering that it is not full circulatory support and does not provide a routine survival advantage in infarct-related cardiogenic shock. Avoid significant aortic regurgitation and aortic dissection; assess severe peripheral vascular disease, bleeding and vascular access risk.

**Examiner emphasis:** Candidates commonly used imprecise cardiac-cycle terminology, struggled to identify the dicrotic notch and confused increased diastolic coronary perfusion with systolic unloading. Link each named point to aortic valve opening/closure and LV pressure–volume work.

**Sources:** ANZCA 2022.1 Chair’s Report, p. 18. Pass rate 49.7%. · [ANZCA Final Exam reports and papers](https://www.anzca.edu.au/education-and-training/anaesthesia-training-and-pathways/anaesthesia-training-program/anaesthesia-exams) · [ANZCA Blue Book 2021, RV dysfunction after separation and right ventricular failure](https://www.anzca.edu.au/safety-and-advocacy/advocacy/college-publications/australasian-anaesthesia-%28the-blue-book%29) · [IABP-SHOCK II](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1208410), [DanGer Shock](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa2312572), and [ECLS-SHOCK](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa2307227)

items.title: 2020.2 Q1: Heart transplant recipient for laparoscopic cholecystectomy
items.q: You are asked to assess and anaesthetise a 54-year-old patient for a laparoscopic cholecystectomy. They received a heart transplant ten years ago. Discuss the issues relevant for this patient.
items.model:
## Preoperative — graft, infection and organ reserve

Establish time since transplantation, rejection episodes, exercise tolerance, heart-failure symptoms and transplant follow-up. Examine current ECG, echocardiography, graft systolic/diastolic function, pulmonary pressure, known allograft vasculopathy and any prior coronary surveillance. **Cardiac allograft vasculopathy can present without typical angina** because sensory innervation is reduced; new fatigue, arrhythmia or LV impairment may indicate ischaemia or rejection. Look for renal dysfunction, hypertension, diabetes, infection and malignancy associated with long-term immunosuppression. Check FBC, electrolytes (especially potassium and magnesium), creatinine/eGFR and clinically indicated drug levels. Continue tacrolimus/ciclosporin, mycophenolate and corticosteroids as prescribed, arranging an alternative route if fasting; review drug interactions (macrolides, azoles, QT drugs), anaemia and infection prophylaxis. Discuss significant graft dysfunction or suspected rejection with transplant cardiology before elective surgery.

## Denervated cardiac physiology and drugs

The transplanted heart typically has a higher resting rate, diminished immediate reflex tachycardia with hypotension and a blunted chronotropic response to pain or hypovolaemia. Cardiac output is more dependent on venous return/stroke volume, especially with limited graft reserve; do not rely on heart-rate response to judge anaesthetic depth or volume status. **Direct-acting** agents (adrenaline, noradrenaline, phenylephrine and isoprenaline) act at adrenergic receptors; **indirect** agents such as ephedrine have variable efficacy. Atropine often has little chronotropic effect in a denervated heart (later reinnervation is variable). Have direct-acting chronotrope, pacing and defibrillation available. Any arrhythmia may have haemodynamic consequences, especially with CAV or rejection.

## Laparoscopy and intraoperative management

Pneumoperitoneum **reduces venous return**, can increase SVR and PVR, increases airway pressures and may cause hypercarbia; reverse Trendelenburg for upper abdominal surgery further reduces preload. These are specific risks that the 2020.2 examiners highlighted. Discuss a low insufflation pressure and gradual positioning, and be ready to release insufflation if output falls. Standard monitoring is reasonable with a stable graft but obtain an arterial line/TOE when disease or surgical risk warrants. Use carefully titrated induction, maintain intravascular volume without overload, avoid hypoxia/hypercarbia/acidosis and provide a safe airway/ventilation plan. Use meticulous asepsis and appropriate perioperative antibiotic prophylaxis. Do not give unnecessary nephrotoxic or interacting drugs.

## Postoperative

Resume immunosuppression promptly; monitor graft perfusion, renal function, glucose, infection and wound healing. Discuss the need for stress-dose steroids based on actual chronic steroid use/adrenal suppression, not transplant status alone. New hypotension, arrhythmia or reduced urine output should prompt usual surgical assessment and consideration of graft rejection, infection or silent ischaemia.

**Sources:** ANZCA 2020.2 Chair’s Report, p. 11. Pass rate 61.6%. · [ANZCA Final Exam reports and papers](https://www.anzca.edu.au/education-and-training/anaesthesia-training-and-pathways/anaesthesia-training-program/anaesthesia-exams) · [ISHLT guidelines for the care of heart transplant recipients](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37080658/)

Explains denervation, fixed chronotropic response and preload dependence
Gives direct- versus indirect-acting cardiovascular drug implications
Maintains immunosuppression and considers interactions, renal and infection risk
Explicitly explains pneumoperitoneum and reverse Trendelenburg effects
Plans monitoring, haemodynamics, analgesia, rescue pacing and ventilation
Arranges postoperative graft, medication, wound and renal surveillance

items.title: 2019.2 Q1: Deep hypothermic circulatory arrest: rationale and consequences
items.q: Describe the rationale for the use of deep hypothermic circulatory arrest and outline the pathophysiological consequences of this technique.
items.model:
## Rationale

**Deep hypothermic circulatory arrest (DHCA)** stops the circulation completely at a core temperature of about 18 to 20 degrees Celsius, giving a **bloodless, cannula-free field** for aortic arch surgery, type A dissection, some thoracoabdominal and congenital operations and pulmonary thromboendarterectomy. The cost is ischaemia of every organ, and the aim is **cerebral protection**.

Cooling reduces the **cerebral metabolic rate** by about 6 to 7% per degree, to roughly 20 to 25% of normal at 18 degrees, and reduces excitatory neurotransmitter release and free-radical injury. An approximate 30–40-minute window for isolated arrest is often cited, but neurological risk is continuous and modified by adjunct antegrade cerebral perfusion; no fixed duration is guaranteed safe.

## Technique

**Cerebral perfusion is the variable that alters acceptable arrest duration.** Deep hypothermia in isolation does not guarantee a fixed duration without neurological injury: the operative anatomy, temperature attained, baseline cerebrovascular disease and use of selective antegrade cerebral perfusion all matter. In contemporary arch surgery, moderate hypothermia with antegrade cerebral perfusion is an accepted alternative to isolated DHCA. Track brain and body temperature at appropriate sites, arterial pressure and cerebral oximetry. Rewarm gradually and avoid cerebral hyperthermia. Confirm appropriate anticoagulation during cooling and plan haemostasis before rewarming; hypothermia-associated platelet dysfunction can persist after apparent temperature correction.

- Cool on bypass over 20 to 30 minutes, keeping the gradient between blood and body at 10 degrees or less; confirm brain cooling (nasopharyngeal and bladder or rectal temperature, EEG silence or cerebral oximetry).
- Adjuncts: head ice, steroids, a barbiturate or propofol, glucose control, an alpha-stat or pH-stat strategy (pH-stat favours cerebral blood flow during cooling), and **selective antegrade cerebral perfusion** or retrograde perfusion to extend the safe time.
- Rewarm slowly, keeping the outflow temperature below 37 degrees, to avoid gas emboli and cerebral hyperthermia.

## Pathophysiological consequences

| System | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **Neurological** | Stroke, delirium, seizures, cognitive deficit, choreoathetosis in children; risk rises with arrest time |
| **Coagulation** | Platelet dysfunction, slowed enzyme activity, fibrinolysis, haemodilution and heparin: major bleeding |
| **Cardiac** | Bradycardia, VF below about 28 degrees, arrhythmias on rewarming, myocardial stunning |
| **Respiratory** | Left shift of the oxygen–haemoglobin curve, altered gas solubility and pH, lung injury |
| **Renal and visceral** | Ischaemia–reperfusion injury, acute kidney injury, gut ischaemia, cold diuresis |
| **Metabolic and inflammatory** | Hyperglycaemia (insulin resistance), acidosis, electrolyte shifts and a systemic inflammatory response that can lead to **vasoplegia** after rewarming |

Postoperatively expect prolonged ventilation, delayed awakening, bleeding and tamponade. DHCA is a distinct technique from cardioplegic arrest (a chemically arrested, perfused heart) and from ECMO (circulatory support).

**Updated reference:** [2024 EACTS/EACTAIC/EBCP CPB guideline — hypothermia and cerebral protection](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947607/).

**Sources:** ANZCA 2019.2 report, Q1. items.title: 2016.2 Q10: Considerations for successful weaning from bypass after CABG
items.q: Outline the considerations for successful weaning from cardiopulmonary bypass after coronary artery graft surgery.
items.model:
## Principle

Weaning is the **return of the native circulation and ventilation** once the heart and patient are ready. Prepare before the surgeon removes the clamp and complete a checklist.

## 1. Native circulation

**An ordered handover prevents missed mechanical causes.** Before asking the perfusionist to reduce flow, confirm graft patency and de-airing with the surgeon; use TOE for segmental and global function, ventricular filling, valve competence and unexpected LVOT obstruction. Each weaning attempt should identify which variable failed as pump support reduced—pressure, oxygen delivery, rhythm, ventricle or surgical anatomy. If the RV dilates while the LV empties, treat RV afterload/perfusion and consider coronary air. If the LV is hyperdynamic yet pressure remains low, assess low SVR or dynamic obstruction before choosing a drug.

- **Rate and rhythm:** aim for sinus rhythm or pacing at a rate titrated to filling and output. Use synchronised cardioversion for unstable organised tachyarrhythmia and defibrillation for VF. Test epicardial sensing and capture with backup available and use AV synchrony when appropriate. Correct important potassium and magnesium abnormalities.
- **Volume and MAP:** adequate preload by TOE and CVP; an individualised arterial pressure supported with a vasopressor when needed. Vasopressin can be relatively pulmonary-sparing at commonly used doses and may reduce catecholamine requirements; monitor PVR and clinical response. Vasoplegia is likelier with ACE inhibitors or ARB use, long bypass and poor ventricular function; milrinone worsens vasodilation.
- **Contractility and ischaemia:** good function on TOE, no new regional wall motion abnormality, graft flows checked.
- **De-airing** of the heart, vents off, cross-clamp off. Air in the anterior right coronary ostium is a classic cause of RV failure.
- **RV protection:** FiO2 1.0, no hypercarbia or acidosis, avoiding excessive tidal volume or PEEP; for patients with pulmonary hypertension or poor RV function start an inhaled pulmonary vasodilator (nitric oxide 10 to 20 ppm, up to 40) before bypass ends. Protamine can cause pulmonary hypertension, so give it slowly.

## 2. Native ventilation

Lungs **re-expanded** under vision (recruitment; check for pneumothorax or secretions), FiO2 1.0 and a working circuit before ventilation restarts.

## 3. Metabolic and haematological

- **Temperature** above 36 degrees (nasopharyngeal) with a small core-to-periphery gradient.
- **Acid-base, gases and electrolytes** normal; ionised calcium above 1.0.
- **Haemoglobin** adequate (about 70 to 80 g/L or above) and glucose controlled.
- **Coagulation:** Assess bleeding risk and prepare haemostatic testing. Once stable separation has been confirmed and the team agrees it is safe to reverse, titrate protamine and recheck anticoagulation and haemostasis.

## 4. Anaesthesia and equipment

Adequate depth and analgesia, transducers zeroed, TOE ready, defibrillator pads, and inotropes, vasopressors and vasodilators (GTN, nitric oxide) prepared.

## 5. The process

Communicate with the surgeon and perfusionist; wean gradually (partial then full clamping of the venous line) watching the heart, pressures and TOE; have a failure plan: reinstitute bypass, optimise preload, rate, contractility and afterload, then IABP or mechanical support.

**Sources:** ANZCA 2016.2 report, Q10. Pass rate 71.1%. · [ANZCA Final Exam reports and papers](https://www.anzca.edu.au/education-and-training/anaesthesia-training-and-pathways/anaesthesia-training-program/anaesthesia-exams) · [EACTS/EACTAIC/EBCP adult CPB guideline](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947607/) · [ANZCA Blue Book 2021, RV dysfunction after separation and right ventricular failure](https://www.anzca.edu.au/safety-and-advocacy/advocacy/college-publications/australasian-anaesthesia-%28the-blue-book%29) · [BJA Education epicardial pacing (2023)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10433321/)

items.title: 2015.2 Q2: Previous orthotopic heart transplant presenting for non-cardiac surgery
items.q: A 50-year-old patient has received an orthotopic heart transplant 10 years ago. He now presents for elective non-cardiac surgery. Outline the issues a prior heart transplant may present for the anaesthetist AND describe how these will affect anaesthetic management.
items.model:
## Relevant transplant-specific problems

The transplanted heart is initially **denervated** after surgical division of sympathetic and parasympathetic inputs. Resting tachycardia is common, and normal immediate baroreflex responses are attenuated. Tachycardia during hypovolaemia is not a reliable sign. Heart-rate responses to exertion depend on circulating catecholamines, and atropine is generally ineffective for vagally mediated bradycardia in a denervated graft; reinnervation may occur variably with time. Because stroke volume may be particularly important when rapid chronotropic compensation is blunted, avoid abrupt reductions in preload. **Direct-acting** vasoactive drugs and pacing are preferred for predictable emergency responses; indirect sympathomimetics may be unreliable.

Ten years after orthotopic transplant, the main additional threats are **cardiac allograft vasculopathy** (often clinically silent, with absent typical angina), prior/recurrent rejection and graft dysfunction, accelerated coronary disease, arrhythmia and conduction disease, and chronic immunosuppression. Calcineurin inhibitors predispose to chronic kidney disease, hypertension, glucose intolerance and electrolyte disturbances; other drugs may cause marrow suppression or interact with anaesthetic/antimicrobial therapy. Infection risk and wound-healing impairment depend on degree and type of immunosuppression. Steroid adrenal suppression may require perioperative supplementation if chronically exposed.

## Preoperative assessment and optimisation

Obtain graft history, rejection and CAV surveillance results, functional capacity, examination findings and recent ECG/echo. Assess LV/RV performance, pulmonary pressures and known coronary disease; investigate new symptoms, arrhythmia or change in function with the transplant team before elective surgery. Review current immunosuppressive doses, timing and blood-level monitoring, renal function, glucose, K/Mg, infection markers, full blood count and medication interactions. Continue immunosuppression with an agreed fasting plan; withholding several doses may risk rejection. Provide ordinary surgical risk assessment tailored to graft reserve and operation magnitude.

## Anaesthetic implications

Choose GA or regional according to surgery, not transplant status alone, but titrate induction to avoid hypotension and significant venous pooling. Arterial monitoring is appropriate for major surgery or abnormal graft function. If hypotensive, assess preload, bleeding, vasodilatation and graft ischaemia; correct the mechanism and use titrated direct-acting agents when needed. Atropine cannot be relied on for bradycardia; have isoprenaline, adrenaline and pacing available, with individual patient response monitored. Control hypoxaemia, hypercarbia and acidosis, particularly if pulmonary pressure or RV dysfunction is present. For laparoscopic operations, pneumoperitoneum/positioning can reduce venous return; discuss insufflation pressure and positioning in advance. Maintain meticulous asepsis and prophylaxis, and avoid avoidable nephrotoxins.

## Recovery

Resume all immunosuppression promptly with therapeutic monitoring where required, prevent infection and monitor renal/metabolic complications. New low-output symptoms or arrhythmias may represent rejection, CAV or another perioperative complication; take a low threshold for transplant-specialist and echocardiographic review.

**Sources:** ANZCA 2015.2 report, Q2. Pass rate 60.9%. · [ANZCA Final Exam reports and papers](https://www.anzca.edu.au/education-and-training/anaesthesia-training-and-pathways/anaesthesia-training-program/anaesthesia-exams) · [ISHLT guidelines for the care of heart transplant recipients](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37080658/)

items.title: 2012.2 Q3: Prerequisites for separation and causes of post-bypass hypotension
items.q: 1. What are the prerequisites for separation from standard cardiopulmonary bypass after uneventful coronary artery bypass surgery? (50%) 2. What are the likely causes of hypotension in the immediate post-separation period? (50%)
items.model:
## 1. Prerequisites for separation (50%)

**Native circulation and ventilation restored**
- **Rhythm and rate:** sinus or paced at 70 to 90 per minute (pacing capture threshold under 5 mA, wires tested), no block or ectopy.
- **Contractility and ischaemia:** good function and no new regional abnormality on TOE; grafts flowing; heart de-aired.
- **Volume and pressure:** adequate filling by TOE and pressure trends, with arterial pressure suited to organ and graft perfusion.
- **Lungs** re-expanded and ventilating with FiO2 1.0, no pneumothorax.

**Correction of the disturbances of surgery and bypass**
- **Temperature** above 36 degrees nasopharyngeal.
- **Acid-base and electrolytes:** pH, gases, K 4.5 to 5.5, ionised calcium and magnesium.
- **Anaemia and coagulation:** haemoglobin 70 to 80 g/L or higher; heparin reversed (ACT back to baseline), platelets and fibrinogen assessed.

**Anaesthesia and equipment:** adequate depth, zeroed monitors, TOE, pacing, defibrillator, and drugs drawn up.

## 2. Causes of hypotension after separation (50%)

**Make the bedside differential operational.** First check the arterial waveform and transducer, rhythm and TOE while asking the perfusionist to maintain support if needed. An empty LV may mean insufficient pump return, reduced venous return, RV failure or tamponade, whereas a dilated poorly contracting LV suggests myocardial stunning or graft-related ischaemia. Hyperdynamic flow with low vascular resistance suggests vasoplegia, but high-output distributive physiology is not unique to vasoplegia. A hyperdynamic LV with SAM and late-peaking LVOT gradient instead needs preload/afterload and less inotropy. The correct action follows the mechanism; blind boluses of catecholamine may worsen either RV ischaemia or LVOTO.

| Group | Examples |
|---|---|
| **Pump failure** | LV stunning or ischaemia from graft problems or air; **RV failure** (air in the right coronary artery, pulmonary hypertension, prolonged bypass, inadequate protection); valve dysfunction |
| **Rate and rhythm** | Bradycardia, heart block, AF, ventricular arrhythmia |
| **Preload** | Hypovolaemia and bleeding, venous pooling from vasodilators, **tamponade**, tension pneumothorax, high PEEP |
| **Afterload** | **Vasoplegia** (bypass inflammation, ACE inhibitor or ARB use, prolonged bypass, milrinone), **protamine reaction**, anaphylaxis, sepsis |
| **Other** | Residual anaesthetic, acidosis, hypocalcaemia, hypothermia, LVOT obstruction (inotropes, hypovolaemia) |

**Protamine**, given once separation is stable, may cause systemic hypotension, acute pulmonary vasoconstriction and RV failure, or anaphylaxis. Ask about previous protamine reactions and protamine-containing insulin. Slow, monitored dosing mitigates rate-related hypotension. Stop administration and initiate phenotype-specific resuscitation if a severe reaction occurs.

**Approach:** exclude low cardiac output first, because vasoplegia commonly has a preserved or elevated output and low SVR (cardiac index above 2.5, SVR index below 800, normal or high SvO2). Use TOE and the PA catheter to separate causes. After cardiac surgery the femoral pressure often exceeds the radial in vasoplegia, so check a central pressure before treating a low radial reading. Treat the cause and communicate with the surgeon.

**Sources:** ANZCA 2012.2 report, Q3. Pass rate 59.1%. · [ANZCA Final Exam reports and papers](https://www.anzca.edu.au/education-and-training/anaesthesia-training-and-pathways/anaesthesia-training-program/anaesthesia-exams) · [EACTS/EACTAIC/EBCP adult CPB guideline](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947607/) · [ANZCA Blue Book 2021, RV dysfunction after separation and right ventricular failure](https://www.anzca.edu.au/safety-and-advocacy/advocacy/college-publications/australasian-anaesthesia-%28the-blue-book%29) · [ANZCA Blue Book 2023, Intravenous heparin and non-cardiac anaesthesia](https://www.anzca.edu.au/safety-and-advocacy/advocacy/college-publications/australasian-anaesthesia-%28the-blue-book%29)

items.title: 2008.2 Q12: Intra-aortic balloon pump: indications, contraindications and optimisation
items.q: List the indications and contra-indications for the use of an intra-aortic balloon pump. Describe how its performance is optimised.
items.model:
## Principle

A 30 to 50 mL helium-filled balloon sits in the **descending thoracic aorta**, **inflating in diastole and deflating just before systole**. The 2022.1 examiners' two core points are: diastolic inflation raises aortic root diastolic pressure and so **coronary perfusion**, and systolic deflation lowers **afterload**, improving myocardial oxygen supply against demand. Augmentation of output is modest (about 0.5 to 1 L/min), and it needs some native contractility and reliable triggering (ECG or arterial-pressure trigger). The examiners noted poor knowledge of the cardiac cycle, so describe timing against the dicrotic notch.

## Indications

- Cardiogenic shock or severe failure awaiting recovery or definitive treatment.
- **Failure to wean from bypass**, or low output after cardiac surgery; the Blue Book also supports it in RV failure to promote right coronary flow.
- Post-infarction: refractory angina, ventricular arrhythmia, **mechanical complications** (acute mitral regurgitation, VSD) awaiting surgery.
- High-risk revascularisation (left main disease, poor LV function), bridge to transplant or VAD, and LV unloading with VA-ECMO.

## Contraindications

- **Aortic regurgitation** more than mild (the examiners stress that even mild AR can become severe with an IABP, because diastolic augmentation worsens it).
- **Aortic dissection or aneurysm**, and severe aorto-iliac or peripheral vascular disease.
- Relative: coagulopathy, sepsis, uncontrolled tachyarrhythmia, bleeding.

## Optimising performance

**Timing is confirmed on the arterial waveform at 1:2 assistance.** Inflation should coincide with aortic valve closure at the dicrotic notch, raising diastolic aortic pressure; deflation just before the next systole reduces assisted end-diastolic pressure and LV afterload. Early inflation opposes ejection, late inflation reduces diastolic augmentation, early deflation sacrifices sustained coronary augmentation and late deflation increases systolic afterload. With tachyarrhythmia or poor ECG signal, pressure triggering can still permit operation—irregular rhythm is a limitation, not an absolute contraindication. Poor augmentation also warrants assessment of balloon volume/position and haemodynamic state, not timing alone.

- **Position:** tip just distal to the left subclavian artery (about 2 cm below the aortic knob on chest X-ray).
- **Balloon volume:** full inflation for the patient's size.
- **Timing (1:2 mode):** inflation at the **dicrotic notch** (aortic valve closure); too early closes the valve prematurely and reduces stroke volume, too late loses augmentation. Deflation **just before systole**, at end-diastole; late deflation raises afterload. A good trace shows a diastolic peak above the unassisted systolic peak and an assisted end-diastolic pressure below the unassisted one.
- **Trigger:** ECG or arterial waveform; regular rhythm and rate (AF, tachycardia and pacing artefact degrade timing).
- Maintain MAP and preload, treat arrhythmias, keep the leg straight, anticoagulate as appropriate, and check limb perfusion, platelets and haemolysis. Trials in infarct shock (IABP-SHOCK II) showed no mortality benefit (from memory).

**Sources:** ANZCA 2008.2 report, Q12. Pass rate 59%. · [ANZCA Final Exam reports and papers](https://www.anzca.edu.au/education-and-training/anaesthesia-training-and-pathways/anaesthesia-training-program/anaesthesia-exams) · [ANZCA Blue Book 2021, RV dysfunction after separation and right ventricular failure](https://www.anzca.edu.au/safety-and-advocacy/advocacy/college-publications/australasian-anaesthesia-%28the-blue-book%29) · [IABP-SHOCK II](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1208410), [DanGer Shock](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa2312572), and [ECLS-SHOCK](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa2307227)

items.title: How would you reduce anxiety in a patient presenting for cardiac surgery?
items.sub: Before bypass: assessment, risk, preparation and anxiolysis
items.eyebrow: Before bypass: assessment, risk, preparation and anxiolysis
items.q: How would you reduce anxiety in a patient presenting for cardiac surgery?
items.a:
- Clear information and honest discussion of expectations.
- Pre-op education, prehabilitation, avoid routine sedative premedication.
- Anxiolysis only if needed, taking care to avoid hypoventilation.
- Plan for early mobilisation and pain control.

> **Closing point:** Information reduces anxiety more than drugs.

Sources: BJA Educ 2021

items.title: What are the issues with redo cardiac surgery?
items.sub: Before bypass: assessment, risk, preparation and anxiolysis
items.eyebrow: Before bypass: assessment, risk, preparation and anxiolysis
items.q: What are the issues with redo cardiac surgery?
items.a:
- Re-entry risk: patent LIMA graft or RV behind the sternum.
- Use CT to map re-entry risk. Consider peripheral access or bypass before re-entry in selected high-risk cases.
- External pads, large-bore access, blood and cell salvage ready.
- Longer CPB, more bleeding, higher mortality.

> **Closing point:** Prepare for haemorrhage at re-entry.

items.title: What monitoring is used for a standard cardiac surgical case?
items.sub: Before bypass: assessment, risk, preparation and anxiolysis
items.eyebrow: Before bypass: assessment, risk, preparation and anxiolysis
items.q: What monitoring is used for a standard cardiac surgical case?
items.a:
- ECG with ST analysis, arterial line before induction, CVC (± PAC).
- TOE, NIRS, temperature, urine output.
- ACT, blood gases, glucose and haemoglobin.
- Pacing wires and defibrillator pads.

> **Closing point:** Invasive monitoring before induction.

items.title: Outline the surgical steps of coronary artery bypass grafting.
items.sub: The surgical procedures: what is actually being done
items.eyebrow: The surgical procedures: what is actually being done
items.q: Outline the surgical steps of coronary artery bypass grafting.
items.a:
- Sternotomy, conduit harvest (LIMA, radial, saphenous vein).
- Heparin, cannulation, bypass, cross-clamp and cardioplegia.
- Distal and proximal anastomoses, rewarming and weaning.
- Protamine, haemostasis, pacing wires and chest closure.

> **Closing point:** Off-pump avoids CPB and the clamp.

items.title: What are the haemodynamic goals for coronary artery bypass anaesthesia?
items.sub: The surgical procedures: what is actually being done
items.eyebrow: The surgical procedures: what is actually being done
items.q: What are the haemodynamic goals for coronary artery bypass anaesthesia?
items.a:
- Maintain coronary perfusion pressure.
- Heart rate 60 to 80; avoid tachycardia.
- Avoid hypotension and hypertension; treat ischaemia.
- Continue beta-blocker; withhold ACE inhibitor.

> **Closing point:** Balance oxygen supply and demand.

items.title: How does cardiac displacement during off-pump CABG cause hypotension, and what should you do first?
items.sub: The surgical procedures: what is actually being done
items.eyebrow: The surgical procedures: what is actually being done
items.q: How does cardiac displacement during off-pump CABG cause hypotension, and what should you do first?
items.a:
- Lifting/rotating the heart compresses RV/atria and restricts filling; stabilisers can produce regional ischaemia.
- Look for loss of pulsatility, CVP rise, regional ST or TOE changes and arrhythmia.
- Ask surgeon to **release or reposition** the heart; optimise preload carefully, vasopressor as indicated, stabilise rate/rhythm and oxygenation.
- Persistent collapse or ischaemia requires readiness to convert to CPB.

> **Closing point:** Correct mechanical displacement before giving litres of fluid or escalating inotropes.

items.title: What are the haemodynamic goals in severe aortic stenosis?
items.sub: The surgical procedures: what is actually being done
items.eyebrow: The surgical procedures: what is actually being done
items.q: What are the haemodynamic goals in severe aortic stenosis?
items.a:
- Maintain sinus rhythm and preload.
- Maintain afterload and coronary perfusion; use phenylephrine or noradrenaline.
- Avoid tachycardia and bradycardia.
- Cardiovert AF promptly.

> **Closing point:** A fixed obstruction needs a fixed pressure head.

items.title: What are the anaesthetic considerations for TAVI?
items.sub: The surgical procedures: what is actually being done
items.eyebrow: The surgical procedures: what is actually being done
items.q: What are the anaesthetic considerations for TAVI?
items.a:
- Hybrid theatre with surgical and perfusion back-up.
- Local with sedation or GA; TOE with GA.
- Rapid ventricular pacing during deployment causes hypotension.
- Complications: vascular injury, annular rupture, conduction block, stroke, leak.

> **Closing point:** Plan for conversion to open surgery.

items.title: Compare surgical aortic valve replacement and TAVI.
items.sub: The surgical procedures: what is actually being done
items.eyebrow: The surgical procedures: what is actually being done
items.q: Compare surgical aortic valve replacement and TAVI.
items.a:
- Surgical AVR: younger, low risk, bicuspid, concomitant surgery.
- TAVI: elderly, high risk, transfemoral access.
- TAVI risks: pacemaker, vascular injury, leak, stroke.
- Heart Team decision using STS or EuroSCORE.

> **Closing point:** Selection is a team decision.

items.title: What haemodynamic goals differ between severe mitral regurgitation and mitral stenosis?
items.sub: The surgical procedures: what is actually being done
items.eyebrow: The surgical procedures: what is actually being done
items.q: What haemodynamic goals differ between severe mitral regurgitation and mitral stenosis?
items.a:
- Chronic **MR:** avoid bradycardia and large increases in SVR; maintain forward output and coronary perfusion; high pre-op EF may conceal poor effective forward contractility.
- **MS:** slow–normal HR and sinus rhythm/AV synchrony where possible; avoid fluid overload and rises in PVR due to hypoxaemia, hypercarbia or acidosis.
- After MR repair anticipate **afterload mismatch**, RV failure and SAM/LVOT obstruction.

> **Closing point:** The repair changes LV afterload; postoperative hypotension must be diagnosed by TOE.

items.title: What are the main steps and TOE checks in mitral valve repair or replacement?
items.sub: The surgical procedures: what is actually being done
items.eyebrow: The surgical procedures: what is actually being done
items.q: What are the main steps and TOE checks in mitral valve repair or replacement?
items.a:
- CPB and cross-clamp → left atrial or transseptal access → inspect leaflets/chordae → repair (ring, leaflet/chordal technique) or replacement while preserving subvalvular structures where possible.
- Close atrium, de-air, reperfuse and wean.
- TOE: residual MR, functional MS/mean gradient, LVOT/SAM, prosthetic seating, LV/RV function and de-airing.

> **Closing point:** Correct anatomy is necessary but physiological function must be checked at appropriate loading.

items.title: What did CORONARY and ROOBY show about on-pump versus off-pump CABG?
items.sub: The surgical procedures: what is actually being done
items.eyebrow: The surgical procedures: what is actually being done
items.q: What did CORONARY and ROOBY show about on-pump versus off-pump CABG?
items.a:
> **Evidence:** [BJA Education: CABG Part 1, 2026 corrected proof; full text read via ClinicalKey](https://www-clinicalkey-com-au.ezproxy.anzca.edu.au/#!/content/journal/1-s2.0-S205853492600079X); supplied expanded Set 13 notes.

- **CORONARY (five-year follow-up):** in 4,752 randomised CABG patients, the composite of death, stroke, MI, renal failure or repeat revascularisation was **23.1% off-pump vs 23.6% on-pump**, without a significant difference.
- **ROOBY (five-year follow-up):** in a predominantly male veteran population, death was **15.2% off-pump vs 11.9% on-pump**, favouring on-pump in that setting.
- **Interpretation:** surgeon/centre experience, target anatomy, complete revascularisation and aortic manipulation matter. Off-pump is **not universally better**; trial findings should not be extrapolated uncritically to every centre.

> **Closing point:** Avoid claiming that eliminating CPB always reduces important long-term outcomes.

> **Source:** Expanded Set 13 chapters

items.title: What are the components of a cardiopulmonary bypass circuit?
items.sub: Cardiopulmonary bypass: make the machine understandable
items.eyebrow: Cardiopulmonary bypass: make the machine understandable
items.q: What are the components of a cardiopulmonary bypass circuit?
items.a:
- Venous cannula and reservoir.
- Pump (roller or centrifugal).
- Membrane oxygenator with heat exchanger.
- Arterial filter and return cannula.

> **Closing point:** Blood leaves the right atrium and returns to the aorta.

items.title: Why can normal MAP on bypass coexist with inadequate oxygen delivery?
items.sub: Cardiopulmonary bypass: make the machine understandable
items.eyebrow: Cardiopulmonary bypass: make the machine understandable
items.q: Why can normal MAP on bypass coexist with inadequate oxygen delivery?
items.a:
- Systemic DO₂ = pump blood flow × arterial oxygen content; oxygen content depends mainly on **haemoglobin and arterial saturation**.
- Low pump flow, profound haemodilution, oxygenator malfunction or maldistribution can lower DO₂ despite a normal resistance-driven MAP.
- Check flow index, Hb/Hct, arterial and venous gases, SvO₂, lactate, temperature and NIRS; correct the cause.

> **Closing point:** Pressure is not equivalent to flow or oxygen delivery.

items.title: What are the first actions for low MAP with high arterial-line pressure during CPB?
items.sub: Cardiopulmonary bypass: make the machine understandable
items.eyebrow: Cardiopulmonary bypass: make the machine understandable
items.q: What are the first actions for low MAP with high arterial-line pressure during CPB?
items.a:
- Call a **CPB circuit emergency**; avoid blindly escalating pump pressure.
- Check for clamp, kink, cannula obstruction/malposition or aortic dissection/false lumen.
- Review patient radial/femoral pressures, NIRS, pump flow and circuit pressure; use TOE/epiaortic imaging and surgical assessment.
- Correct obstruction or recannulate while perfusionist maintains safe oxygen delivery.

> **Closing point:** High circuit pressure with poor patient perfusion is a delivery problem.

items.title: How do you recognise and manage oxygenator or sweep-gas failure on CPB?
items.sub: Cardiopulmonary bypass: make the machine understandable
items.eyebrow: Cardiopulmonary bypass: make the machine understandable
items.q: How do you recognise and manage oxygenator or sweep-gas failure on CPB?
items.a:
- Falling post-oxygenator PaO₂ or rising PaCO₂ despite appropriate flow suggests gas exchange failure.
- Confirm gas source, oxygen fraction/blender, sweep-flow tubing, connectors, blood-gas samples and membrane pressure gradient.
- Maintain safe patient perfusion, alert perfusionist/surgeon and prepare oxygenator exchange per local circuit protocol.

> **Closing point:** Separate oxygenator gas failure from low pump flow or arterial obstruction.

items.title: How does aortic atheroma influence aortic cannulation?
items.sub: Cardiopulmonary bypass: make the machine understandable
items.eyebrow: Cardiopulmonary bypass: make the machine understandable
items.q: How does aortic atheroma influence aortic cannulation?
items.a:
- Risk of embolic stroke and dissection.
- Epiaortic ultrasound and TOE grade the atheroma.
- Alternative cannulation: axillary, femoral or innominate.
- No-touch or off-pump techniques.

> **Closing point:** Assess the aorta before clamping.

items.title: How much heparin is given for bypass and how is it monitored?
items.sub: Anticoagulation, blood conservation and protamine
items.eyebrow: Anticoagulation, blood conservation and protamine
items.q: How much heparin is given for bypass and how is it monitored?
items.a:
- 300 to 400 units/kg.
- Confirm the circuit- and assay-specific ACT target before bypass, often around 480 seconds.
- ACT repeated every 20 to 30 minutes.
- Suspect heparin resistance when the expected dose fails to reach the bypass target.

> **Closing point:** Check the ACT before the cannulae are connected.

Sources: BJA Educ 2022

items.title: What are the causes of heparin resistance?
items.sub: Anticoagulation, blood conservation and protamine
items.eyebrow: Anticoagulation, blood conservation and protamine
items.q: What are the causes of heparin resistance?
items.a:
- Antithrombin deficiency, congenital or acquired.
- Preoperative heparin, liver disease, DIC.
- Non-specific heparin binding to platelet factor 4, fibrinogen and factor VIII.
- Andexanet alfa; pseudo-resistance from assay error.

> **Closing point:** Antithrombin or fresh frozen plasma often corrects it.

Sources: Blue Book 2023

items.title: How do you manage heparin-induced thrombocytopenia for cardiac surgery?
items.sub: Anticoagulation, blood conservation and protamine
items.eyebrow: Anticoagulation, blood conservation and protamine
items.q: How do you manage heparin-induced thrombocytopenia for cardiac surgery?
items.a:
- 4T score and antibody test; stop all heparin.
- Delay non-urgent surgery until antibodies clear.
- Urgent: bivalirudin (or argatroban in renal failure); or heparin with an antiplatelet drug.
- LMWH is contraindicated.

> **Closing point:** Type 2 HIT is immune mediated and prothrombotic.

Sources: BJA Educ 2023

items.title: How does protamine reverse heparin and what is the dose?
items.sub: Anticoagulation, blood conservation and protamine
items.eyebrow: Anticoagulation, blood conservation and protamine
items.q: How does protamine reverse heparin and what is the dose?
items.a:
- Cationic protein binds anionic heparin 1:1.
- Titrate to residual heparin or a validated local protocol.
- Onset within 5 minutes, half-life about 7 to 10 minutes.
- Excess protamine has anticoagulant effects.

> **Closing point:** Give slowly.

Sources: Blue Book 2023

items.title: What are the adverse effects of protamine?
items.sub: Anticoagulation, blood conservation and protamine
items.eyebrow: Anticoagulation, blood conservation and protamine
items.q: What are the adverse effects of protamine?
items.a:
- Hypotension from vasodilation.
- Pulmonary hypertension and RV failure (0.6%).
- Anaphylaxis and anaphylactoid reactions (about 0.2%).
- Coagulopathy and heparin rebound.

> **Closing point:** Prior reactions and protamine-containing insulin are relevant when assessing risk.

Sources: BJA Educ 2022

items.title: What is the mechanism of tranexamic acid?
items.sub: Anticoagulation, blood conservation and protamine
items.eyebrow: Anticoagulation, blood conservation and protamine
items.q: What is the mechanism of tranexamic acid?
items.a:
- Lysine analogue that binds plasminogen.
- Blocks plasmin formation and fibrin breakdown.
- Renally cleared; dose-reduce in renal impairment.
- High doses cause seizures.

> **Closing point:** It is antifibrinolytic, not procoagulant.

items.title: What do TRICS III and ATACAS mean for cardiac-surgical blood conservation?
items.sub: Anticoagulation, blood conservation and protamine
items.eyebrow: Anticoagulation, blood conservation and protamine
items.q: What do TRICS III and ATACAS mean for cardiac-surgical blood conservation?
items.a:
> **Evidence:** [2024 EACTS/EACTAIC patient blood management guideline](https://www.eacts.org/clinical-practice-guideline/2024-eacts-eactaic-guidelines-on-patient-blood-management-in-adult-cardiac-surgery-in-collaboration-with-ebcp/) · [2024 EACTS/EACTAIC/EBCP CPB guideline (published 2025)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11826095/); supplied expanded Set 13 notes.

- **TRICS III:** in moderate/high-risk cardiac surgery, a **restrictive RBC threshold around Hb 75 g/L** was **non-inferior** to a liberal strategy for a major composite of death, MI, stroke and new dialysis (11.4% vs 12.5%). It is not a rule for unstable haemorrhage or active ischaemia.
- **ATACAS:** **tranexamic acid** reduced blood-product use and reoperation for bleeding/tamponade, but increased **seizures**; no significant primary composite thrombotic/death benefit. Choose dose using renal function, seizure risk and local protocol.
- Practical application: use a **patient-blood-management programme**, treat surgical bleeding and specific coagulation deficits, and interpret the trial population before changing care.

> **Closing point:** Restrictive transfusion is contextual, and TXA benefits must be weighed against dose-related harm.

> **Source:** Expanded Set 13 chapters

items.title: What is cardioplegia and how is it delivered?
items.sub: Myocardial, cerebral and whole-body protection on bypass
items.eyebrow: Myocardial, cerebral and whole-body protection on bypass
items.q: What is cardioplegia and how is it delivered?
items.a:
- High-potassium solution induces diastolic arrest.
- Cold or warm blood or crystalloid (St Thomas, del Nido).
- Antegrade via the aortic root; retrograde via the coronary sinus.
- Repeated every 20 to 30 minutes.

> **Closing point:** It lowers oxygen demand during the cross-clamp.

Sources: BJA Educ 2026

items.title: What causes myocardial reperfusion injury after aortic cross-clamp removal?
items.sub: Myocardial, cerebral and whole-body protection on bypass
items.eyebrow: Myocardial, cerebral and whole-body protection on bypass
items.q: What causes myocardial reperfusion injury after aortic cross-clamp removal?
items.a:
- Reperfusion of ischaemic myocardium triggers reactive oxygen species, calcium overload, mitochondrial permeability transition, endothelial dysfunction and inflammation.
- Consequences include arrhythmias, transient stunning, microvascular dysfunction and occasionally irreversible damage.
- Reduce risk with adequate cardioplegia, controlled reperfusion and avoiding prolonged ischaemia; ischaemic conditioning has biologic plausibility but inconsistent clinical outcome benefits.

> **Closing point:** Reopening the coronary circulation does not immediately restore normal myocardial function.

items.title: What is the rationale for deep hypothermic circulatory arrest?
items.sub: Myocardial, cerebral and whole-body protection on bypass
items.eyebrow: Myocardial, cerebral and whole-body protection on bypass
items.q: What is the rationale for deep hypothermic circulatory arrest?
items.a:
- Cerebral protection when circulation stops.
- Cerebral metabolic rate falls about 6 to 7% per degree Celsius.
- Gives a bloodless field for arch surgery at 18 to 20 °C.
- Safe time about 30 minutes; selective cerebral perfusion extends it.

> **Closing point:** The aim is brain protection.

Sources: Exam report 2019.2

items.title: What are the consequences of deep hypothermic circulatory arrest?
items.sub: Myocardial, cerebral and whole-body protection on bypass
items.eyebrow: Myocardial, cerebral and whole-body protection on bypass
items.q: What are the consequences of deep hypothermic circulatory arrest?
items.a:
- Neurological injury: stroke, delirium, seizures, cognitive decline.
- Coagulopathy: platelet dysfunction, fibrinolysis.
- Arrhythmias on cooling and rewarming; renal and visceral injury.
- Hyperglycaemia and inflammatory response.

> **Closing point:** Not the same as cardioplegia or ECMO.

Sources: Exam report 2019.2

items.title: What are the problems with rewarming after bypass?
items.sub: Myocardial, cerebral and whole-body protection on bypass
items.eyebrow: Myocardial, cerebral and whole-body protection on bypass
items.q: What are the problems with rewarming after bypass?
items.a:
- Rewarm slowly; outflow temperature at most 37 °C.
- Cerebral hyperthermia and gas emboli.
- After-drop, shivering, vasodilation and bleeding.
- Target nasopharyngeal 36 to 37 °C before separation.

> **Closing point:** Avoid overshooting.

items.title: What are the cardiac effects of hypothermia?
items.sub: Myocardial, cerebral and whole-body protection on bypass
items.eyebrow: Myocardial, cerebral and whole-body protection on bypass
items.q: What are the cardiac effects of hypothermia?
items.a:
- Bradycardia and conduction slowing (J waves).
- VF below about 28 °C.
- Reduced oxygen demand and better protection.
- Arrhythmias on rewarming.

> **Closing point:** Cooling protects but makes the heart unstable.

items.title: Which neurological complications follow cardiac surgery?
items.sub: Myocardial, cerebral and whole-body protection on bypass
items.eyebrow: Myocardial, cerebral and whole-body protection on bypass
items.q: Which neurological complications follow cardiac surgery?
items.a:
- Stroke (1 to 3%) and TIA; delirium and cognitive decline.
- Embolic, hypoperfusion and inflammatory mechanisms.
- Strategies: no-touch aorta, MAP targets, avoid hyperthermia, NIRS.
- Delirium screening and avoidance of benzodiazepines.

> **Closing point:** Aortic manipulation is a key embolic source.

items.title: Compare alpha-stat and pH-stat blood-gas management during hypothermic CPB.
items.sub: Myocardial, cerebral and whole-body protection on bypass
items.eyebrow: Myocardial, cerebral and whole-body protection on bypass
items.q: Compare alpha-stat and pH-stat blood-gas management during hypothermic CPB.
items.a:
> **Evidence:** [2024 EACTS/EACTAIC/EBCP CPB guideline (published 2025)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11826095/) · [Consensus on hypothermia in aortic arch surgery (temperature definitions)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3741830/); supplied expanded Set 13 notes.

- **Alpha-stat:** interpret and target blood-gas values as measured at **37°C** without temperature correction. During cooling, actual in-vivo PaCO₂ falls and pH rises; cerebral autoregulation and protein charge regulation tend to be preserved. Common in **adult CPB**.
- **pH-stat:** add CO₂ during cooling so **temperature-corrected** pH ≈ 7.40 and PaCO₂ ≈ 40 mmHg. Cerebral vasodilation can improve cooling uniformity but may increase embolic delivery and blunt autoregulation.
- pH-stat has a role in selected **paediatric/deep-cooling** protocols; neither is universally superior for every operation.

> **Closing point:** The difference is which temperature the blood gas is interpreted at—and how CO₂ changes cerebral flow.

> **Source:** Expanded Set 13 chapters

items.title: List the prerequisites for separation from cardiopulmonary bypass.
items.sub: Separation from cardiopulmonary bypass: the high-yield chapter
items.eyebrow: Separation from cardiopulmonary bypass: the high-yield chapter
items.q: List the prerequisites for separation from cardiopulmonary bypass.
items.a:
- Stable rhythm and rate, effective ejection, adequate filling and an individualised arterial pressure.
- Lungs re-expanded and ventilating with FiO2 1.0.
- Temperature above 36 °C; acid-base, K, calcium and Hb corrected; coagulation addressed.
- Adequate anaesthesia; pacing wires, defibrillator and drugs ready.

> **Closing point:** Heart, lungs, metabolic state, equipment.

items.title: What are the causes of hypotension immediately after separation from bypass?
items.sub: Separation from cardiopulmonary bypass: the high-yield chapter
items.eyebrow: Separation from cardiopulmonary bypass: the high-yield chapter
items.q: What are the causes of hypotension immediately after separation from bypass?
items.a:
- Pump failure: LV stunning or ischaemia, RV failure, valve problem.
- Rate and rhythm disturbance, heart block.
- Preload: hypovolaemia, bleeding, tamponade, tension pneumothorax.
- Afterload: vasoplegia, protamine reaction, anaphylaxis.

> **Closing point:** Use TOE to tell them apart.

items.title: What are the first steps when a patient fails to wean from bypass?
items.sub: Separation from cardiopulmonary bypass: the high-yield chapter
items.eyebrow: Separation from cardiopulmonary bypass: the high-yield chapter
items.q: What are the first steps when a patient fails to wean from bypass?
items.a:
- Stay on bypass and keep the heart empty and perfused.
- Check rate, rhythm, electrolytes, temperature, ventilation and anaesthesia.
- TOE for LV, RV, valve, air and tamponade; surgeon checks grafts.
- Optimise preload, contractility and afterload; escalate to IABP or ECMO.

> **Closing point:** Diagnose before escalating inotropes.

items.title: How do you recognise and treat right ventricular failure after bypass?
items.sub: Separation from cardiopulmonary bypass: the high-yield chapter
items.eyebrow: Separation from cardiopulmonary bypass: the high-yield chapter
items.q: How do you recognise and treat right ventricular failure after bypass?
items.a:
- Rising CVP, poor forward flow, a dilated or poorly contracting RV and septal flattening on TOE.
- Causes: right coronary air, protamine, pulmonary hypertension, poor protection.
- Pace, vasopressin for perfusion, dobutamine or adrenaline, inhaled nitric oxide.
- Return to CPB if unstable. Consider RVAD or VA-ECMO for refractory failure.

> **Closing point:** Protect RV coronary perfusion and lower PVR.

Sources: Blue Book 2021

items.title: What is vasoplegia after bypass and how is it treated?
items.sub: Separation from cardiopulmonary bypass: the high-yield chapter
items.eyebrow: Separation from cardiopulmonary bypass: the high-yield chapter
items.q: What is vasoplegia after bypass and how is it treated?
items.a:
- Low SVR with a good or high cardiac output after CPB.
- Causes: inflammatory response, nitric oxide, vasopressin deficiency, ACE inhibitors.
- Start titrated noradrenaline. Add vasopressin when appropriate and discuss rescue agents for refractory shock.
- Exclude protamine reaction and hypovolaemia.

> **Closing point:** A multimodal vasopressor approach works best.

Sources: BJA Education 2025

items.title: How do you set up epicardial pacing for complete heart block?
items.sub: Separation from cardiopulmonary bypass: the high-yield chapter
items.eyebrow: Separation from cardiopulmonary bypass: the high-yield chapter
items.q: How do you set up epicardial pacing for complete heart block?
items.a:
- DDD when both atrial/ventricular wires function and atrial rhythm is sinus; VVI if AF or ventricular-only wires.
- Individualise rate and AV delay for pressure/output; emergency asynchronous DOO/VOO is for the supervised theatre or arrest setting, not routine unattended ICU pacing.
- Output at 2 to 3 times the capture threshold; sensitivity with a safety margin.
- Confirm mechanical capture on the arterial trace.

> **Closing point:** Justify the rate and mode for the patient.

Sources: Exam report 2026.1

items.title: How do you troubleshoot intermittent failure to capture in a pacing-dependent patient?
items.sub: Separation from cardiopulmonary bypass: the high-yield chapter
items.eyebrow: Separation from cardiopulmonary bypass: the high-yield chapter
items.q: How do you troubleshoot intermittent failure to capture in a pacing-dependent patient?
items.a:
- Check the patient: haemodynamics, electrolytes, acidosis, ischaemia, drugs.
- Check temporary epicardial wires and all connections/cables; change cables or generator as appropriate.
- Check the generator: battery, output, over-sensing; use asynchronous mode.
- Alternatives: transcutaneous pads, transvenous wire, chronotropes, permanent pacemaker.

> **Closing point:** Patient, lead, generator.

Sources: Exam report 2026.1

items.title: What are the effects of protamine on the right ventricle?
items.sub: Separation from cardiopulmonary bypass: the high-yield chapter
items.eyebrow: Separation from cardiopulmonary bypass: the high-yield chapter
items.q: What are the effects of protamine on the right ventricle?
items.a:
- Pulmonary vasoconstriction (thromboxane) in the first 3 to 5 minutes.
- Raised PA pressure and acute RV failure with hypotension.
- Treat: stop protamine, inhaled nitric oxide or prostacyclin, vasopressor.
- Return to bypass if refractory.

> **Closing point:** Slow administration reduces the risk.

Sources: BJA Educ 2022

items.title: What TOE findings would you look for when weaning from bypass?
items.sub: Separation from cardiopulmonary bypass: the high-yield chapter
items.eyebrow: Separation from cardiopulmonary bypass: the high-yield chapter
items.q: What TOE findings would you look for when weaning from bypass?
items.a:
- LV function and regional wall motion, filling and outflow obstruction.
- RV size and function (TAPSE), septal position, tricuspid regurgitation.
- Valve function and paravalvular leak; air in the chambers.
- Pericardial collection and aortic integrity.

> **Closing point:** TOE is the main tool for the difficult wean.

items.title: Why can adrenaline worsen hypotension after mitral repair?
items.sub: Separation from cardiopulmonary bypass: the high-yield chapter
items.eyebrow: Separation from cardiopulmonary bypass: the high-yield chapter
items.q: Why can adrenaline worsen hypotension after mitral repair?
items.a:
- Hyperdynamic underfilled LV and changed mitral geometry can cause **SAM and dynamic LVOT obstruction** with secondary MR.
- Inotropy, tachycardia, reduced preload and low afterload worsen the gradient.
- TOE shows small LV, SAM and late-peaking LVOT gradient.
- Stop/limit inotrope, restore preload carefully, raise afterload, consider esmolol and surgical revision if refractory.

> **Closing point:** Distinguish obstruction from true low contractility before choosing an inotrope.

items.title: What does a new regional wall-motion abnormality immediately after CABG suggest?
items.sub: Separation from cardiopulmonary bypass: the high-yield chapter
items.eyebrow: Separation from cardiopulmonary bypass: the high-yield chapter
items.q: What does a new regional wall-motion abnormality immediately after CABG suggest?
items.a:
- New graft-territory RWMA may indicate graft kink/occlusion/spasm, coronary air, anastomotic error or inadequate myocardial protection.
- Correlate with ST changes, graft-flow assessment, pressures and TOE; restore coronary perfusion and ask surgeon to inspect/revise graft if needed.
- Avoid treating severe ischaemia solely by catecholamine escalation.

> **Closing point:** New regional dysfunction is an ischaemia/surgical diagnosis until excluded.

items.title: What is internal defibrillation?
items.sub: Separation from cardiopulmonary bypass: the high-yield chapter
items.eyebrow: Separation from cardiopulmonary bypass: the high-yield chapter
items.q: What is internal defibrillation?
items.a:
- Sterile paddles applied directly to the heart with an open chest.
- 10 to 20 J biphasic.
- Safe energy is lower than external because impedance is bypassed.
- Used in theatre or after resternotomy.

> **Closing point:** Open chest, low energy.

items.title: What is the role of cardioversion for intraoperative arrhythmias?
items.sub: Separation from cardiopulmonary bypass: the high-yield chapter
items.eyebrow: Separation from cardiopulmonary bypass: the high-yield chapter
items.q: What is the role of cardioversion for intraoperative arrhythmias?
items.a:
- For haemodynamically significant organised tachyarrhythmia, synchronised cardioversion is appropriate; VF/pulseless VT requires unsynchronised defibrillation and resuscitation.
- Treat oxygenation, perfusion, electrolyte/ischaemic and surgical triggers in parallel, because recurrence is likely if the cause persists.
- An already anaesthetised patient still needs adequate depth, monitoring and a safe shock/pacing plan.
- Do not shock sinus tachycardia as a compensatory automatic rhythm; stable arrhythmias require diagnosis and considered drug/rhythm treatment rather than a universal electrical-first rule.

items.title: What makes cardioversion safe?
items.sub: Separation from cardiopulmonary bypass: the high-yield chapter
items.eyebrow: Separation from cardiopulmonary bypass: the high-yield chapter
items.q: What makes cardioversion safe?
items.a:
- For elective AF >24 hours/uncertain onset, ESC 2024 requires ≥3 weeks effective anticoagulation or TOE exclusion of thrombus with periprocedural anticoagulation; most require ≥4 weeks afterwards.
- Long-term therapy follows stroke/valve risk despite successful conversion; verify adherence and device/valve-specific eligibility.
- Assess airway/aspiration, cardiac disease, electrolytes and digoxin toxicity; consent and provide short monitored anaesthesia with capnography and rescue equipment.
- Confirm R-wave synchronisation and oxygen/fire safety; anticipate hypotension, brady/asystole and VF. Unstable AF needs urgent cardioversion without delaying for elective anticoagulation.

items.title: How does an intra-aortic balloon pump work?
items.sub: Mechanical circulatory support: IABP and ventricular assist devices
items.eyebrow: Mechanical circulatory support: IABP and ventricular assist devices
items.q: How does an intra-aortic balloon pump work?
items.a:
- Balloon in the descending aorta inflates in diastole and deflates before systole.
- Augments diastolic pressure and coronary flow; lowers afterload and oxygen demand.
- Provides modest assisted output; needs native cardiac activity, and arterial pressure triggering may work in an irregular rhythm.
- Triggered by ECG or arterial waveform.

> **Closing point:** Diastolic augmentation and systolic unloading.

items.title: List the indications for an IABP.
items.sub: Mechanical circulatory support: IABP and ventricular assist devices
items.eyebrow: Mechanical circulatory support: IABP and ventricular assist devices
items.q: List the indications for an IABP.
items.a:
- Cardiogenic shock or severe cardiac failure awaiting recovery or treatment.
- Failure to wean from bypass; post-infarction.
- Mechanical complications: acute MR, VSD.
- High-risk revascularisation; LV decompression on VA-ECMO.

> **Closing point:** A bridge to recovery or definitive treatment.

Sources: Exam report 2008.2

items.title: List the contraindications to an IABP.
items.sub: Mechanical circulatory support: IABP and ventricular assist devices
items.eyebrow: Mechanical circulatory support: IABP and ventricular assist devices
items.q: List the contraindications to an IABP.
items.a:
- Clinically important aortic regurgitation (assess severity; balloon inflation can exacerbate regurgitation).
- Aortic dissection or aneurysm.
- Severe aorto-iliac or peripheral vascular disease.
- Relative: coagulopathy, local sepsis.

> **Closing point:** Even mild regurgitation can worsen.

Sources: Exam report 2008.2

items.title: How is IABP timing set and what are the errors?
items.sub: Mechanical circulatory support: IABP and ventricular assist devices
items.eyebrow: Mechanical circulatory support: IABP and ventricular assist devices
items.q: How is IABP timing set and what are the errors?
items.a:
- Inflate at the dicrotic notch; deflate just before systole.
- Early inflation closes the aortic valve early; late inflation reduces augmentation.
- Early deflation loses unloading; late deflation increases afterload.
- Check reliable ECG or arterial pressure triggering and position distal to the left subclavian artery.

> **Closing point:** Check the waveform on a 1:2 ratio.

items.title: What are the complications of an IABP?
items.sub: Mechanical circulatory support: IABP and ventricular assist devices
items.eyebrow: Mechanical circulatory support: IABP and ventricular assist devices
items.q: What are the complications of an IABP?
items.a:
- Limb ischaemia (commonest), bleeding and retroperitoneal haematoma.
- Thrombocytopenia and haemolysis.
- Aortic dissection, stroke or embolism, visceral or left arm malperfusion.
- Infection and balloon rupture.

> **Closing point:** Check limb perfusion every hour.

items.title: What types of durable LVAD exist and how do they work?
items.sub: Mechanical circulatory support: IABP and ventricular assist devices
items.eyebrow: Mechanical circulatory support: IABP and ventricular assist devices
items.q: What types of durable LVAD exist and how do they work?
items.a:
- Continuous-flow pumps: axial (HeartMate II) or centrifugal (HeartMate 3, HVAD).
- Drain the LV apex and return blood to the ascending aorta via a driveline.
- Little or no pulse; preload and afterload dependent.
- Indications: bridge to transplant or candidacy, recovery, destination therapy.

> **Closing point:** Pulse and standard monitoring are unreliable.

Sources: Blue Book 2021

items.title: What are the anaesthetic principles for a patient with an LVAD?
items.sub: Mechanical circulatory support: IABP and ventricular assist devices
items.eyebrow: Mechanical circulatory support: IABP and ventricular assist devices
items.q: What are the anaesthetic principles for a patient with an LVAD?
items.a:
- Multidisciplinary plan; VAD specialist present; spare batteries.
- Arterial line, NIRS, TOE; pulse oximetry may be unreliable.
- Maintain preload and RV function, limit PVR and excessive afterload; agree an individual MAP goal and consider neuraxial only with safe anticoagulation management.
- HeartMate 3 may use VKA without aspirin (ARIES-HM3); interrupt/bridge/reverse anticoagulation only under a device- and surgery-specific VAD-team plan.

> **Closing point:** Protect the right ventricle.

Sources: Blue Book 2021

items.title: What are the complications of an LVAD?
items.sub: Mechanical circulatory support: IABP and ventricular assist devices
items.eyebrow: Mechanical circulatory support: IABP and ventricular assist devices
items.q: What are the complications of an LVAD?
items.a:
- Bleeding (gastrointestinal, intracranial) and infection of the driveline.
- Stroke, pump thrombosis.
- Right heart failure and arrhythmia.
- Aortic regurgitation and device malfunction.

> **Closing point:** Bleeding and infection dominate.

Sources: Blue Book 2021

items.title: Compare IABP, Impella and VA-ECMO.
items.sub: Mechanical circulatory support: IABP and ventricular assist devices
items.eyebrow: Mechanical circulatory support: IABP and ventricular assist devices
items.q: Compare IABP, Impella and VA-ECMO.
items.a:
- IABP: modest augmentation (0.8 L/min), needs rhythm and contractility.
- Impella: 2.5 to 5 L/min LV unloading; haemolysis and vascular complications.
- VA-ECMO: full cardiorespiratory support up to 7 L/min but increases LV afterload.
- Use the least support that achieves the goal.

> **Closing point:** More support brings more complications.

Sources: BJA Educ 2023

items.title: How do you recognise cardiac arrest in a continuous-flow LVAD patient?
items.sub: Mechanical circulatory support: IABP and ventricular assist devices
items.eyebrow: Mechanical circulatory support: IABP and ventricular assist devices
items.q: How do you recognise cardiac arrest in a continuous-flow LVAD patient?
items.a:
- Absence of a palpable pulse alone is not arrest. Assess responsiveness, breathing, colour/capillary refill, MAP, ETCO2 and device function.
- If perfusion is inadequate, start appropriate resuscitation including compressions while another rescuer checks power, controller, driveline and alarms.
- Contact the VAD centre, treat arrhythmia and reversible causes and use echo where available without delaying support.
- Preserved perfusion despite an abnormal rhythm requires urgent management but does not automatically need compressions; AHA 2025 emphasises the perfusion distinction.

items.title: What changed in HeartMate 3 antithrombotic teaching after ARIES-HM3?
items.sub: Mechanical circulatory support: IABP and ventricular assist devices
items.eyebrow: Mechanical circulatory support: IABP and ventricular assist devices
items.q: What changed in HeartMate 3 antithrombotic teaching after ARIES-HM3?
items.a:
- In HM3 patients on VKA, aspirin avoidance was non-inferior for the trial’s haemocompatibility endpoint and reduced nonsurgical bleeding.
- Do not teach aspirin as mandatory for every HM3 recipient solely because of the pump.
- Verify other vascular indications and the device-centre regimen; VKA/INR targets remain individualised, commonly 2–3 for HM3.
- This does not establish routine DOAC substitution or automatic avoidance of bridging/reversal; surgery decisions balance device, thrombosis and bleeding risk.
