items.title: What are the indications for VV ECMO?
items.sub: ECMO and extracorporeal support beyond conventional cardiac bypass
items.eyebrow: ECMO and extracorporeal support beyond conventional cardiac bypass
items.q: What are the indications for VV ECMO?
items.a:
- Reversible respiratory failure with predicted mortality above 50%.
- PaO2/FiO2 below 150 on FiO2 0.9 and a high Murray score.
- Uncompensated hypercapnia, graft failure, severe asthma.
- Referral to an ECMO centre (CESAR, EOLIA).

> **Closing point:** VV supports gas exchange, VA supports circulation.

Sources: Blue Book 2017

items.title: Compare VV and VA ECMO.
items.sub: ECMO and extracorporeal support beyond conventional cardiac bypass
items.eyebrow: ECMO and extracorporeal support beyond conventional cardiac bypass
items.q: Compare VV and VA ECMO.
items.a:
- VV: drains the vena cava, returns to the right atrium; respiratory support only.
- VA: drains venous blood, returns to an artery; supports circulation and oxygenation.
- VA risks: increased LV afterload, differential hypoxia, limb ischaemia.
- Both need anticoagulation.

> **Closing point:** Choose by whether the heart needs support.

Sources: Blue Book 2017

items.title: What are the complications of ECMO?
items.sub: ECMO and extracorporeal support beyond conventional cardiac bypass
items.eyebrow: ECMO and extracorporeal support beyond conventional cardiac bypass
items.q: What are the complications of ECMO?
items.a:
- Bleeding and intracranial haemorrhage.
- Circuit clotting, haemolysis, air embolism.
- Limb ischaemia (VA), infection, renal injury.
- Harlequin syndrome in peripheral VA ECMO.

> **Closing point:** Intracranial haemorrhage is the most devastating.

Sources: Blue Book 2017

items.title: What does low effective ECMO blood flow do, and what does increasing sweep do?
items.sub: ECMO and extracorporeal support beyond conventional cardiac bypass
items.eyebrow: ECMO and extracorporeal support beyond conventional cardiac bypass
items.q: What does low effective ECMO blood flow do, and what does increasing sweep do?
items.a:
Oxygenation depends on effective circuit blood flow relative to cardiac output, recirculation, haemoglobin, oxygenator function and the native lungs. Sweep primarily controls CO₂ clearance. Check gas oxygen fraction, cannula position, actual flow and pre/post-membrane gases. Assess oxygen delivery alongside arterial saturation.

**Sources:** [BJA Education VV ECMO physiology (2026)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2058534926000296)

items.title: Which non-cardiac surgeries may need bypass or ECMO support?
items.sub: ECMO and extracorporeal support beyond conventional cardiac bypass
items.eyebrow: ECMO and extracorporeal support beyond conventional cardiac bypass
items.q: Which non-cardiac surgeries may need bypass or ECMO support?
items.a:
- Tumour with caval or atrial extension.
- Critical airway or tracheal surgery; lung transplant.
- Massive pulmonary embolism; rewarming after severe hypothermia.
- Cardiac arrest (E-CPR).

> **Closing point:** A plan for cannulation and anticoagulation is needed.

Sources: Blue Book 2017

items.title: Explain VV versus V-V, VV-V, V-AV and dual-lumen nomenclature.
items.sub: ECMO and extracorporeal support beyond conventional cardiac bypass
items.eyebrow: ECMO and extracorporeal support beyond conventional cardiac bypass
items.q: Explain VV versus V-V, VV-V, V-AV and dual-lumen nomenclature.
items.a:
- Mode describes support: VV gas exchange; VA direct circulatory/respiratory support.
- Configuration uses a hyphen at the membrane lung: drainage left, return right. V-V has one venous drainage and one venous return cannula.
- VV-V has two venous drainage cannulae and one return; V-AV returns to arterial and venous sites, for selected combined/upper-body oxygenation problems.
- (dl)V-V uses a dual-lumen cannula; state actual sites, tip/jet position and purpose as well as letters.

items.title: How is VV ECMO weaned and how does this differ from VA ECMO?
items.sub: ECMO and extracorporeal support beyond conventional cardiac bypass
items.eyebrow: ECMO and extracorporeal support beyond conventional cardiac bypass
items.q: How is VV ECMO weaned and how does this differ from VA ECMO?
items.a:
- Demonstrate recovering lung function with acceptable work of breathing, gases and haemodynamics on safe ventilator support.
- Reduce sweep/delivered gas oxygen and perform a supervised off-sweep assessment according to centre protocol while maintaining adequate circuit blood flow to avoid thrombosis.
- Do not assume reducing VV pump flow is the same as testing native cardiac recovery on VA support. VA weaning uses controlled flow reduction with echo and haemodynamic assessment.
- Decannulate with an anticoagulation, haemostasis, vascular and respiratory rescue plan; failure prompts reassessment rather than forcing a time target.

items.title: What are the common causes of low cardiac output after cardiac surgery?
items.sub: Immediate cardiac surgical ICU: the patient after bypass
items.eyebrow: Immediate cardiac surgical ICU: the patient after bypass
items.q: What are the common causes of low cardiac output after cardiac surgery?
items.a:
- Myocardial stunning or ischaemia from graft failure.
- Tamponade, hypovolaemia and bleeding.
- RV failure, arrhythmia and heart block.
- Vasoplegia, tension pneumothorax, valve dysfunction.

> **Closing point:** TOE and a PA catheter help sort the cause.

items.title: How do you recognise and treat tamponade after cardiac surgery?
items.sub: Immediate cardiac surgical ICU: the patient after bypass
items.eyebrow: Immediate cardiac surgical ICU: the patient after bypass
items.q: How do you recognise and treat tamponade after cardiac surgery?
items.a:
- Falling drain output, rising CVP, narrow pulse pressure, hypotension.
- Echo (TOE) shows localised clot; drains may be blocked.
- Emergency resternotomy; drainage.
- In arrest, resternotomy within 5 minutes.

> **Closing point:** Consider tamponade in any low output state.

items.title: Why can stopped chest drains be more worrying than heavy drainage after CABG?
items.sub: Immediate cardiac surgical ICU: the patient after bypass
items.eyebrow: Immediate cardiac surgical ICU: the patient after bypass
items.q: Why can stopped chest drains be more worrying than heavy drainage after CABG?
items.a:
- Sudden drain cessation with shock may reflect a blocked drain and **retained localised haematoma/tamponade**.
- Rising filling pressure, low output and often a deceptively small or atypical effusion on TTE; use TOE if unstable.
- Call surgeon early, support circulation and arrange urgent surgical decompression; do not wait for a classic Beck triad.

> **Closing point:** Little blood in the bottle does not mean little blood in the chest.

items.title: How is bleeding managed after cardiac surgery?
items.sub: Immediate cardiac surgical ICU: the patient after bypass
items.eyebrow: Immediate cardiac surgical ICU: the patient after bypass
items.q: How is bleeding managed after cardiac surgery?
items.a:
- Separate surgical from coagulopathic bleeding.
- Restore temperature, calcium and pH; check ACT and viscoelastic tests.
- Targeted platelets, fibrinogen, PCC and TXA (below 100 mg/kg).
- Return to theatre early.

> **Closing point:** Resternotomy carries a mortality of about 15%.

Sources: BJA Educ 2021

items.title: What is the incidence and treatment of AF after cardiac surgery?
items.sub: Immediate cardiac surgical ICU: the patient after bypass
items.eyebrow: Immediate cardiac surgical ICU: the patient after bypass
items.q: What is the incidence and treatment of AF after cardiac surgery?
items.a:
- About 30%, peaking on days 2 to 3.
- Correct K and Mg; beta-blocker or amiodarone.
- Synchronised cardioversion if unstable.
- Anticoagulation by CHA2DS2-VASc and bleeding risk.

> **Closing point:** Check electrolytes first.

items.title: What is the risk of acute kidney injury after cardiac surgery?
items.sub: Immediate cardiac surgical ICU: the patient after bypass
items.eyebrow: Immediate cardiac surgical ICU: the patient after bypass
items.q: What is the risk of acute kidney injury after cardiac surgery?
items.a:
- Up to 30%; 2 to 5% need renal replacement.
- Mechanisms: ischaemia–reperfusion, haemolysis, inflammation.
- Risk factors: CKD, diabetes, low EF, long CPB.
- Prevention: avoid hypotension and nephrotoxins; KDIGO bundle.

> **Closing point:** Prevention is more effective than drug therapy.

Sources: BJA Educ 2025

items.title: What changes in the arrest algorithm after cardiac surgery?
items.sub: Immediate cardiac surgical ICU: the patient after bypass
items.eyebrow: Immediate cardiac surgical ICU: the patient after bypass
items.q: What changes in the arrest algorithm after cardiac surgery?
items.a:
- ANZCOR 11.10 (2026)/CALS-ANZ: up to three promptly stacked shocks for witnessed monitored VF/pulseless VT; emergency DOO pacing for severe bradycardia/asystole with epicardial wires.
- Withhold compressions for up to 60 seconds only while delivering indicated immediate rhythm interventions. If circulation does not return, start compressions and continue while preparing to reopen.
- Aim for skilled emergency resternotomy within five minutes; avoid routine indiscriminate adrenaline boluses during the initial cause-directed actions.

> **Closing point:** Reversible causes include tamponade and bleeding.

In paced PEA, briefly pause pacing to exclude hidden VF.

items.title: Which factors influence the duration of ventilation after cardiac surgery?
items.sub: Fast-track cardiac surgery and postoperative ventilation
items.eyebrow: Fast-track cardiac surgery and postoperative ventilation
items.q: Which factors influence the duration of ventilation after cardiac surgery?
items.a:
- Patient: age, COPD, obesity, poor LV function, renal disease.
- Surgical: emergency, redo, long CPB, bleeding.
- Anaesthetic: long-acting opioids, hypothermia, residual block.
- Postoperative: instability, lung injury, AKI, delirium.

> **Closing point:** Fast-track suits low-risk patients only.

items.title: What is fast-track cardiac anaesthesia?
items.sub: Fast-track cardiac surgery and postoperative ventilation
items.eyebrow: Fast-track cardiac surgery and postoperative ventilation
items.q: What is fast-track cardiac anaesthesia?
items.a:
- Early extubation within about 6 hours.
- Short-acting drugs and multimodal opioid-sparing analgesia.
- Normothermia, minimal bleeding, haemodynamic stability.
- Now part of enhanced recovery (ERAS Cardiac) with early mobilisation.

> **Closing point:** Do not extubate an unstable or bleeding patient to meet a target.

Sources: BJA Educ 2021

items.title: What are the major complications of percutaneous coronary intervention?
items.sub: Anaesthesia for interventional cardiology: the cath lab and its emergencies
items.eyebrow: Anaesthesia for interventional cardiology: the cath lab and its emergencies
items.q: What are the major complications of percutaneous coronary intervention?
items.a:
- Coronary perforation and tamponade.
- Vessel closure, no-reflow and infarction.
- Arrhythmia, access-site bleeding and retroperitoneal haematoma.
- Contrast reaction, AKI and stroke.

> **Closing point:** Know them before the call comes.

items.title: How do you manage coronary perforation?
items.sub: Anaesthesia for interventional cardiology: the cath lab and its emergencies
items.eyebrow: Anaesthesia for interventional cardiology: the cath lab and its emergencies
items.q: How do you manage coronary perforation?
items.a:
- Reverse heparin with protamine.
- Balloon tamponade, covered stent.
- Pericardiocentesis for tamponade.
- Surgical repair if refractory.

> **Closing point:** Call the surgeon early.

items.title: What are the complications of TAVI?
items.sub: Anaesthesia for interventional cardiology: the cath lab and its emergencies
items.eyebrow: Anaesthesia for interventional cardiology: the cath lab and its emergencies
items.q: What are the complications of TAVI?
items.a:
- Vascular injury, annular rupture, coronary obstruction.
- Aortic dissection, valve embolisation, paravalvular leak.
- Conduction block needing a pacemaker.
- Stroke and tamponade.

> **Closing point:** Surgical standby is essential.

items.title: After TAVI deployment there is sudden hypotension and new ST elevation. What are your first differentials?
items.sub: Anaesthesia for interventional cardiology: the cath lab and its emergencies
items.eyebrow: Anaesthesia for interventional cardiology: the cath lab and its emergencies
items.q: After TAVI deployment there is sudden hypotension and new ST elevation. What are your first differentials?
items.a:
- **Coronary ostial obstruction** by displaced leaflet/calcification; also annular rupture/tamponade, severe AR, valve embolisation or complete heart block.
- Call for angiography/TOE, assess valve function/pericardium, prepare coronary rescue and pacing/defibrillation, and escalate to surgery/MCS if required.

> **Closing point:** Match collapse mechanism to the structural intervention.

items.title: What are the complications of AF ablation?
items.sub: Anaesthesia for interventional cardiology: the cath lab and its emergencies
items.eyebrow: Anaesthesia for interventional cardiology: the cath lab and its emergencies
items.q: What are the complications of AF ablation?
items.a:
- Tamponade (about 1%).
- Stroke or air embolism.
- Atrio-oesophageal fistula (delayed).
- Phrenic nerve injury and pulmonary vein stenosis.

> **Closing point:** About 2% major complications.

Sources: Blue Book 2021

items.title: What are the early and delayed life-threatening complications of AF ablation?
items.sub: Anaesthesia for interventional cardiology: the cath lab and its emergencies
items.eyebrow: Anaesthesia for interventional cardiology: the cath lab and its emergencies
items.q: What are the early and delayed life-threatening complications of AF ablation?
items.a:
- Early: perforation/tamponade, air or thromboembolism/stroke, vascular bleeding, arrhythmia and phrenic nerve injury.
- Delayed: atrio-oesophageal fistula, often with fever, neurological signs or sepsis weeks later.
- Suspected fistula needs emergency specialist imaging and surgery; **avoid oesophageal instrumentation**.

> **Closing point:** A delayed fever/stroke after AF ablation is not simply infection until fistula is excluded.

items.title: Why is the catheter laboratory a high-risk location for anaesthesia?
items.sub: Anaesthesia for interventional cardiology: the cath lab and its emergencies
items.eyebrow: Anaesthesia for interventional cardiology: the cath lab and its emergencies
items.q: Why is the catheter laboratory a high-risk location for anaesthesia?
items.a:
- Remote site with limited access and radiation.
- Anticoagulation and antiplatelet therapy.
- Unfamiliar team and equipment.
- Need for surgical and perfusion back-up.

> **Closing point:** Plan for crisis before the case starts.

items.title: What is rapid ventricular pacing in TAVI?
items.sub: Anaesthesia for interventional cardiology: the cath lab and its emergencies
items.eyebrow: Anaesthesia for interventional cardiology: the cath lab and its emergencies
items.q: What is rapid ventricular pacing in TAVI?
items.a:
- Rapid pacing transiently reduces forward output during selected valvuloplasty/deployment steps; often 180–220/min for balloon-expandable procedures.
- Rate/duration depend on device and tolerance; not every valve step needs the same manoeuvre.
- Confirm capture, communicate start/stop, prepare vasopressors and assess rhythm/perfusion recovery.
- Persistent collapse needs immediate assessment for coronary obstruction, severe AR, tamponade or vascular bleeding.

Source: BJA Educ 2021

items.title: Why is the donor right ventricle vulnerable immediately after heart transplantation?
items.sub: Heart transplantation: the operation and the patient with a previous graft
items.eyebrow: Heart transplantation: the operation and the patient with a previous graft
items.q: Why is the donor right ventricle vulnerable immediately after heart transplantation?
items.a:
- Donor RV is adapted to low PVR and may face the recipient's elevated PVR, plus ischaemia–reperfusion injury and graft dysfunction.
- Avoid hypoxaemia, hypercarbia, acidosis and excessive PEEP; preserve coronary perfusion and optimise preload judiciously.
- Use inotrope and inhaled pulmonary vasodilator as indicated; escalate to mechanical support if refractory.

> **Closing point:** Donor RV failure is a leading mechanism of failed transplant-graft separation.

items.title: What changes when a patient with a previous heart transplant requires non-cardiac anaesthesia?
items.sub: Heart transplantation: the operation and the patient with a previous graft
items.eyebrow: Heart transplantation: the operation and the patient with a previous graft
items.q: What changes when a patient with a previous heart transplant requires non-cardiac anaesthesia?
items.a:
- Denervation causes attenuated baroreflex tachycardia; assess preload/haemodynamics rather than HR alone.
- Direct-acting vasoactives and pacing are reliable rescue choices; atropine and indirect agents may be less effective.
- Screen for graft vasculopathy/rejection, impaired function, infection, renal dysfunction and immunosuppression interactions; continue immunosuppressants.
- Pneumoperitoneum and head-up positioning may reduce venous return.

> **Closing point:** Think graft function + denervation + immunosuppression + procedural physiology.

items.title: 1. Redo cardiac surgery
items.q: Outline the specific anaesthetic and surgical issues associated with redo cardiac surgery.
items.a:
## Why redo surgery is high risk

Adhesions between the sternum and heart/grafts cause a risk of **catastrophic haemorrhage on resternotomy** (RV, aorta, vein grafts, and a patent LIMA graft); longer operating and bypass times; more coagulopathy; and patients are older and sicker. Operative mortality is higher than first-time surgery.

## Preoperative

- **CT of the chest** to show the relationship between the sternum, RV, aorta and grafts; plan peripheral cannulation (femoral or axillary) and **bypass before sternotomy** if the heart or grafts lie directly beneath the sternum.
- Assess ventricular function, graft status and comorbidity; antiplatelet and anticoagulant management.
- **Two large-bore IV lines, arterial line and defibrillator pads on** before sternotomy; cross-matched blood available; perfusionist ready with the circuit primed.
- Cell salvage.

## Intraoperative

**Re-entry planning starts before anaesthetic induction.** Review prior operation notes for patent internal mammary and vein graft courses; an adherent RV or ascending aorta immediately behind the sternum creates a potential exsanguinating injury. CT helps identify structures at risk and informs whether femoral/axillary cannulation should precede sternotomy. Agree a stop/rescue phrase with the surgeon and perfusionist, obtain blood and cell salvage, and confirm how rapid CPB would be instituted if the heart or great vessel is torn. If a patent LIMA–LAD graft remains patent across the operative field, preserve its flow and plan myocardial protection that recognises persistent regional perfusion despite aortic clamping. Following re-entry, expect prolonged CPB, platelet dysfunction and higher organ injury risk.

- Oscillating saw resternotomy with pauses, and surgeon-led dissection; ventilation held at apnoea during sternal division.
- If injury occurs: **immediate pressure**, urgent institution of bypass via femoral vessels, and volume resuscitation from the pump.
- Plan for **longer procedures and bypass times**, anticoagulation to the circuit-specific ACT target, cardioprotection for patent grafts (cross-clamp avoided when possible), and managing the RV.

## Haemostasis

Higher bleeding risk from dissection surfaces and prolonged bypass: antifibrinolytic, protamine reversal, fibrinogen, platelets and viscoelastic-guided therapy.

## Postoperative

Expect more bleeding and tamponade, vasoplegia, AKI and arrhythmia, a need for pacing wires, and a higher chance of prolonged ventilation; mechanical support may be needed.

## Anaesthetic summary

Anticipate bleeding, prepare for emergency bypass, maintain haemodynamic stability, and communicate closely with the surgeon.

## Practical points

The surgical team should say in advance whether the sternum will be opened before or after the circulation is supported, and the anaesthetist should have the necessary lines and cross-matched blood in place by then. Rehearse who controls the injury, gives blood and initiates bypass. Pre-entry bypass can reduce the consequences of re-entry injury in selected patients, but exposes the patient to anticoagulation during dissection and adds bypass time. Plan ICU care around operative complexity and organ reserve.

**Sources:** [BJA Education repeat sternotomy (2024)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10941097/) · [ANZCA Blue Book 2023, Intravenous heparin and non-cardiac anaesthesia](https://www.anzca.edu.au/safety-and-advocacy/advocacy/college-publications/australasian-anaesthesia-%28the-blue-book%29)

## Self-marking checklist

- Describes the re-entry hazard and patent graft risk
- Preoperative CT planning and cannulation alternatives
- Longer CPB, bleeding and poorer protection
- Large-bore access, pads before sternotomy and cell salvage
- Plan for femoral bypass at re-entry
- Blood products, TXA and viscoelastic tests
- ICU and postoperative complications

items.title: 2. On-pump CABG: surgical steps and anaesthetic technique
items.q: Outline the surgical steps and the anaesthetic technique for an on-pump coronary artery bypass graft in a patient with triple vessel disease and an ejection fraction of 40%.
items.a:
## Preoperative

Assess ventricular function, coronary anatomy (left main or triple-vessel disease), valve disease, carotid disease, renal function, diabetes and pulmonary disease. **Continue beta-blockers** (they reduce POAF and ischaemia); consider holding **ACE inhibitors and ARBs** (vasoplegia risk); manage antiplatelets (clopidogrel stopped about 5 days); avoid long fasting and hypotension; premedicate lightly.

## Pre-bypass

- **Monitoring:** five-lead ECG with ST analysis, arterial line before induction, central venous access (PA catheter if poor function), TOE, temperature, urine output and processed EEG or NIRS.
- **Induction:** haemodynamic stability with titrated opioid, hypnotic and rocuronium; avoid tachycardia, hypotension and hypertension. Maintain coronary perfusion pressure (diastolic pressure minus LVEDP) and a low-normal heart rate.
- **Sternotomy** is the most stimulating moment; anticipate hypertension and bradycardia.
- **Heparin and haemostasis:** administer heparin and confirm the circuit-specific ACT target before going on bypass. Use a local antifibrinolytic regimen where appropriate.

## On bypass

**Link the surgical steps to specific hazards.** The LIMA–LAD graft is particularly vulnerable to interruption of flow during mammary harvest and manipulation. During off-pump grafting, posterior-wall exposure may compress the RV, distort mitral/tricuspid filling and cause severe hypotension; request immediate repositioning rather than giving repeated large fluid boluses, and retain a plan for conversion to CPB. Throughout conventional CPB check mixed venous oxygenation, haemoglobin, perfusion pressure and lactate: a normal MAP with low pump flow can still produce inadequate oxygen delivery. Before separation review graft flow and TOE for new regional dysfunction, assess aortic de-airing and allow reperfusion time. A new RWMA after grafting is a mechanical/ischaemic problem until proven otherwise, not an indication simply to increase inotropy.

Maintain anaesthesia through a compatible oxygenator or by TIVA and confirm delivery. Adjust flow and pressure to oxygen delivery and patient risk, integrating haemoglobin, arterial saturation, venous saturation and lactate. Follow temperature, glucose, gases and ACT. Use ventilation or CPAP on bypass according to the surgical and perfusion plan.

## Separation

Follow a checklist (rate and rhythm, ventilation, temperature, electrolytes, de-airing, graft flow): see 2016.2-10. Treat RV failure or vasoplegia promptly.

## Post-bypass and ICU

Protamine slowly, haemostasis and coagulation testing, ST monitoring, epicardial pacing wires, transfer with monitors, and **fast-track** extubation. Surgical technique matters: on-pump versus **off-pump**, with off-pump needing careful positioning, with hypotension and RV compression during lifting, atrial wires and vasopressor-supported pressure.

Complications to anticipate: perioperative infarction, AF, bleeding, AKI, stroke, delirium and sternal wound infection.

## Practical points

Brief the team before induction on the plan for heparin, the order of cannulation and the target pressure during bypass. Check that the pacing wires, the defibrillator and the vasopressor infusions are ready before weaning, and decide in advance who will manage the TOE during separation.

**Sources:** [BJA Education CABG Part 1 (2026)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2026.08.003) · [EACTS/EACTAIC/EBCP adult CPB guideline](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947607/)

## Self-marking checklist

- Describes sternotomy, conduit harvest, heparin, cannulation and CPB
- Describes cardioplegia and cross-clamp, anastomoses and weaning
- Mentions off-pump alternative
- Preoperative review and drug management
- Monitoring including TOE and arterial line
- Induction and maintenance aims (avoid tachycardia and hypotension)
- Management during CPB and transfer to ICU

items.title: 3. Off-pump CABG and haemodynamic collapse on displacement
items.q: Outline the surgical steps and anaesthetic management of off-pump CABG, including haemodynamic collapse during cardiac displacement.
items.a:
## Surgical strategy and preparation

Off-pump CABG constructs anastomoses on the beating heart using displacement and local stabilisation rather than planned CPB/cardioplegic arrest. Sternotomy and conduit harvest are followed by systemic heparinisation to the off-pump protocol, exposure of each target, local stabiliser/intracoronary shunt where required, distal/proximal anastomoses and graft-flow assessment. A proximal aortic clamp may still be used: off-pump does **not** automatically mean no aortic manipulation. An anaortic/no-touch strategy is a separate surgical choice. Limited-access/robotic CABG may additionally require lung isolation and restrict emergency access.

Assess coronary anatomy, LV/RV function, valve disease, aortic atheroma and anticipated target access. Establish arterial pressure, ECG/ST, central access and TOE as appropriate, with defibrillation/pacing and a perfusionist/primed CPB rescue plan. Maintain anaesthesia, temperature, oxygenation, normal relevant electrolytes and myocardial supply–demand balance; off-pump does not remove blood-loss, awareness or anticoagulation risk. Have volume/vasoactive support ready before displacement, particularly for lateral/posterior targets.

## Why displacement causes instability

Lifting/rotating the heart can compress the RV, obstruct venous return, distort valves, impair filling and cause ischaemia/arrhythmia. Coronary occlusion during anastomosis can add regional dysfunction. A small underfilled LV and reduced output may reflect mechanical restriction rather than a need for a large fluid load. Observe TOE, pressure, ECG and the surgeon’s manoeuvres together.

For sudden hypotension, announce the change immediately, reduce/stop displacement or stabiliser pressure and restore the heart towards its normal position. Check rhythm, oxygenation, filling, regional ischaemia and the adequacy of the surgical shunt; treat arrhythmia, maintain coronary pressure with appropriate vasopressor and give small assessed volume increments only if helpful. Positioning may improve filling but must be coordinated. Avoid persisting with a technically convenient position while perfusion collapses.

## Rescue and postoperative implications

Agree a low threshold for **controlled conversion to CPB** if instability, ischaemia or inadequate exposure persists; emergency conversion after profound shock is riskier. Confirm adequate anticoagulation and a safe cannulation strategy, especially with a diseased aorta. Complete graft-flow/wall-motion checks, haemostasis, protamine when appropriate and postoperative monitoring. Discuss the balance: less extracorporeal exposure/haemodilution may help selected patients, but completeness and durability of revascularisation depend on anatomy and expertise; off-pump is not universally superior in survival, stroke or graft patency. The 2026 CABG review provides the surgical context; the physiological rescue sequence is an educator synthesis.

**Sources:** [BJA Education CABG Part 1 (2026)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2026.08.003) · [EACTS/EACTAIC/EBCP adult CPB guideline](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947607/)

## Self-marking checklist

- **2 marks** — Explains beating-heart/stabilisation steps and aortic-manipulation distinction
- **2 marks** — Plans monitoring, anticoagulation and CPB rescue
- **3 marks** — Links displacement to RV/filling/ischaemia and immediately reverses the manoeuvre
- **2 marks** — Provides targeted support and controlled conversion triggers
- **1 mark** — Checks graft result and explains evidence limitations

items.title: 4. Surgical AVR versus TAVI for aortic stenosis
items.q: Compare surgical aortic valve replacement and transcatheter aortic valve implantation, and outline the anaesthetic considerations for severe aortic stenosis in each.
items.a:
## Pathophysiology of aortic stenosis

Normal valve area is 2.6 to 3.5 cm2; **severe** AS is below 1.0 cm2, peak velocity of at least 4 m/s, mean gradient of at least 40 mmHg, or a velocity ratio below 0.25. Untreated symptomatic severe AS has 1-year mortality approaching 50%. The LV hypertrophies and develops diastolic dysfunction, so it depends on **atrial contraction** (AF is poorly tolerated), preload and **systolic perfusion pressure**. There are four categories: high-gradient; low-flow low-gradient with reduced EF (including pseudo-severe, tested by dobutamine); low-flow low-gradient with preserved EF; and normal-flow low-gradient. Calcium scoring on CT (at least 2000 in men, 1200 in women) supports severity.

## Choice of procedure

STS 30-day mortality risk: low below 4%, intermediate 4 to 8%, high above 8%. **PARTNER A** (high risk) showed TAVI non-inferior to surgery at one year; **PARTNER B** (inoperable) showed lower mortality with TAVI but more stroke. CT is now the standard for planning (annulus size, coronary heights, access vessels). The only absolute contraindication is **active endocarditis**; relative are life expectancy below 2 years, annulus below 18 or above 30 mm, low coronary ostia and bicuspid or heavily calcified anatomy.

## Anaesthetic goals (AS)

**Contrast with mitral disease rather than generalising valve physiology.** Severe mitral stenosis requires slow–normal rate, preserved diastolic filling time and avoidance of hypoxaemia/hypercarbia/acidosis that increase PVR; AF with rapid ventricular response is often poorly tolerated. With chronic MR, avoid excessive bradycardia and major increases in systemic afterload while preserving adequate systemic perfusion. After correcting severe MR, afterload mismatch can reveal impaired LV systolic performance even when preoperative LVEF looked reassuring because ejection into the LA was easy. After mitral repair, new hypotension or high LV velocities with systolic anterior motion should prompt assessment for dynamic LVOT obstruction; increasing catecholamines may make it worse. This complements, rather than replaces, AVR/TAVI management.

- Maintain **sinus rhythm, preload, afterload (SVR) and contractility**; avoid tachycardia and hypotension.
- **Vasopressors** (phenylephrine, noradrenaline) to treat vasodilation; cardiovert unstable AF immediately.
- Slow, titrated induction with arterial line before induction and defibrillator pads on.

## Surgical AVR

Standard cardiac anaesthetic with bypass, protection and postoperative pacing for heart block.

## TAVI

Usually transfemoral under **sedation or light general anaesthesia** with TOE or TTE, arterial line and rapid pacing for valve deployment (hypotension, pacing at 160 to 180); be ready for conversion to open surgery. Complications: annular rupture, coronary obstruction, conduction block needing a pacemaker, paravalvular leak, vascular injury and stroke. Plan for postoperative monitoring, and an arrangement for emergency sternotomy.

**Sources:** [BJA Education TAVI, Part 1](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2021.01.004) and [Part 2](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2058534921000202) · [2025 ESC/EACTS valve guideline](https://academic.oup.com/eurheartj/article/46/44/4635/8234488)

## Self-marking checklist

- Compares surgical AVR and TAVI selection
- Describes aortic stenosis physiology (afterload, rhythm, preload)
- Avoids hypotension and tachycardia; chooses vasopressor
- Surgical AVR anaesthetic points (TOE, pacing, outflow obstruction)
- TAVI: hybrid theatre, pacing, back-up and anaesthetic choice
- Lists TAVI complications and plans
- Follow-up of conduction disturbance

items.title: 5. Mitral repair in severe MR with pulmonary hypertension
items.q: A 66-year-old with severe degenerative mitral regurgitation and pulmonary hypertension presents for surgical mitral valve repair. Discuss the anaesthetic goals and problems you anticipate on separation from bypass.
items.a:
## Preoperative evaluation

Confirm mechanism and severity of MR, LV dimensions and EF, pulmonary artery pressure, RV performance, AF and coronary disease. Regurgitation allows LV emptying into a low-impedance LA, so a seemingly normal EF can overstate effective forward systolic function. Severe chronic MR causes LA enlargement, pulmonary venous hypertension and potentially secondary pulmonary hypertension/RV dysfunction. The team should anticipate that correction abruptly removes the low-resistance regurgitant pathway, increasing effective LV afterload and possibly **unmasking LV failure**.

**Risk and counselling details.** Explain the likelihood of postoperative low-output syndrome, prolonged inotrope need and atrial arrhythmia to the team, especially when pulmonary hypertension has already reduced RV reserve. Review whether there is concomitant TR needing repair and whether coronary grafting will also be required. Atrial fibrillation and chronic diuretic therapy change filling and electrolyte management. In complex disease, a pulmonary artery catheter may supplement TOE but pressures must be interpreted alongside flow and chamber geometry. A surgical repair is not automatically preferable to replacement if repair durability is uncertain.

## Before and during bypass

The goals of chronic MR are adequate forward cardiac output, avoidance of significant bradycardia and large increases in SVR, while preserving perfusion. Do not induce profound vasodilation or reduce coronary/RV perfusion; consider carefully titrated induction with arterial monitoring and TOE. Maintain oxygenation, normocapnia and acid-base balance to protect the pressure-loaded RV. Determine with TOE the baseline leaflet pathology, LV and RV function, TR, pulmonary pressure estimate and any associated valve disease. Heparinisation, ACT checks, adequate perfusion flow/oxygen delivery, cardioplegia and de-airing follow standard cardiac practice. Repair typically involves annular reduction, leaflet/chordal work and test of competence; after reperfusion, assess geometry as well as leak.

## Separation: anticipate three specific failures

**Afterload mismatch:** systemic pressure falls with low LV output after MR correction, possibly despite previously preserved EF. TOE shows global LV impairment and insufficient forward stroke volume; check ischaemia, volume and acid–base status, then provide carefully titrated inotropy/mechanical support as needed. **RV failure:** pulmonary hypertension, coronary air, poor protection or hypoxia increase PVR; TOE shows dilated RV and septal shift, rising CVP and reduced LV filling. Optimise RV perfusion pressure, pulmonary afterload and selective inotropic support; inhaled pulmonary vasodilator may help. **SAM/dynamic LVOTO:** after repair, a small hyperdynamic ventricle and anterior mitral leaflet motion cause obstruction and sometimes recurrent MR. This worsens with adrenaline/vasodilation and improves with preload, increased afterload and reduced inotropy; refractory SAM may require surgical revision. Also exclude residual MR, functional MS, prosthetic dysfunction, AV block, tamponade and coronary ischaemia.

## End point and handover

Complete TOE after loading/pressure normalise: grade MR and transmitral gradient, LVOT gradient, LV/RV function and residual defects. Hand over pulmonary-hypertension strategy, pacer requirements, bleeding and ICU haemodynamic targets. The exam distinction is that **the same hypotension can require opposite treatment** for low LV contractility versus SAM.

**Sources:** [2025 ESC/EACTS valve guideline](https://academic.oup.com/eurheartj/article/46/44/4635/8234488) · [EACTS/EACTAIC/EBCP adult CPB guideline](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947607/) · [ANZCA Blue Book 2021, RV dysfunction after separation and right ventricular failure](https://www.anzca.edu.au/safety-and-advocacy/advocacy/college-publications/australasian-anaesthesia-%28the-blue-book%29)

## Self-marking checklist

- Evaluates mechanism and severity of MR and pre-existing LV/RV reserve
- Explains forward EF versus regurgitant EF and afterload mismatch
- States preoperative/induction goals including SVR, rate, perfusion and PVR
- Describes mitral repair and key TOE checkpoints
- Differentiates LV failure, RV failure and SAM/LVOTO after bypass
- Provides distinct management for each mechanism, including surgical correction
- Concludes with TOE reassessment and comprehensive ICU handover

items.title: 6. Mitral valve replacement: surgical steps and anaesthetic technique
items.q: Describe the surgical steps and an appropriate anaesthetic technique for mitral valve replacement, distinguishing mitral stenosis from regurgitation and problems after separation.
items.a:
## Assess lesion and reserve

Review mechanism/severity, symptoms, LV and RV function, pulmonary hypertension, rhythm, prior embolism/endocarditis, anticoagulation and coronary disease. Severe **mitral stenosis** obstructs diastolic filling: avoid tachycardia, preserve sinus rhythm/AV contribution if possible, maintain appropriate preload without pulmonary oedema, preserve systemic perfusion and avoid increases in PVR. In **chronic MR**, forward flow benefits from avoiding bradycardia and excessive systemic afterload; maintain contractility and a suitable normal-to-moderate rate, with adequate rather than excessive preload. Acute MR or ventricular failure may need more urgent afterload/contractility support. These are lesion-specific goals, not a single fixed HR for every patient.

## Surgical steps

Sternotomy (or selected right thoracic access), systemic heparinisation, arterial/venous cannulation and CPB are followed by cross-clamp/cardioplegia and left atrial exposure. The diseased valve is excised as appropriate, preserving chordal/subvalvular continuity where feasible to maintain LV geometry. Size and seat the mechanical or tissue prosthesis, confirm unhindered leaflet/disc movement, close the atrium, de-air the left heart, reperfuse/rewarm and separate. Choice of prosthesis balances durability, anticoagulation, pregnancy considerations where applicable and patient preferences.

## Anaesthetic conduct

Use titrated cardiac GA with arterial pressure, central access, TOE, temperature, anticoagulation and gas/metabolic monitoring. Select a PAC for significant pulmonary hypertension/RV disease where its data will change treatment. Prepare pacing, vasopressors, inotropes and inhaled pulmonary vasodilator support. Maintain anaesthesia on CPB, adequate myocardial protection, anticoagulation and oxygen delivery. A minimally invasive approach may require OLV, peripheral CPB, specialised venous drainage and careful TOE guidance; an endoaortic balloon may migrate and compromise arch-vessel or coronary flow, requiring bilateral pressure/cerebral monitoring according to the technique. Plan external defibrillation and conversion access.

## Separation and postoperative checks

TOE assesses prosthesis movement/seating, residual/paravalvular regurgitation, gradients interpreted against flow/HR, LV/RV function, new regional changes, air and outflow obstruction. Exclude circumflex coronary injury, which may cause new lateral wall dysfunction. After correcting MR, removing the low-impedance regurgitant outlet can expose **afterload mismatch** and previously hidden LV dysfunction. Treat with appropriate inotropy/afterload/perfusion support and exclude ischaemia or a mechanical lesion. RV failure can follow longstanding pulmonary hypertension or perioperative injury.

If a repair rather than replacement has been performed, assess residual MR/stenosis and **SAM/LVOT obstruction**. For SAM, optimise filling and afterload, reduce excessive inotropy/tachycardia and seek surgical reassessment if persistent. Do not treat all post-mitral hypotension with an inotrope. Plan prosthesis-specific anticoagulation, bleeding surveillance, pacing/conduction review and ICU handover. Mechanical mitral valves require VKA-based long-term anticoagulation rather than a DOAC.

**Sources:** [2025 ESC/EACTS valve guideline](https://academic.oup.com/eurheartj/article/46/44/4635/8234488) · [EACTS/EACTAIC/EBCP adult CPB guideline](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947607/) · [ANZCA Blue Book 2021, RV dysfunction after separation and right ventricular failure](https://www.anzca.edu.au/safety-and-advocacy/advocacy/college-publications/australasian-anaesthesia-%28the-blue-book%29)

## Self-marking checklist

- **2 marks** — Contrasts MS and MR physiological goals
- **2 marks** — Describes surgical sequence and chordal/prosthesis considerations
- **2 marks** — Plans cardiac anaesthesia/TOE and minimally invasive modifications
- **3 marks** — Checks prosthesis, circumflex injury, afterload mismatch, RV and SAM
- **1 mark** — Provides ICU and prosthesis-specific anticoagulation plan

items.title: 7. Anaesthetic issues on bypass and aortic cannulation
items.q: Outline the anaesthetic issues during cardiopulmonary bypass, including the implications of aortic disease for aortic cannulation.
items.a:
## The circuit

Venous blood drains by gravity or vacuum from the right atrium (or bicaval cannulae) to a **reservoir**, through a **pump** (roller or centrifugal), a **membrane oxygenator with heat exchanger**, arterial filter and bubble trap, and returns via an **aortic cannula**. Added: cardiotomy suction, vent, cell saver, cardioplegia delivery and haemofilter.

## Cannulation

- **Aortic:** ascending aorta; risks are dissection, atheroemboli and malposition (high line pressure, asymmetric arm pressures). Alternatives are femoral or axillary in dissection or porcelain aorta.
- **Venous:** two-stage right atrial, or bicaval cannulation for right-sided opening; risks are air lock, arrhythmia and poor drainage with hypotension.
- **Confirm heparinisation before cannulation.**

## Anticoagulation

Give unfractionated heparin according to the circuit protocol, often 300–400 units/kg. Confirm the assay-specific ACT target before bypass and repeat regularly during bypass. If ACT is inadequate, verify administration, sampling and assay, consider heparin concentration and antithrombin deficiency, and agree targeted correction with perfusion. Once separation is stable, titrate protamine to residual heparin and reassess anticoagulation and haemostasis. Watch for hypotension, pulmonary vasoconstriction and anaphylaxis.

## Myocardial protection

The aim is a still, bloodless, protected heart after **aortic cross-clamping**. **Cardioplegia** (hyperkalaemic, cold blood or crystalloid, antegrade via the aortic root or retrograde via the coronary sinus, repeated about every 20 to 30 minutes) causes depolarised diastolic arrest, with hypothermia and a reduced metabolic rate. The heart is vulnerable to poor distribution (severe coronary disease, LV hypertrophy, aortic regurgitation causing LV distension), so check for aortic regurgitation before cross-clamping (LV vent) and check the left ventricle is not distended.

## Anaesthetic role on bypass

**A crisis checklist belongs inside CPB management.** In arterial-line hypertension with falling patient MAP, immediately consider a kink, clamp, dissection, malposition or circuit obstruction rather than increasing pump pressure. With falling venous return, inspect venous cannula position, reservoir level and air lock, and communicate before reducing flow. If oxygenator gas exchange fails, check oxygen source, sweep gas, connectors, membrane pressures and blood gas sampling; maintain patient perfusion and prepare emergency oxygenator/circuit exchange with the perfusionist. If arterial air is suspected, stop unsafe delivery according to local protocol, identify its source and coordinate de-airing and cerebral-protection actions. Use a structured perfusion safety checklist and preserve anaesthesia through all emergencies.

Maintain anaesthesia and relaxation, individualised MAP and goal-directed oxygen delivery (traditional flow ≈2.2–2.4 L/min/m² is an initial setting, not a guarantee of tissue perfusion), temperature, glucose and electrolytes, review ACT, and watch for hypotension (haemodilution, vasodilation), inadequate venous drainage, high arterial line pressure, awareness and cerebral perfusion.

**Contemporary CPB reference:** [EACTS/EACTAIC/EBCP 2024 guidelines](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947607/).

**Sources:** [EACTS/EACTAIC/EBCP adult CPB guideline](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947607/) · [ANZCA Blue Book 2023, Intravenous heparin and non-cardiac anaesthesia](https://www.anzca.edu.au/safety-and-advocacy/advocacy/college-publications/australasian-anaesthesia-%28the-blue-book%29) · [BJA Education CABG Part 1 (2026)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2026.08.003)

## Self-marking checklist

- Describes the circuit and flow, pressure and temperature targets
- Heparin dose and ACT; heparin resistance and HIT
- Protamine reversal and its hazards
- Maintains anaesthesia and monitors during CPB
- Aortic disease and the risk of embolism or dissection
- Alternative cannulation and epiaortic or TOE assessment
- Myocardial protection with cardioplegia

items.title: 8. Falling MAP with rising arterial-line pressure on CPB
items.q: A 64-year-old undergoing valve replacement has a sudden fall in systemic MAP during CPB. The perfusionist reports rising arterial-line pressure; NIRS is falling. Explain your immediate differential diagnosis and management.
items.a:
## Recognition and first actions

A high **post-oxygenator arterial-line pressure** with low patient MAP is an arterial outflow problem until proven otherwise: a kink or clamp, occluded filter/cannula, aortic cannula malposition, intimal injury or delivery into a false lumen. Falling NIRS indicates possible cerebral malperfusion. Immediately **announce a CPB perfusion emergency** and coordinate anaesthetist, perfusionist and surgeon. Do not blindly raise pump RPM against an obstruction. Continue an appropriate, safe perfusion strategy under perfusionist control while diagnosing the fault. Confirm the arterial transducer and pressure sites, check circuit tubing, pump and cannula orientation, and inspect the operative field.

## Differential and targeted troubleshooting

An **arterial obstruction** produces high circuit pressure, potentially reduced flow and inadequate patient perfusion: relieve kinks/clamps or correct the catheter. **Aortic dissection or cannulation into the false lumen** may show asymmetric radial/femoral pressures, poor venous return, cerebral NIRS change or TOE evidence of flap/poor true-lumen perfusion. Stop unsafe flow distribution; assess aorta with TOE/epiaortic imaging and surgical inspection; switch the arterial cannulation site if needed. An **oxygenator failure** usually causes abnormal pre/post-oxygenator gas measurements or pressure gradient and desaturation, not simply low MAP: confirm gas supply, sweep, oxygen blender and membrane integrity; prepare backup circuit/oxygenator exchange. **Air entry or an arterial air event** requires immediate source isolation, circuit air-handling actions and coordination of de-airing and organ protection. **Venous drainage failure** is suggested by poor reservoir volume or negative venous pressure, not necessarily high arterial line pressure; check cannula, snare, venous air lock and filling.

**Team communication and decision points.** State aloud which readings are circuit pressures and which are patient pressures: they can move in opposite directions and are not interchangeable. Identify the perfusionist as the operator of pump and oxygenator adjustments while the surgeon manages cannula position and possible aortic injury; the anaesthetist tracks myocardial, cerebral and systemic endpoints and preserves anaesthesia. If true-lumen malperfusion is suspected, continuing apparently normal numerical pump flow can worsen regional ischaemia. Agree when to recannulate, revise the aorta or briefly interrupt unsafe flow according to local emergency protocol.

## Patient and organ protection

Use a continuously repeated team checklist: pump flow and venous saturation; arterial/circuit pressures; bilateral patient pressures where available; FiO₂/sweep and blood gases; haemoglobin, temperature, glucose, acid–base and cerebral NIRS. Calculate/estimate systemic oxygen delivery rather than assuming adequate MAP guarantees it. Assess the brain and circulation by cerebral oximetry, arterial gas/lactate and urine output. When repairs are complete, confirm stable systemic pressure, oxygenation and absence of cerebral malperfusion before continuing the operation. Keep depth of anaesthesia and anticoagulation adequate throughout the interruption, record the event, and plan a focused postoperative neurological/renal assessment.

**Sources:** [EACTS/EACTAIC/EBCP adult CPB guideline](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947607/)

## Self-marking checklist

- Identifies arterial obstruction/malposition or dissection as leading differential
- Calls for immediate surgeon–anaesthetist–perfusionist communication and avoids increasing pressure blindly
- Distinguishes oxygenator/sweep failure, arterial air and inadequate venous drainage
- Uses circuit and patient pressure sites, blood gases, TOE/epiaortic imaging and NIRS
- Describes targeted surgical/circuit correction and alternative cannulation when necessary
- Maintains organ oxygen delivery, anticoagulation and anaesthesia
- Plans neurological/renal follow-up and documents event

items.title: 9. Failure to reach target ACT and HIT for bypass
items.q: A patient fails to reach an ACT of 480 seconds after 400 units/kg of heparin before cardiopulmonary bypass. Outline your approach, and describe the management of a patient with heparin-induced thrombocytopenia requiring bypass.
items.a:
## Heparin resistance

**Definition:** inability to reach the target ACT despite adequate dose: non-bypass more than 35,000 units over 24 hours; bypass more than **500 units/kg** to reach an ACT of 400 to 480 seconds (occurs in up to 20%).

**Causes:** **antithrombin deficiency**, congenital (about 1 in 5000) or acquired (heparin therapy lowers antithrombin 5 to 7% per day; liver disease; DIC; nephrotic syndrome; oestrogen), increased heparin binding proteins, thrombocytosis, high factor VIII or fibrinogen, and a wrong ACT test (haemodilution or hypothermia changes ACT).

**Management:** check dose, drug and ACT cartridge; give more heparin, then **antithrombin concentrate** (1000 units) or FFP if resistance persists. Confirm the anti-Xa activity rather than aPTT or ACT alone, preferably on the same sample.

## Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT)

**Do not conflate expected post-CPB thrombocytopenia with HIT.** Most patients have a transient platelet fall during the first 1–3 postoperative days because of haemodilution, consumption and circuit exposure. Immune HIT more typically causes a second fall around days 5–10 or a very early fall following recent heparin exposure; consider thrombosis and apply the 4Ts score before laboratory testing. Immunoassays detect antibodies but are not identical to functional platelet-activation tests. Urgent bypass in acute HIT requires joint haematology–perfusion planning, often bivalirudin with modified circuit and monitoring protocols; unlike heparin, there is no reliable protamine reversal. Remote HIT with negative functional assays is a different scenario and may allow intraoperative heparin in a tightly defined plan.

**Type 2 HIT** is immune mediated: IgG antibodies to platelet factor 4–heparin complex cause platelet activation, thrombocytopenia and **thrombosis** (about 0.3% in vascular surgery), typically day 5 to 11 (earlier with recent exposure). Thrombotic mortality is up to 30%. Use the **4T score** (thrombocytopenia, timing, thrombosis, other causes) and confirm with immunoassay and functional assay.

**Management:** stop all heparin including flushes and heparin-coated lines, **no LMWH**; start a non-heparin anticoagulant (argatroban, which is hepatically cleared, or bivalirudin, which undergoes proteolysis and partial renal clearance; dose adjustment and monitoring are needed in renal impairment), avoid platelet transfusion unless bleeding, and avoid warfarin until platelets recover.

## Cardiac surgery with HIT

- **Acute or subacute HIT (antibody positive):** delay elective surgery until antibody-negative; if urgent, use **bivalirudin** for bypass.
- **Remote HIT (antibody negative):** a single dose of heparin for bypass may be used, with non-heparin anticoagulant before and after.
- Monitor with ACT (ecarin clotting time where available) and ensure the pump prime is free of heparin.

## Anaesthetic points

Anticipate bleeding (no simple reversal for bivalirudin or argatroban), use cell salvage and viscoelastic testing, and involve haematology.

## Practical points

Tell the perfusionist about any history of heparin exposure or previous HIT before the case, and check the platelet count trend. If there is any doubt about HIT, avoid heparin flushes on all lines until the test result is available.

**Sources:** [ANZCA Blue Book 2023, Intravenous heparin and non-cardiac anaesthesia](https://www.anzca.edu.au/safety-and-advocacy/advocacy/college-publications/australasian-anaesthesia-%28the-blue-book%29) · [EACTS/EACTAIC/EBCP adult CPB guideline](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947607/) · [BJA Education anticoagulation for CPB, Part 1 (2023)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2022.12.003) · [ASH HIT guideline](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6258919/)

## Self-marking checklist

- Defines heparin resistance on CPB
- Lists causes (antithrombin deficiency, non-specific binding)
- Distinguishes true from pseudo-resistance
- Treats with extra heparin, antithrombin or plasma
- Distinguishes HIT type 1 and type 2 and the 4T score
- Bivalirudin or argatroban for urgent surgery; LMWH contraindicated
- Notes the timing of surgery and the HIT-free window

items.title: 10. Bleeding 400 mL/hour after CABG
items.q: A patient is bleeding 400 mL/hour from the chest drains two hours after CABG. Outline your assessment and management.
items.a:
## Causes

| Cause | Detail |
|---|---|
| **Surgical bleeding** | Anastomoses, sternal edges, cannulation sites; needs surgical re-exploration |
| **Heparin effect** | Inadequate protamine or **heparin rebound** |
| **Platelet dysfunction** | Bypass activation, hypothermia, antiplatelet drugs (aspirin, clopidogrel, ticagrelor) |
| **Dilutional and consumptive coagulopathy** | Low fibrinogen is the earliest and strongest deficit; factor consumption |
| **Hyperfibrinolysis** | Bypass, DHCA, redo surgery |
| **Hypothermia, acidosis, hypocalcaemia** | Slow enzymatic coagulation |
| **Preoperative** | DOACs, warfarin, liver disease, renal failure, von Willebrand disease |

## Protamine

Titrate protamine against measured residual heparin or the local reversal algorithm. Excess protamine can impair haemostasis. Give slowly with haemodynamic monitoring. Recognise systemic vasodilation, acute pulmonary vasoconstriction with RV failure, and anaphylaxis. Previous protamine reactions and use of protamine-containing insulin warrant particular attention.

## Assessment

**Resuscitate and decide on re-exploration in parallel.** First alert the surgeon, assess haemodynamic stability and ensure cross-matched products and rapid infuser are available. Look for the pattern of drainage, surgical field information, tamponade on TOE and the possibility that drains are blocked by clot. A normal ACT does not exclude residual heparin; compare heparin-sensitive and heparinase viscoelastic channels when available. VHA-guided management distinguishes fibrinogen deficiency (e.g. low FIBTEM amplitude), platelet dysfunction/deficiency, factor deficiency and fibrinolysis. Avoid indiscriminate PCC, plasma, platelet and protamine administration; excess protamine itself impairs coagulation. Recheck coagulopathy after therapy, but do not postpone surgery if output or haemodynamics suggest a surgical source.

Confirm **ACT or heparin concentration at baseline**, platelet count, fibrinogen, and **viscoelastic testing** (ROTEM or TEG) to separate heparin effect, fibrinogen, platelet and fibrinolytic problems; check temperature, pH, ionised calcium and chest drain volume.

## Management

- **1.** **Correct physiology first:** warm above 36 degrees, calcium, pH, MAP control.
- **2.** **Heparin:** extra protamine if ACT elevated with a heparin effect.
- **3.** **Targeted products:** fibrinogen concentrate or cryoprecipitate for active bleeding with demonstrated fibrinogen deficiency; platelets if dysfunction (low count or antiplatelet); prothrombin complex or plasma for factor deficiency.
- **4.** **Antifibrinolytic:** tranexamic acid, with dose restraint due to seizure risk at high doses.
- **5.** **Desmopressin** in von Willebrand disease or uraemia; cell salvage.
- **6.** **Surgical re-exploration** for tamponade, instability, suspected surgical bleeding or persistent high output using the local surgical pathway.

Transfuse to a rational threshold and treat massive bleeding with the massive transfusion protocol.

## Practical points

Do not wait for the laboratory when bleeding is brisk: if drain output is above 400 mL per hour with a falling pressure, discuss re-exploration at once. Send repeated viscoelastic tests after each product, and keep calcium and temperature in range, since these are the commonest reversible contributors.

**Sources:** [ANZCA Blue Book 2025, viscoelastic testing chapter, pp. 62–63](https://doi.org/10.60115/11055/1305) · [ANZCA Blue Book 2023, Intravenous heparin and non-cardiac anaesthesia](https://www.anzca.edu.au/safety-and-advocacy/advocacy/college-publications/australasian-anaesthesia-%28the-blue-book%29) · [EACTS/EACTAIC patient blood management guideline](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12257489/) · [BJA Education anticoagulation for CPB, Part 1 (2023)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2022.12.003)

## Self-marking checklist

- Differentiates surgical bleeding from coagulopathy and recognises tamponade
- Lists causes (heparin, protamine, platelet, fibrinogen, physiology)
- Restores temperature, calcium and acid-base
- Uses viscoelastic or laboratory tests
- Targets products (platelets, fibrinogen, PCC, TXA)
- Re-explores early
- Mentions limits of rescue agents and transfusion risks

items.title: 11. Hypotension and pulmonary hypertension during protamine
items.q: A patient develops severe hypotension and pulmonary hypertension during protamine administration after CPB. Explain the differential diagnosis and management.
items.a:
## Recognise the syndrome and act

Stop protamine, announce the reaction, call surgeon/perfusionist for immediate support, give 100% oxygen and assess ECG, arterial/CVP/PA pressures, TOE and the operative field. Check timing, dose/rate and other concurrent drugs. Hypotension may reflect rapid-infusion systemic vasodilation, immune/non-immune anaphylaxis, or catastrophic pulmonary vasoconstriction with acute RV failure. Also exclude haemorrhage, coronary air/ischaemia, tamponade, mechanical obstruction and inadequate ventricular function; more than one process can coexist.

## Phenotype-specific treatment

**Vasodilatory hypotension:** support perfusion with titrated vasopressor and assessed volume if underfilled. Rapid protamine administration can worsen systemic vasodilation; do not keep giving it while trying to counteract the fall in pressure.

**Anaphylaxis:** follow the perioperative anaphylaxis protocol, using titrated IV adrenaline in an appropriately monitored cardiac operating room, airway/ventilation support and volume to the phenotype. Treat bronchospasm and obtain timed tryptase when feasible after resuscitation. Steroids/antihistamines are not first-line substitutes for adrenaline or perfusion support. Severe anaphylaxis can present without obvious skin signs.

**Pulmonary hypertensive reaction/RV failure:** sudden high RV afterload causes RV dilation, impaired LV filling and systemic collapse; PA pressure may later fall with profound RV failure. Maintain systemic/RV coronary perfusion, correct hypoxaemia/hypercarbia/acidaemia and excessive airway pressures, give an appropriate inotrope and inhaled nitric oxide/prostacyclin where available. Avoid uncontrolled fluid loading of a distended RV. If refractory, urgently re-establish CPB with adequate **re-heparinisation** and perfusion-team coordination; the prior heparin has been reversed. Consider ongoing RV/cardiopulmonary support if required.

## Prevention and follow-through

Base reversal on residual heparin or a validated titration protocol, give slowly with close haemodynamic observation, and anticipate risk with prior protamine reaction or protamine-containing insulin. Fish allergy/vasectomy alone is not proof of a contraindication. A small test dose cannot rule out severe reaction. Excess protamine can impair platelet/coagulation function and prolong ACT; repeated dosing for any prolonged ACT can worsen bleeding. Use measured heparin/heparinase comparison and the whole haemostatic picture.

Do not restart protamine automatically. Balance residual-heparin bleeding against recurrent reaction with surgeon, perfusionist and haematology; document the exact exposure/phenotype, allergy referral where appropriate and future planning. Monitor RV function, oxygenation, haemostasis and organ perfusion in ICU. The distinction between dose-rate hypotension, anaphylaxis and pulmonary vasoconstriction explains why no single rescue drug treats every protamine reaction.

**Sources:** [BJA Education anticoagulation for CPB, Part 1 (2023)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2022.12.003) · [ANZCA Blue Book 2023, Intravenous heparin and non-cardiac anaesthesia](https://www.anzca.edu.au/safety-and-advocacy/advocacy/college-publications/australasian-anaesthesia-%28the-blue-book%29) · [ANZCA Blue Book 2021, RV dysfunction after separation and right ventricular failure](https://www.anzca.edu.au/safety-and-advocacy/advocacy/college-publications/australasian-anaesthesia-%28the-blue-book%29) · [EACTS/EACTAIC patient blood management guideline](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12257489/)

## Self-marking checklist

- **2 marks** — Stops protamine and rapidly assesses competing causes
- **2 marks** — Distinguishes vasodilation, anaphylaxis and pulmonary/RV failure
- **3 marks** — Provides phenotype-directed perfusion/adrenaline/pulmonary therapy
- **1 mark** — Plans re-heparinised return to CPB when refractory
- **2 marks** — Explains titrated reversal, testing limits and future documentation

items.title: 12. Haematological and inflammatory effects of CPB
items.q: Explain the haematological and inflammatory effects of CPB, the role of antifibrinolytics, and the clinical implications of reperfusion injury and ischaemic preconditioning.
items.a:
## Blood–circuit interaction and haemostasis

Contact with artificial surfaces, tissue injury, blood–air interface and cardiotomy suction activate coagulation/contact pathways, complement, platelets and leukocytes. Haemodilution lowers Hb, platelet and factor concentrations. Platelet activation/consumption, dysfunction from CPB and antiplatelet drugs, fibrinogen depletion, fibrinolysis, residual heparin, excess protamine, hypothermia, acidosis and low ionised calcium can combine to cause bleeding. Shear/excessive suction can cause haemolysis, with free Hb/iron contributing to renal injury and NO scavenging. Microthrombi/embolism and postoperative thrombosis may coexist with bleeding: a long clotting time does not mean all thrombotic risk is absent.

Clinical management combines careful surgery, limited unnecessary dilution/suction, adequate anticoagulation on CPB, temperature/pH/calcium correction, titrated reversal and algorithm-guided haemostatic treatment. Use platelet count/function, fibrinogen, conventional tests and appropriate viscoelastic/heparinase channels to identify the problem; avoid treating every abnormality with plasma or protamine.

## Antifibrinolytics in cardiac surgery

TXA is a lysine analogue that interferes with plasminogen binding/activation on fibrin, reducing fibrinolysis, blood loss and transfusion/re-exploration. Give a validated local cardiac regimen matched to renal function rather than borrowing an obstetric or hip-arthroplasty dose. Higher exposure can increase seizures, particularly with renal accumulation. Discuss thrombosis risk in context, avoid wrong-route administration and do not claim TXA repairs a surgical anastomotic leak. Aminocaproic acid is another lysine analogue. Aprotinin inhibits serine proteases and has efficacy but important renal/allergy/regulatory restrictions; the 2007.2 Q9 answer works through the historical debate. ACT assay selection matters with aprotinin. Antifibrinolysis is one part of patient blood management, not a substitute for diagnosis.

## Inflammation and organ consequences

DAMPs, cytokines, complement and endothelial/glycocalyx injury increase permeability, oedema, vasodilation and microcirculatory heterogeneity. NO signalling and vascular hyporesponsiveness contribute to vasoplegia. Myocardial, pulmonary, renal, gut and cerebral injury can follow, particularly after prolonged CPB, poor oxygen delivery or marked haemolysis. The inflammatory phenotype does not automatically prove infection or justify routine steroids for everyone; continue to look for treatable low output, bleeding, obstruction and sepsis.

## Reperfusion and preconditioning

After ischaemia, reoxygenation can generate reactive oxygen species, calcium overload, mitochondrial dysfunction, inflammatory activation and endothelial injury. Clinically this contributes to myocardial stunning, arrhythmia, oedema, microvascular no-reflow and remote organ injury. Minimise ischaemic time, provide effective cardioplegia, avoid distension and restore perfusion/oxygen delivery/metabolic conditions carefully; allow time for recovery before concluding permanent failure, while excluding graft/valve lesions.

Ischaemic preconditioning describes brief sublethal ischaemic episodes activating endogenous protective signalling; remote conditioning applies a stimulus elsewhere, commonly limb cuff cycles. Mechanistic plausibility and small-study effects have not produced a consistent major-outcome benefit in large cardiac trials, so it is not a universal routine requirement. Similarly, volatile-agent conditioning mechanisms do not establish guaranteed outcome superiority over well-conducted TIVA. Explain mechanism, evidence and applicability separately.

**Sources:** [BJA Education anticoagulation for CPB, Part 1 (2023)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2022.12.003) · [EACTS/EACTAIC patient blood management guideline](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12257489/) · [ANZCA Blue Book 2025, viscoelastic testing chapter, pp. 62–63](https://doi.org/10.60115/11055/1305) · [BJA Education cardiac surgery-associated AKI (2026)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2025.11.001)

## Self-marking checklist

- **2 marks** — Explains circuit/dilution/platelet/factor/fibrinolytic changes
- **2 marks** — Links inflammation/haemolysis to organ injury and vasoplegia
- **2 marks** — Explains TXA mechanism, benefit and renal/seizure/route precautions
- **2 marks** — Explains reperfusion injury and practical prevention
- **2 marks** — Explains preconditioning and limitations of outcome evidence

items.title: 13. Myocardial protection during CPB
items.q: Describe intraoperative myocardial protection during CPB, including cardioplegia delivery problems and assessment after reperfusion.
items.a:
## Objective and pre-bypass information

Maintain myocardial viability during interruption of normal coronary flow, reduce oxygen demand and prevent distension/ischaemia–reperfusion injury while permitting repair. Review coronary distribution/stenoses/grafts, ventricular hypertrophy/function, AR and planned cross-clamp time. Agree the solution, route, pressure, temperature, redose interval and rescue strategy with surgeon/perfusionist; no single formulation or fixed 20-minute interval suits every operation.

## Arrest, cooling and delivery

Hyperkalaemic cardioplegia causes depolarised arrest, reducing electrical/mechanical work. Blood or crystalloid solutions, cold/warm strategies and intermittent/continuous delivery are selected according to the operation and team protocol. Arrest does not abolish metabolism; adequate distribution, temperature and repeat delivery remain essential. Systemic cooling can add metabolic protection but is distinct from cardioplegia and from global circulatory arrest.

**Antegrade aortic-root delivery** uses normal coronary flow direction after cross-clamping. Severe proximal coronary stenosis can produce maldistribution; significant AR allows solution into the LV, causing distension and inadequate coronary protection. Use direct ostial delivery or another agreed route where necessary, with an LV vent. Monitor root pressure and the heart’s arrest/temperature/distension; an expected dose delivered does not prove tissue protection.

**Retrograde coronary-sinus delivery** can bypass proximal arterial obstruction and assist with AR or patent graft washout. Correct catheter position and pressure are essential: excessive pressure can injure the sinus, and RV protection may be incomplete because some venous drainage bypasses the sinus. Combining routes may improve distribution; do not assume retrograde alone protects every territory equally. Patent IMA/other graft flow in redo surgery can wash out cardioplegia and rewarm a region, requiring a tailored surgical strategy.

## Ongoing anaesthetic/perfusion role

Maintain adequate systemic oxygen delivery and anticoagulation, record clamp/cardioplegia times, watch electrical activity and myocardial distension, and communicate unexpected return of activity or delivery-pressure changes. Avoid unnecessary LV distension, which increases wall stress and impairs subendocardial perfusion. Account for cardioplegia-related K and volume load, glucose/calcium/acid-base changes and temperature. Verify anaesthesia continues while heart/ventilation signs are absent.

## Reperfusion and separation

De-air carefully before restoring ejection; maintain coronary driving pressure, correct major electrolyte/acidaemic abnormalities, restore a suitable rhythm/pacing and allow reperfusion. Assess TOE for new regional wall-motion changes versus global stunning, RV failure, residual valve/outflow lesions and air; the surgeon checks graft flow and repair. Treat ischaemia, spasm or a mechanical problem directly. If function remains poor, support/rest on CPB and select inotropic/mechanical support by phenotype rather than rushing separation. Reperfusion arrhythmias, calcium/oxidant injury and stunning can occur despite technically adequate cardioplegia; preconditioning/volatile mechanisms are not proof of universal clinical benefit.

**Sources:** [BJA Education CABG Part 1 (2026)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2026.08.003) · [EACTS/EACTAIC/EBCP adult CPB guideline](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947607/) · [BJA Education repeat sternotomy (2024)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10941097/)

## Self-marking checklist

- **2 marks** — Defines objective and relevant coronary/valve/anatomical assessment
- **2 marks** — Explains arrest, temperature and repeat delivery
- **3 marks** — Contrasts antegrade/retrograde failure modes and distension
- **1 mark** — Monitors delivery, systemic perfusion and metabolic load
- **2 marks** — Assesses reperfusion/regional dysfunction and provides a failed-wean plan

items.title: 14. Cooling and rewarming on CPB
items.q: Discuss the physiological effects of cooling during routine cardiopulmonary bypass, and explain how to manage rewarming safely.
items.a:
## Why cool on bypass

Hypothermia reduces **metabolic rate** (about 6 to 7% per degree for the brain, roughly halving at 28 degrees and falling to about 20 to 25% of normal at 18 degrees), allowing lower flows and protecting organs, and enables circulatory arrest. Classification: mild 32 to 35, moderate 28 to 32, deep 18 to 28 degrees, with deep hypothermic arrest at 18 to 20.

## Physiological effects

| System | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Cardiac** | Bradycardia, prolonged conduction (PR, QRS, QT), **VF below about 28 degrees**, reduced contractility; Osborn J waves |
| **Cerebral** | Reduced metabolic rate and flow; autoregulation lost at deep levels |
| **Respiratory/blood gas** | Gases become more soluble, so measured PaCO2 and pH at 37 degrees differ from the patient's; left shift of the oxygen–haemoglobin curve and impaired tissue oxygen release |
| **Coagulation** | Platelet dysfunction, slowed enzyme cascade, fibrinolysis |
| **Renal and metabolic** | Cold diuresis, insulin resistance and hyperglycaemia, reduced drug metabolism |
| **Immune/wound** | Infection risk |

## Acid-base strategy

**Temperature management is an active safety intervention.** Hypothermia changes the partition of anaesthetic drugs, ionised electrolyte concentrations, blood gas solubility, coagulation function and myocardial excitability. A core temperature does not always represent cerebral temperature during rapid cooling or rewarming; use appropriate nasopharyngeal and other sites. During rewarming, cerebral hyperthermia and microembolisation are particular hazards. Contemporary CPB guidance limits arterial oxygenator outlet temperature to 37°C, and discourages excessive heat-exchanger gradients. With arch surgery, selective antegrade cerebral perfusion can permit less profound hypothermia; the decision is procedural and patient-specific. A quoted 30–40-minute DHCA window is only a risk reference for isolated arrest, not a universally guaranteed safe period.

**Alpha-stat** (gases interpreted at 37 degrees, no CO2 added; preserves enzyme function and cerebral autoregulation) is usual in adults; **pH-stat** (CO2 added to correct for temperature; increases cerebral blood flow, uncoupling it from metabolism) is used in deep cooling and paediatrics.

## Management on bypass

- Cool and rewarm at controlled rates; keep the gradient between arterial blood and body at 10 degrees or less, and arterial oxygenator outlet temperature no higher than 37°C (2024 EACTS/EACTAIC/EBCP) to reduce gas microembolisation and cerebral hyperthermia.
- Maintain anaesthesia and relaxation (shivering after rewarming raises oxygen demand), and monitor brain temperature (nasopharyngeal) with core (bladder or rectal) readings.
- Recheck potassium, glucose and ionised calcium and anticipate rewarming vasodilation.
- After bypass, avoid **afterdrop** by rewarming to over 36 degrees with warming blankets and warmed fluids, and remember that cooling lowers drug requirement but residual hypothermia prolongs recovery.

**Contemporary CPB reference:** [EACTS/EACTAIC/EBCP 2024 guidelines](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947607/).

**Sources:** [EACTS/EACTAIC/EBCP adult CPB guideline](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947607/)

## Self-marking checklist

- Gives the reduction in metabolic rate with cooling and temperature grades
- Describes CNS, cardiac, coagulation and metabolic effects
- Explains the oxygen–haemoglobin shift and gas solubility
- Describes rewarming rate and cerebral hyperthermia risk
- Mentions after-drop and shivering
- Gives practical warming and temperature targets

items.title: 15. Neurological complications of cardiac surgery
items.q: Discuss the neurological complications of cardiac surgery with cardiopulmonary bypass and the strategies to reduce them.
items.a:
## Stroke and delirium after cardiac surgery

Stroke occurs in about 1 to 5% of cardiac operations (higher with valve and aortic surgery), and delirium in up to 30 to 50%. Both increase mortality, stay and long-term cognitive decline.

## Mechanisms

- **Embolic:** atheroma from aortic manipulation (cannulation, cross-clamp), particulate and **gaseous** emboli (see the gas embolism chapter), valve debris, left atrial thrombus, and AF; **postoperative AF** is associated with a higher stroke risk (OR 3.5 in the POISE cohort).
- **Hypoperfusion:** hypotension on or off bypass, carotid or intracranial stenosis, low cardiac output.
- **Inflammation and microvascular injury**, hyperglycaemia, hyperthermia on rewarming, and cerebral oedema.
- **Delirium:** age, preexisting cognitive impairment, alcohol, sleep deprivation, drugs (benzodiazepines, anticholinergics, high-dose opioids), pain, infection and metabolic disturbance.

## Neuroprotection and prevention

**Target the mechanisms that can actually be modified.** Cerebral embolism from aortic instrumentation is addressed by reviewing aortic atheroma with epiaortic scanning and choosing no-touch or alternative cannulation when indicated. Perfusion decisions should be based on oxygen delivery, pressure and cerebral monitoring together; a regional cerebral saturation decrease needs a sequential response (head/venous drainage, PaCO₂, oxygen content, flow, pressure and haematocrit) rather than automatically adding vasopressors. NIRS is useful for detecting regional change, but its impact on hard neurological outcomes is not consistently proven. Avoid cerebral hyperthermia during rewarming and actively reassess new focal deficit for time-sensitive thrombectomy eligibility after recent surgery.

- **1.** **Preoperative:** carotid assessment, identify cognitive impairment and alcohol use, and anticoagulate AF appropriately.
- **2.** **Surgical:** no-touch or epiaortic scanning for atheroma, off-pump or minimal aortic manipulation, de-airing and carbon dioxide field flooding.
- **3.** **Perfusion:** adequate MAP (above 65 to 70, higher in cerebrovascular disease), alpha-stat management, avoid hyperthermia above 37 degrees, arterial filter, and glucose below about 10 mmol/L.
